body.text: Ratnakīrti Nibandhāvalī //
body.translated_text: <s>Ratnakīrti Nibandhāvalī</s> (The Collected Works of <s>Ratnakīrti</s>).

body.text: // sarvajñasiddhiḥ //
body.translated_text: <s>Sarvajñasiddhi</s> (Proof of Omniscience).

children.translated_text: Homage to <s>Tārā</s>, in whom there is no ignorance, in whom there is no birth in hell, and in whom devotion grants all desires;

children.text: avyāhataṃ yo jagadekabandhuḥ sa jñāyate sarvavidatra nirmalam //
children.translated_text: he who is the sole friend of the world, who is known as omniscient — him, the immaculate, [I salute].

body.text: iha hi dharmajñādaparama navaśeṣajñamanicchannapi kumārilo dharmajña eva kevale pratiṣiddhe vedamupādeyamabhimanyamānaḥ paṭhati
body.translated_text: For here, even <s>Kumārila</s>, who does not desire [to admit] a knower beyond the knower of <s>dharma</s> (duty), while maintaining the <s>Veda</s> as authoritative when a mere knower of <s>dharma</s> alone is refuted, reads [the verse]:

children.translated_text: 'The refutation of the knowledge of <s>dharma</s> is applicable only when it stands alone;
but by what is a person who knows everything else prevented?'

body.text: iti /
body.translated_text: Thus.

body.text: tadayamācāryo 'pi sarvasarvajñacaraṇareṇusanāthaṃ yāvadākāśaṃ jagadicchannapi tribhuvanacūḍāmaṇībhūtasaparikaraheyopādeyatattvajñapuruṣapuṇḍarīkaprasādhanādapyapramāṇakajaḍavaidikaśabdarāśipramukhasakaladurmatipravādapratihatirityantarnayannāha
body.translated_text: Therefore this teacher too, while wishing to establish the world extending as far as the sky, blessed by the dust of the feet of the Omniscient One, and while wishing also to accomplish the lotus-man who knows the reality of what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted, the crest-jewel of the three worlds together with his retinue — yet [recognizing that] the refutation of all false doctrines, headed by the mass of <s>Vedic</s> words [propounded by] dull, proof-less [thinkers], [is necessary] — says, leading [the discussion] inward:

children.translated_text: 'He who knows the reality of what is to be abandoned and adopted, together with the means [thereto],

children.text: yaḥ pramāṇamasāviṣṭo na tu sarvasya vedakaḥ //
children.translated_text: is an authority; but he is not a knower of everything.'

body.text: ityādi //
body.translated_text: And so forth.

body.text: tadidānīmupayuktasarvajñameva tāvat prasādhayāmaḥ / paryante tu sarvasarvajñadohadamapyapaneṣyāmaḥ / svāsthyamāsthīyatām /
body.translated_text: Therefore, let us now first establish the omniscient one who is [omniscient only] with respect to what is useful. At the end, however, we shall also dispel the longing for one who is omniscient about everything. Let there be equanimity.

body.text: yo yaḥ sādaranirantaradīrghakālābhyāsasahitacetoguṇaḥ sa sarvaḥ sphuṭībhāvayogyaḥ /
body.translated_text: [Thesis:] Every mental quality (<s>cetoguṇa</s>) that is accompanied by practice (<s>abhyāsa</s>) that is attentive, uninterrupted, and of long duration, is capable of becoming clear (<s>sphuṭībhāva</s>);

body.text: yathā yuvatyākāraḥ kāminaḥ puruṣasya /
body.translated_text: just as the form of a young woman [becomes clear] in the [mind of] a man filled with desire.

body.text: yathoktābhyāsasahitacetoguṇāśvāmī caturāryasatyaviṣayā ākārā iti svabhāvo hetuḥ /
body.translated_text: The mental images (<s>ākāra</s>) whose object is the Four Noble Truths (<s>caturāryasatya</s>), which are mental qualities accompanied by the aforementioned practice — [this is] the natural reason (<s>svabhāvahetu</s>).

body.text: tatra na tāvadāśrayadvāreṇa hetudvāreṇa vāsiddhisaṃbhāvanā / saṃkalparūḍhānāṃ caturāryasatyākārāṇāṃ cetoguṇatvamātrasya ca hetoḥ pratyātmavedyatvāt / nāpi sādaranirantaradīrghakālābhyāsalakṣaṇaṃ hetuviśeṣaṇamasaṃbhāvanīyam / tathā hi saṃsārasvabhāvaṃ (#Nibandh 2#) duḥkhātiśayamapanetumiyaṃ saṃkalpārūḍhā caturāryasatyākārabhāvanā prārabdhā / asyāścāsaṃbhāvanā nāma kiṃ (1) bhāvyasya saṃkalpārūḍhatvāsaṃbhavāt (2) anarthitvāt (3) heyarūpāniścayāt (4) heyasya nityatvāt (5) tasyāhetutvāt (6) taddhetornityatvāt (7)heyahetvaparijñānāt (8) tadbādhakābhāvāt (9) bādhakāparijñānāt (10) cittasya doṣātmakatvāt (11) tasya vyavasthitaguṇatvāt (12) bhavāntarābhāvāt (13) dhvastadoṣapunarudbhavād veti trayodaśa vikalpāḥ //
body.translated_text: In this [argument], there is no possibility of the defect of non-establishment (<s>asiddhi</s>), either through the substratum or through the reason. For the mental quality of the images of the Four Noble Truths, which have been taken up through volition, and the reason consisting merely in being a mental quality, are known through introspection (<s>pratyātmavedya</s>). Nor is the qualifier of the reason — namely, [being accompanied by] practice characterized as attentive, uninterrupted, and of long duration — inconceivable. For the meditation on the images of the Four Noble Truths, taken up through volition, has been undertaken in order to remove suffering, which by its very nature belongs to <s>saṃsāra</s> (cyclic existence), in its extreme form. Now, the impossibility of this [meditation] could be [alleged on] which [ground]? (1) Because the object of meditation cannot be taken up through volition? (2) Because of lack of desire [to remove suffering]? (3) Because what is to be abandoned is not ascertained? (4) Because what is to be abandoned is permanent? (5) Because it is uncaused? (6) Because its cause is permanent? (7) Because the cause of what is to be abandoned is not known? (8) Because of the absence of an antidote? (9) Because the antidote is not known? (10) Because the mind is essentially defiled? (11) Because [the mind] has fixed qualities? (12) Because there are no future lives? (13) Because destroyed defilements arise again? — these are the thirteen alternatives.

body.text: tatra na tāvadādyaḥ pakṣaḥ / saparikaraheyopādeyātmakasya caturāryasatyākārasya bhāvyasya vikalpārūḍhasya pratyātmavedyatvāt //
body.translated_text: Among these, the first alternative does not hold, because the object of meditation — the image of the Four Noble Truths, which is of the nature of what is to be abandoned and adopted together with its retinue — is known through introspection as having been taken up through volition.

body.text: nāpi dvitīyaḥ / duḥkhamātrasyāpi parityāgārthitvena vyāpteḥ sarvajanānubhavasiddhatvāt //
body.translated_text: Nor [does] the second [hold], because even the desire to abandon suffering alone is established through the experience of all people, being pervaded [by that desire].

body.text: nāpi tṛtīyaḥ / saṃsārātmano duḥkhasvarūpasya pratīteḥ / kathamasya duḥkhātmakatvamiti cet / saṃkṣepataḥ
body.translated_text: Nor [does] the third [hold], because <s>saṃsāra</s> (cyclic existence) is perceived as being of the nature of suffering. 'How is it of the nature of suffering?' If [asked], in brief:

children.translated_text: It has been said: Hell, by its very nature directly suffering, the realms of hungry ghosts and animals,
in the human realm there is happiness somewhere, but even that is engulfed by misery;
and for the gods, when the store of merit that serves as provisions is exhausted,
alas, those very enjoyments emit the mingling of fierce flames. Thus.

body.text: na ca caturthaḥ / vārtamānikapañcaskandhātmakasya duḥkhasyotpādadarśanāt // na ca pañcamaḥ / duḥkhasya kādācitkatvāt // nāpi ṣaṣṭhaḥ / kāryakādācitkatvasya anityahetukatvena vyāptatvāt //
body.translated_text: Nor [does] the fourth [hold], because suffering, which consists of the present five <s>skandhas</s> (aggregates), is observed to arise [and perish]. Nor [does] the fifth, because suffering is occasional (<s>kādācitka</s>). Nor [does] the sixth, because the occasional nature of the effect is pervaded by [its] having a non-eternal cause.

body.text: nāpiṃ saptamaḥ / duḥkhe viparyāsatṛṣṇāpravṛtiśaktikarmabhiḥ sahitasyātmadṛṣṭilakṣaṇasya hetoḥ sāṃsārikapañcaskandhalakṣaṇakāryānyathānupapattito niścayāt / yadāhuḥ
body.translated_text: Nor [does] the seventh [hold], because the cause — characterized as the view of self (<s>ātmadṛṣṭi</s>) — together with distorted perception (<s>viparyāsa</s>), craving (<s>tṛṣṇā</s>), the force of activity (<s>pravṛtti</s>), and <s>karma</s>, is ascertained through the impossibility-otherwise (<s>anyathānupapatti</s>) of the effect characterized as the <s>saṃsāric</s> five aggregates. As they say:

children.translated_text: First egoism (<s>ahaṃkāra</s>), then possessiveness (<s>mamakāra</s>), born from both of those is passion (<s>rāga</s>) and the rest; from malevolence toward what is harmful, the fire of hatred (<s>dveṣa</s>);

children.text: tataḥ śeṣaḥ kleśastata udayinaḥ karmavisarādvisārī saṃsāraḥ śaraṇarahito dāruṇataraḥ //
children.translated_text: from that, the remaining afflictions (<s>kleśa</s>); from those arise <s>karmas</s>; from the proliferation of <s>karma</s>, <s>saṃsāra</s> spreads — shelterless, most terrible.
Therefore, craving and distorted perception, preceded by the view of self,
are ascertained as producers of the <s>saṃsāric</s> aggregates, through [the inference from] cause and effect.

body.text: ātmadarśanasya cāvidyātvamātmapratikṣepato draṣṭavyam / tadabhāve 'pi kṣaṇabhaṅgaprastāve paralokādikamanākulamavasthāpitam //
body.translated_text: And the nature of the self-view as <s>avidyā</s> (ignorance) should be understood from its being the opposite of [the view of] <s>anātman</s> (non-self). Even in the absence of [proof for] that, the discussion of momentariness establishes future lives and so forth without confusion.

body.text: na cāṣṭamaḥ / ātmadṛṣṭirūpāyāḥ avidyāyāḥ pratipakṣabhūtasya nairātmyadarśanasya saṃbhavāt //
body.translated_text: Nor [does] the eighth [hold], because the antidote — namely, the vision of <s>nairātmya</s> (selflessness), which is the counterpart of <s>avidyā</s> in the form of the self-view — is possible.

body.text:
(#Nibandh 3#)
nāpinavamaḥ / nairātmyadarśanasya mārgaśabdavācyasya pramāṇato niścitatvāt //
body.translated_text: Nor [does] the ninth [hold], because the vision of selflessness, denoted by the word <s>mārga</s> (path), is ascertained through <s>pramāṇa</s> (valid means of knowledge).

body.text: daśamo 'pyasaṃbhavī / doṣāvasthāyāṃ cittasya saṃskārāpekṣatvāt / yo hi yatsvabhāvastasmin svabhāve vyavasthito na saṃskāramapekṣate / yathā doṣamapanīya tapanīyamakṣayadaśāyāmavasthitam / apekṣate ca cittamavidyāvasthāyāṃ saṃskāramiti vyāpakaviruddhopalabdhiḥ / pratiṣedhyasya tatsvabhāvatvasya yadvyāpakaṃ saṃskāranirapekṣatvaṃ tadviruddhaṃ tadapekṣatvamiti cittasya doṣātmakatvakṣatiḥ //
body.translated_text: The tenth too is impossible, because the mind, in its state of defilement, depends on conditioning (<s>saṃskāra</s>). For whatever is of a certain nature, being established in that nature, does not depend on conditioning — just as gold, once the impurities have been removed, is established in an imperishable state. But the mind in its state of <s>avidyā</s> does depend on conditioning — this is a proof through the apprehension of what is contradictory to the pervader (<s>vyāpakaviruddhopalabdhi</s>). That which pervades the thing to be refuted — namely, its being of that nature — is non-dependence on conditioning; what is contradictory to that is dependence on conditioning. Thus, the [claim of the mind's] essential defiledness is undermined.

body.text: ekādaśo 'pyayuktaḥ / cetasastattatsaṃskārātiśaye prajñātiśayadarśanāt //
body.translated_text: The eleventh too is unjustified, because when there is an increase of the relevant conditioning in the mind, an increase of wisdom is observed.

body.text: na ca dvādaśaḥ / paralokaprasādhanāt / tathā hi,
body.translated_text: Nor [does] the twelfth [hold], because of the establishment of future lives. That is to say:

body.text:
yaccittaṃ taccittāntaraṃ pratisandhatte /
yathedānīntanaṃ cittam /
cittaṃ ca maraṇakālabhāvīti svabhāvahetuḥ /

na cārhaccaramacittena vyabhicāraḥ / tasyāgamamātrataḥ pratītatvāt / niḥkleśacittāntarajananād vā / hetorvā kleśe satīti viśeṣaṇādityanāgatabhavasiddhiḥ / evaṃ yaccittaṃ taccittāntarapūrvakaṃ yathedānīntanaṃ cittam / cittaṃ ca janmasamayabhāvītyarthataḥ kāryaheturityatītabhavasiddhiḥ //
body.translated_text: Nor is there deviation [from the rule] with respect to the final mind of an <s>Arhat</s> (Worthy One), because that is known merely from scripture (<s>āgama</s>); or because it generates a mind-moment free from afflictions. Or, [the reason is qualified:] 'when there is affliction' — thus, through the qualifier, the establishment of future existence [follows]. Similarly, whatever is a mind is preceded by another mind, just like the present mind; and the mind exists at the time of birth — thus, the proof of the past existence is [established] through the reason in the form of effect.

body.text: na ca trayodaśaḥ / doṣakāraṇasyātmadarśanasya yadviruddhaṃ nairātmyadarśanaṃ tasya nirupadravatvāt / bhūtārthatvāt / svabhāvatvācca / sarvadāvasthiteḥ / tannāyaṃ viśeṣaṇāsiddho 'pi hetuḥ / tathāpī dṛśo 'bhyāso na kasya cid dṝśyata iti cet / na dṛśyatām / saṃbhāvanā tāvadaśakyapratiṣedhā / idānīntanajanapravṛtiścāvyāhateti nāparaṃ gamyate / ata evedaṃ saṃbhāvanānumānamucyate //
body.translated_text: Nor [does] the thirteenth [hold], because the vision of selflessness (<s>nairātmya</s>), which is the opposite of the self-view that is the cause of defilement, is free from relapse; because it grasps reality; because it is of the nature [of things]; and because it persists always. Therefore this reason is not defective even if the qualifier is unestablished. 'Even so, the practice of [this] vision is not seen in anyone' — if [objected], let it not be seen; the possibility (<s>saṃbhāvanā</s>) at least cannot be refuted. And the activity of present-day people is unobstructed; hence nothing further follows. For this very reason, this is called a possibility-inference (<s>saṃbhāvanānumāna</s>).

body.text: na caiṣa viruddho hetuḥ / sapakṣe kāminyākāre saṃbhavāt / na cānaikāntikaḥ / abhyāsasahitaceto guṇasphuṭapratibhāsayoḥ kāryakāraṇayorghaṭakumbhakārayoriva sarvopasaṃhāreṇa pratyakṣānupalambhataḥ kāryakāraṇabhāvasiddhāvabhyāsasahitacetoguṇatvasya sādhanasya sphuṭapratibhāsakaraṇayogyatayā vyāptisiddheḥ / tathā hi vyāptyadhikaraṇe kāmāturavartini yuvatyākāre sādaranirantaradīrghakālābhyāsasahitacetoguṇāt pūrvamanupalabdhiḥ sphuṭābhasya / paścādabhyāsasaṃvedanaṃ sphuṭābhasaṃvedanamiti / trividhapratyakṣānupalambhasādhyaḥ kāryakāraṇabhāvaḥ sphuṭapratibhāsābhyāsasacivacittākārayoriyamupapannā sarvopasaṃhāravatī vyāptiḥ / ato 'naikāntikatāpyasaṃbhavinītyanavadyo hetuḥ //
body.translated_text: Nor is this a contradictory reason (<s>viruddha hetu</s>), because it is possible in the sapakṣa (similar case), namely the image of a young woman [in the mind of a lover]. Nor is it inconclusive (<s>anaikāntika</s>), because the causal relation between the mental quality accompanied by practice and clear manifestation — [established] like the causal relation between a potter and a pot — is established through a comprehensive negative perception (<s>sarvopasaṃhāra pratyakṣānupalambha</s>): [i.e.,] in the domain of pervasion, regarding the image of a young woman present in the continuum of one afflicted with desire, prior to the attentive, uninterrupted, long-term practice as a mental quality, there is non-perception of clear manifestation; afterwards, the perception of practice [co-occurs with] the perception of clear manifestation. The causal relation, established through the threefold negative perception, between clear manifestation and the mental image accompanied by practice, constitutes this well-established pervasion with comprehensive scope. Therefore, inconclusiveness too is impossible — hence the reason is faultless.

body.text: nanu kathamanumānataḥ sarvajñasiddhipratyāśā / tasya parokṣatvena tatpratibaddhaliṅgāniścayāt (#Nibandh 4#) kiṃ ca sarvajñasattāsādhane sarvo heturna trayīṃ doṣajātimatipatati / sarvajñe hi dharmiṇyasiddhatvam / asarvajñe hi viruddhatvam / ubhayātmakepyanaikāntikatvamiti //
body.translated_text: Objection: How can there be expectation of proving omniscience through inference? Since [omniscience] is imperceptible, the mark (<s>liṅga</s>) that is invariably connected to it cannot be ascertained. Moreover, in proving the existence of an omniscient being, every reason falls into one of the three categories of defects: with respect to the omniscient as the subject (<s>dharmin</s>), there is non-establishment (<s>asiddhatva</s>); with respect to the non-omniscient, there is contradiction (<s>viruddhatva</s>); and with respect to what partakes of both natures, there is inconclusiveness (<s>anaikāntikatva</s>).

body.text: api ca abhyāsāt kāraṇātkāryasya sphuṭābhasya pratītau nāvaśyaṃ kāraṇāni kāryavanti bhavantītyanaikāntikatā / atha sphuṭībhāvayogyatānumīyate / sāpi śaktirucyate / sā ca kārye 'nantarā sāntarā vā / tatrādyā kāryasamadhigamyā / na cādhigatakāryasya tayā kaścidupayogaḥ / dvitīyā tu kāryāvasāyamaikāntikaṃ na sādhayet //
body.translated_text: Furthermore, even if the effect — clear manifestation — is understood from the cause, practice, it does not follow that causes necessarily have effects — hence inconclusiveness. Now, if it is the capacity for becoming clear that is inferred — that too is called a power (<s>śakti</s>). And that is either immediately prior to the effect or remote from it. Of these, the first is known together with the effect; and for one who has already ascertained the effect, that [capacity] serves no purpose. The second, however, would not conclusively establish the occurrence of the effect.

body.text: na ca kāryāpratītau yogyatāniścayaḥ saṃbhavī / nāpi yogyatāmātrasādhanekṛtārthaḥ sāghanavādī / sarvajñajñāne kārye vivādasya tādavasthyād / bhavatu sphuṭībhāvasya siddhiḥ / tathāpi kaḥ prastāvaḥ sarvajñavivāde sādhanamārabdhavataḥ sphuṭatvaṃ cetasaḥ sādhayitum //
body.translated_text: Nor is the ascertainment of the capacity possible in the absence of the effect. Nor is the proponent, who asserts [something] substantive, satisfied with merely proving the capacity; for the dispute concerns the omniscient cognition as the effect, and the situation remains the same. Let clarity [of mind] be established; even so, what is the relevance for one who has undertaken a proof in the dispute about omniscience — [namely,] to prove the clarity of the mind?

body.text: kiṃ ca prasiddhānumāne bhūtalasya dharmiṇaḥ kumbhakāraghaṭayorapi dharmayoḥ pratītatvāt kāryakāraṇabhāvo grahītuṃ śakyata eva / prastute tu kāmāturasantānavartino yuvatyākārasya dharmiṇastatpragatābhyāsasphuṭatvayorapi dharmayoḥ parokṣatvāt / kathaṃ kāryakāraṇagṛhītiḥ / yathā ca naiyāyikaṃ prati yuṣmābhirucyate pratyakṣato na kāryamātraṃ puruṣavyāptaṃ sidhyati / kiṃ tvavāntarameva ghaṭajātīyaṃ kāryamiti tathā nākāramātramabhyāsapūrvakaṃ sidhyati / kiṃ tvavāntarameva yuvatyākārasāmānyamiti vyaktameva / na cābhyāsakāryaḥ sphuṭībhāvaḥ / tadabhāve 'pi svapne darśanāt //
body.translated_text: Moreover, in a well-known inference, since the subject — the ground — and the two properties — the pot-making and the potter — are both perceived, the causal relation can indeed be grasped. But in the present case, since the subject — the image of a young woman present in the continuum of one afflicted with desire — and the two properties — the practice associated with it and the clarity — are imperceptible, how can the causal relation be grasped? And just as you say against the <s>Naiyāyikas</s>: 'From perception, it is not merely the effect that is established as pervaded by a person; rather, it is only a specific, pot-type effect' — so too it is clear that it is not merely any image that is established as preceded by practice, but only a specific one, namely the universal of the image of a young woman. And clarity is not the effect of practice, since it is observed even in dreams in the absence of [practice].

body.text: kiṃ ca sarvavido 'pi yadi caturāryasatyaparijñānataḥ sarvajñatāsthitiḥ, tarhi ghaṭādikatipayavastujñāne 'pi sarvajñateti sādhvī śuddhiḥ / api ca
body.translated_text: Moreover, even if the omniscient knows [only] the Four Noble Truths, and omniscience consists in the knowledge of those, then even in the knowledge of a few things such as a pot, there would be omniscience — what a fine purification [that would be]! Furthermore:

children.translated_text: 'Some person of knowledge is sought in order to understand what he has said —
by those who suspect deception in the instruction of the ignorant.'

body.text: iti yuṣmābhirevocyate / na ca sarvajñānavān viśeṣaniṣṭhatayādhigantuṃ śakyate / na cāsya sattāmātrasiddhau kaścidupayogaḥ, pravṛtteranaṅgatvāditi sarvamasamañjasam //
body.translated_text: Thus is said by you yourselves. But the omniscient cannot be ascertained through any particular [mark of identification]. Nor is there any use in merely establishing his existence, since activity [toward him] would lack a basis. Therefore, all this is incoherent.

body.text:
atrocyate / na vayaṃ sākṣātsarvajñasattāpratijñāyāṃ hetuvyāpāramanumanyāmahe / bhūdharādhīnavahnisattāvat / kintu caturāryasatyākārasvarūpe dharmiṇi sphuṭābhatvasya sādhyasyāyogavyavacchedārthaṃ parvate 'gnimātrāyogavyavacchedavat / sphuṭābhatvaṃ tu kāminyākārādidṛṣṭānte dṛṣṭameva / tacca parvatīyāgnivat / pakṣadharmatābalataḥ satyacatuṣṭayādhikaraṇaṃ sidhyat sarvajñatāmācakṣmahe /
yathoktam
body.translated_text:
To this we reply: We do not sanction the operation of the reason directly for the thesis of the mere existence of the omniscient — like the existence of fire dependent on a mountain. Rather, [we employ the reason] for the purpose of excluding the impossibility (<s>ayogavyavaccheda</s>) of clear manifestation as the <s>sādhya</s> (property to be proved) with respect to the <s>dharmin</s> (subject), which is of the nature of the images of the Four Noble Truths — just as [one excludes] the mere impossibility of fire on a mountain. And clear manifestation is actually observed in the example of the image of a young woman and so forth — just like the fire on a mountain. And when, through the force of the subject-property (<s>pakṣadharmatā</s>), [this clarity] is established as having the Four Truths as its substrate, we call that omniscience.
As has been said:

body.text:
ityabhyāsabalāt parisphuṭadaśākoṭiḥ sphurat saṃbhavī
heyādeyatadaṅgalakṣaṇaguṇaḥ sarvajñatā saiva naḥ // iti /
body.translated_text: 'Therefore, by the force of practice, the quality of mind characterized by what is to be abandoned and adopted and its components — whose culmination is the stage of clear manifestation — arises as possible: that very thing is what we [call] omniscience.' Thus.

body.text: tadatrābhyāsasahitacaturāryasatyākāraḥ samagro dharmī sāmagryamabhyāsaviśiṣṭacetoguṇatvamātraṃ hetuḥ sphuṭībhāvayogyatāsādhyam / yathā sāgnitvānagnitvasandehe (#Nibandh 5#) parvatātmā pramāṇapratīto dharmī / tathātrāpi sarvajñatvāsarvajñatvavivāde 'hi pratyātmaviditaḥ satyacatuṣṭayākāro dharmī / tasmāt sphuṭābhatvena sādhyena dṛṣṭānte vyāptisiddherastyeva tatpratibaddhaliṅganiścayaḥ / sādhyasandehe 'pi dharmiṇaścaturāryasatyākārasya siddherna trividhadoṣajāteravasaraḥ / yogyatāyāḥ prasādhanena ca kāraṇāt kāryapratītāvanaikāntikatvamityapyanabhyupagamapratihatam / yogyatā ca sāntaraiva sādhyate / iyaṃ ca na gamayatu nāmaikāntataḥ kāryasattvam / anupapadyamānaṃ punarasya saṃbhavamākṣipatyeva / tadā bhāvini kārye sandehe 'pi kāraṇayogyatā niścīyata eva / brīhyādau bhāviphalāniścayepi yogyatāniścayena pravṛtteḥ / anyathā śilāśakalāderapyupādānaprasaṅgaḥ /
body.translated_text: Here, the complete <s>dharmin</s> (subject) is the form of the four noble truths together with practice; the <s>hetu</s> (reason) is merely being a mental quality distinguished by practice; and the <s>sādhya</s> (what is to be proved) is the capacity for becoming vivid. Just as, when there is doubt about the presence or absence of fire, the mountain itself — known through a <s>pramāṇa</s> (means of valid knowledge) — is the <s>dharmin</s>; so too here, in the dispute about omniscience and non-omniscience, the form of the four truths, known through one's own experience, is the <s>dharmin</s>. Therefore, since <s>vyāpti</s> (pervasion) is established in the example through the <s>sādhya</s> in the form of non-vividness, there is indeed ascertainment of the <s>liṅga</s> (inferential mark) connected with that. Even when the <s>sādhya</s> is in doubt, since the <s>dharmin</s>, namely the form of the four noble truths, is established, there is no occasion for the threefold set of defects. And the [objection of] <s>anaikāntikatva</s> (inconclusiveness), [namely] that from a cause one should cognize the effect through the establishment of mere capacity — that too is repelled by non-acceptance. For it is capacity-with-a-gap that is being proved. And let this [capacity] not, indeed, conclusively indicate the reality of the effect; nevertheless, what cannot be otherwise accounted for does entail its possibility. Thus, even when the [future] effect is in doubt, the causal capacity is ascertained with certainty — as in the case of rice and the like, where, even when the future fruit is uncertain, one proceeds [to plant] based on the certainty of capacity; otherwise, there would be the absurd consequence that even stone chips could serve as material [for growing].

body.text: tajjātīyasya śarāvasthapaṅkoptasya sāmarthyamupalabdhamiti cet / atrāpi kāminyākāre bhāvanājātīyasya sphuṭībhāvakaraṇayogyatā dṛṣṭeti samānam /
body.translated_text: If [you object]: 'The capacity of that very type [of thing], such as clay in the state of a potsherd, has been observed' — here too, the same [reply applies]: the capacity of that very type of thing, namely <s>bhāvanā</s> (meditative cultivation) in the form of a woman, to produce vividness has been observed.

body.text: evaṃ yogyatāmātrasādhanenaiva kṛtārthaḥ sādhanavādī / sarvajñakāraṇabhāvāttadabhāvavādināṃ nirdalanāt / kāryasya va traikālikasya sambhāvanāprasādhanāt / muttkyarthināṃ ca pravṛtteravirodhāt / vādino 'pi tanmātrasādhanasyābhipretatvāt / ataeva kaḥ prastāvaḥ sarvajñasattāvivāde sphuṭībhāvasādhanasyetyādyapyanavakāśam / sarvajñaśabdena sphuṭībhāvayogyatāyā vivakṣitatvāt / tathā kāryakāraṇapratītirapi saṃbhavatyeva / tathā hi kāminyabhyāsasantatisahacāri saṃbhramakāyavacodarśanameva kāminyākārasya tadbhāvanāyāśca darśanam / tathābhūtakāyavaco 'darśanameva bhāvanāyā adarśanam / evaṃ sphuṭapratibhāsasantatisahacāriviśiṣṭakāyavacodarśanaṃ sphuṭapratibhāsadarśanam / tathāvasthitakāyavaco 'darśanameva sphuṭapratibhāsādarśanamityastyeva prastute 'pi pratyakṣānupalambhataḥ kāryakāraṇabhāvapratītiḥ / iyaṃ ca tathāvasthakāmāturaśarīravacanagrahaṇe tadekadeśabhūtayuvatyākārābhyāsasphuṭapratibhāsagrahaṇavyavasthā vyāvahārikeṇāvaśyaṃ svīkartavyā / anyathā cityacaityarūparasagandhasparśaparamāṇupuñjādyātmakasya kumbhakāraghaṭapradeśāderapi rūpaikadeśagrāhakaṃ cakṣuḥpratyakṣaṃ na samudāyavyavasthāpakamiti sarvavyāvahārikapramāṇocchedaprasaṅgaḥ / tathā bāhyaghaṭakāminyādīnāṃ śaktikṛtasya mahato jātibhedasya saṃbhavādanyajātīyavyāptigrahe 'nyajātīyād buddhimadanumānamayuktam / saṃkalpārūḍhānāṃ tu jalajvalanayuvatyākārādīnāṃ bāhyatvenādhyastānāmapi vijñānaikasvarūpatayaikajātīyatvamastīti bhāvanāsahitākāramātreṇaiva vaiśadyavyāptirastu //
body.translated_text: Thus, the proponent of the proof achieves his purpose merely by proving capacity. [This is] because the position of those who deny omniscience on the ground that its cause is absent is demolished; because the possibility of a temporally extended effect is demonstrated; because there is no contradiction with the activity of those who seek liberation; and because the proponent himself intends to prove just that much. For this very reason, the [objection] 'What occasion is there, in the dispute about the existence of an omniscient being, for proving vividness?' and so forth is also without scope, since what is intended by the word '<s>sarvajña</s>' (omniscient) is the capacity for vividness. Likewise, the cognition of causal relation also obtains. For the seeing of the agitated body and speech that accompanies the stream of practice regarding a woman's [image] is itself the seeing of the woman's form and of that <s>bhāvanā</s> (meditation). Similarly, the non-seeing of such body and speech is the non-seeing of that <s>bhāvanā</s>. Likewise, the seeing of the distinguished body and speech that accompanies a stream of vivid appearances is the seeing of the vivid appearance. And the non-seeing of body and speech in such a state is the non-seeing of the vivid appearance. Thus, even in the present case, the cognition of causal relation obtains from direct perception and non-apprehension. And this determination — that in the apprehension of the body and speech of one who is in the state of being love-sick, there is the apprehension of the vivid appearance of the practice of a young woman's form, which is a part of that [love-sickness] — must necessarily be accepted by those operating at the conventional level. Otherwise, even the visual perception that apprehends one part, namely form, of a potter's pot-locus consisting of consciousness, <s>caitya</s> (mental factors), form, taste, smell, touch, atomic aggregates, and the like, would not be capable of establishing the aggregate — and there would be the absurd consequence of destroying all conventional <s>pramāṇas</s> (means of valid knowledge). Furthermore, since there is a great difference of kind, brought about by capacity, among external [objects] such as pots and women, inferring from one kind's [pervasion] a pervasion with another kind by a mind cognizing [only] that [first kind] is unjustified. But for those [images] that have been taken up in imagination — such as the forms of water, fire, young women, etc., which are superimposed as external even though they are of the sole nature of cognition — since they belong to a single kind, let the pervasion with vividness be [established] by the mere form [of cognition] together with <s>bhāvanā</s> (cultivation).

body.text: na ca svapne sphuṭatāvyabhicāraḥ / bhāvanāsiddhalakṣaṇayorhetvorjātibhede tatkāryayorekatvābhimāne 'pi jātibhedasyāvaśyaṃ svīkartavyatvāt / dṛśyate hi siddhasādhyā vaiśadyajātiranapekṣya viparītabhāvanāṃ nidrāvicchede vicchidyamānā / bhāvanābhāvinī tu na vinā vipakṣābhyāsaṃ jāgrato 'pi yadāhuḥ
body.translated_text: Nor is there a deviation regarding vividness in dream. Since, even when there is a claim that the effects of the two <s>hetus</s> (reasons) — [one] characterized by <s>bhāvanā</s> and [the other] established [independently] — which are of different kinds, are identical, the difference of kind must necessarily be accepted. For one observes that the vividness produced by what is already accomplished, without depending on contrary <s>bhāvanā</s>, ceases upon the interruption of sleep. But [the vividness] produced by <s>bhāvanā</s> does not [cease] even for one who is awake, without practice of the contrary. As they say:

body.text: (#Nibandh 6#)

children.translated_text: Even in dream there is vividness — and likewise [in meditation]; yet there is [claimed to be] identity of these two,
but equality of form alone constitutes the equality [of type] of the genus — this does not hold.
The one is obstructed by the cessation of sleep; the other is obstructed by [contrary] efforts;
vividness [arising] from the power of contrary meditation, as in the case of the difference [between] compassion and cruelty. Thus.

body.translated_text: (Nibandh 6)

body.text: yadapi ghaṭādikatipayajñāne 'pi sarvajñaḥ syādityuktam / tatrāpi
body.translated_text: As for the objection that 'one would be omniscient even from the knowledge of a few things like a pot' — to that too:

children.translated_text: 'Even in complete knowledge of all things beginning with a pot, there is fear [of the objection] on your part;

children.text: dhīyet yadi ko doṣaḥ so 'pi sarvajñatāṃ vrajet /
children.translated_text: if one should fear [that], what fault [is there] — he too would attain omniscience.
But we, desiring liberation from the suffering of <s>saṃsāra</s> (cyclic existence),
would resort to one who knows the means to that, so as to stand on the path proclaimed by him.'

body.text: ityuttaraṃ draṣṭavyam / tathā sattāmātre vipratipannān prati sattaiva kevalā prasādhitā / viśeṣajijñāsāyāṃ tu pramāṇopapannakṣaṇikanairātmyavādina eva sugatasya bhagavataḥ sarvajñatā /
body.translated_text: — this should be seen as the reply. Similarly, against those who dispute the mere existence [of an omniscient being], mere existence itself is proven. But for those who wish to know the specifics, the omniscience belongs to the <s>Bhagavān</s> (Blessed One), the <s>Sugata</s> (Well-gone One), who teaches momentariness and selflessness, [a teaching] supported by <s>pramāṇas</s> (valid means of knowledge).

body.text: ata etadapi nirastaṃ yadāha bhaṭṭaḥ
body.translated_text: Hence this too is refuted, which <s>Bhaṭṭa</s> [<s>Kumārila</s>] says:

children.text: sugato yadi sarvajñaḥ kapilo neti kā pramā /
children.translated_text: 'If the <s>Sugata</s> is omniscient, what proof is there that <s>Kapila</s> is not?

children.text: athobhāvapi sarvajñau matabhedaḥ kathaṃ tayoḥ // iti //
children.translated_text: And if both are omniscient, how [is there] a difference of doctrine between them?' Thus.

body.text: tasmāt
body.translated_text: Therefore:

children.text: uktakrameṇa munirājanaye pramāyāḥ śaktirvyanakti gatimapramitāṃ kṛpāṃ ca /
children.translated_text: 'By the method stated, the king of sages reveals the power of <s>pramāṇa</s> (valid knowledge), an unfathomed course, and [his] compassion;

children.text: anyatra tu dvayamudastamado 'stamāne tenaika eva śaraṇaṃ sa nirātmavādī //
children.translated_text: elsewhere, however, both [power and compassion] are cast off — when pride has set, therefore he alone, the teacher of selflessness, is the refuge.'

body.text: iti viśeṣasiddhirapyanavadyeti sarvamanākulamākulādhayaḥ pare na pratipadyante / sādhane 'sminnavadye 'pi durnītidahanadagdhabuddhayaḥ punarapyetadācakṣate / bādhakapramāṇasadbhāvāt sarvajñasyāsadvyavahāro yuktaḥ sadvyavahārapratiṣedho vā prasādhakapramāṇābhāvādveti //
body.translated_text: Thus, the establishment of the specific [omniscience of the <s>Buddha</s>] too is faultless — all this is tranquil. But those of disturbed minds do not accept it. Even when this proof is faultless, those whose intellects are burned by the fire of bad reasoning again object: 'Because of the existence of a sublating <s>pramāṇa</s>, either the unreal status of the omniscient is justified, or the denial of real status [is justified] because of the absence of a proving <s>pramāṇa</s>.'

body.text: atra vicāryate kiṃ punarasya bhagavato bādhakaṃ pramāṇaṃ pratyakṣamanumānaṃ śabdādikaṃ veti vikalpāḥ //
body.translated_text: Here it is investigated: What, then, is the <s>pramāṇa</s> that sublates the <s>Bhagavān</s> (Blessed One) — is it <s>pratyakṣa</s> (perception), <s>anumāna</s> (inference), <s>śabda</s> (verbal testimony), or the like? These are the alternatives.

body.text: na tāvat pratyakṣam / pratyakṣaṃ hi kevalapradeśādau pravartamānaṃ svapravṛttiyogyameva tatra vastu pratiṣedhati / na vastumātram / na ca sarvajñasya pratyakṣapravṛttiyogyatāsti / svabhāvaviprakṛṣṭatvāttasya //
body.translated_text: Firstly, it is not <s>pratyakṣa</s> (perception). For perception, operating [only] with respect to a mere spatial region and the like, negates [the existence of] only that entity which is fit to be the object of its own operation — not any entity whatsoever. And the omniscient being has no fitness to be an object of perceptual operation, because he is by nature remote [from ordinary perception].

body.text:
(#Nibandh 7#)
syādetat / na vayaṃ pratyakṣaṃ pravartamānamabhāvaṃ sādhayatīti brūmaḥ / kiṃ tarhi / nivartamānam / tathā hi yatra vastuni pratyakṣasya nivṛttistasyāsadbhāvaḥ / yathā śaśaviṣāṇādeḥ / yatra tu pratyakṣasya pravṝttistasya sadbhāvo yathā ghaṭādeḥ / asti ca sarvajñe pratyakṣanivṛttiḥ / tadasyāpyabhāvaḥ kena nivāryata iti //
body.translated_text:
(Nibandh 7)
One might say: 'We do not claim that perception, when operating, proves absence. Rather, [it proves absence] when it ceases to operate. That is to say: where perception ceases [to apprehend] an entity, its non-existence [is established] — as in the case of a hare's horn and the like. But where perception does operate [to apprehend] an entity, its existence [is established] — as in the case of a pot and the like. And there is cessation of perception with respect to the omniscient being; so why cannot his non-existence too [be established]?'

body.text: ucyate / nivartamānaṃ pratyakṣamabhāvaṃ sādhayatīti ko 'rthaḥ / kiṃ pratyakṣasya yā nivṛttistato 'bhāvasiddhiḥ, nivṛttisahitādvā pratyakṣāt, nivṛttādvā pratyakṣāditi /
body.translated_text: We reply: What is meant by 'perception, when ceasing to operate, proves absence'? Does the absence follow (i) from the cessation of perception, or (ii) from perception together with cessation, or (iii) from perception that has ceased?

body.text: nādyaḥ pakṣaḥ / satyapi vastuni pratyakṣanivṛtterupalabhyamānāyā vastvabhāvaniya tatvāsiddheḥ //
body.translated_text: The first alternative is untenable, because since the cessation of perception is observed even when the entity exists, the non-existence of the entity cannot be established — i.e. the thesis is unproven.

body.text: nāpi dvitīyaḥ / svābhāvena saha kasyacit sāhityānupapatteḥ / anyathā tannivṛttatvānupapatteḥ //
body.translated_text: Nor [is] the second [alternative tenable], because nothing can coexist with its own absence; otherwise, the impossibility of its having ceased would follow.

body.text: na ca tṛtīyaḥ / tathā hi nivṛttāt pratyakṣādabhāvasiddhirityasataḥ pratyakṣādityuktaṃ bhavati / na cāsato hetubhāvaḥ saṃbhavati / sarvasāmarthyavirahalakṣaṇatvāttasya / na hi tacca nāsti tena ca pratipattiriti nyāyyam / ato na tāvat pratyakṣaṃ sarvajñabādhakam //
body.translated_text: Nor the third. For 'the establishment of absence from perception that has ceased' amounts to saying 'from non-existent perception' — and a non-existent [thing] cannot serve as a cause, since it is characterized by the absence of all capacity. For it is not reasonable [to say] that something both does not exist and yet produces cognition. Therefore, perception is not, to begin with, a sublator of the omniscient being.

body.text: nāpyanumānam / taddhi trividhaliṅgajatvena trividham / tatra kāryasvabhāvayorvidhisādhanatvāt, pratiṣedhe sādhye 'navasaraḥ / na ca dṛśyānupalambhaḥ tatprabhedo vā kāryānupalabdhyādiryogyānupalambho vā parābhimato 'tra pramāṇam / sarvajñatāyāḥ svabhāvaviprakṛṣṭatvenādṛśyatvāt //
body.translated_text: Nor is <s>anumāna</s> (inference) [a sublator]. For that, being produced by the three types of <s>liṅga</s> (inferential mark), is threefold. Among these, since <s>kārya</s> (effect) and <s>svabhāva</s> (essential nature) [marks] serve to prove [only] positive [assertions], there is no scope for them when the <s>sādhya</s> is a negation. Nor is <s>dṛśyānupalambha</s> (non-apprehension of the perceptible), or its subdivision <s>kāryānupalabdhi</s> (non-apprehension of the effect), or <s>yogyānupalambha</s> (non-apprehension of what is fit to be perceived) — as accepted by the opponent — a <s>pramāṇa</s> here, because omniscience, being by nature remote, is not perceptible.

body.text: nanu kāraṇānupalambhādeva sarvajñatāpratiṣedhaḥ sidhyati / tathā hi tatkāraṇamindriyavijñānaṃ vā mānasaṃ vā bhāvanābalajaṃ vā / bhāvanābalajamapi cākṣuṣaṃ vā, mānasaṃ veti vikalpāḥ /
body.translated_text: Objection: The negation of omniscience is established by the very non-apprehension of its cause. For the cause [of omniscience] is either sensory cognition, or mental cognition, or cognition born of the power of <s>bhāvanā</s> (meditative cultivation). And that which is born of the power of <s>bhāvanā</s> is either visual or mental — these are the alternatives.

body.text: tatra na tāvaccakṣurindriyavijñānamaśeṣārthagrāhi / tasya pratiniyatārthaviṣayatvāt / deśāntare kālāntare [ca] tathaiva pratiniyamaḥ / anyathā hetuphalabhāvābhāvaprasaṅgāt / anekendriyavaiyarthyaprasaṅgācca / tathā ca kārikā
body.translated_text: Among these, firstly, the visual sense-cognition does not apprehend all objects, because it has a specifically delimited range of objects. In other places and other times, the same delimitation [holds]; otherwise, there would be the absurd consequence of the absence of the cause-effect relation [between sense organ and object], and the absurd consequence of the futility of multiple sense organs. And thus the verse:

children.translated_text: 'He who postulates an omniscient being through a single sense-<s>pramāṇa</s> (means of valid knowledge) —

children.text: nūnaṃ sa cakṣuṣā sarvān rasādīn pratipadyate //
children.translated_text: surely he apprehends all tastes and the like through the eye alone!'
'By whatever type of <s>pramāṇas</s> the seeing of whatever type of objects
occurs for people now — so too it was in other times.' Thus.

body.text:
tataścaivaṃ prayogaḥ kartavyaḥ /
buddhacakṣurnātītādiviṣayam /
cakṣustvāt /
smadādicakṣurvat /
(#Nibandh 8#)
acakṣurvā /
atītādiviṣayatvāt /
śabdavat /

iti sarvametat śrotrādāvapi draṣṭavyam / na cakṣurādiprakarṣaḥ svārthamatikramya dṛṣṭa /
kārikā
body.translated_text:
All this should also be seen regarding the ear and other [senses]. No enhancement of the eye and the like has been observed that exceeds its own [proper] object.
The verse:

children.translated_text: Even where enhancement is observed, because it does not exceed its own object,
it would consist in [apprehending] distant and subtle [instances of the same type], not in [apprehending] form from the operation of the ear.

body.text: bṛhaṭṭīkā ca
body.translated_text: The <s>Bṛhaṭṭīkā</s> (Great Commentary) [says]:

children.translated_text: With respect to sounds apprehended by the ear, human superiority is observed
in the apprehension of distant and subtle [sounds], not in the apprehension of form and the like.
Even with the eye, the apprehension of distant and subtle forms
is accomplished through the attainment of enhancement, but not the seeing of sound and the like.

body.text: na caitad vaktavyam / yadi nāmaikaikenendriyeṇa tajjñānena vā sarvasyāgrahaṇaṃ tathāpi pañcabhirindriyaistajjñānairvā svasvaviṣayapravṛttairevātiśayaprāptairbhaviṣyatīti / ekaikasyāpi niḥśeṣasvaviṣayagrahaṇādarśanāt / paracittādyatīndriyāṇāṃ grahaṇā(bhāvā) cca / tadevamindriyamindriyavijñānaṃ vā nāśeṣagrāhīti na prathamaḥ pakṣaḥ //
body.translated_text: Nor should this be said: 'Even if there is no apprehension of everything by each individual sense or its cognition, nevertheless it will be [possible] through the five senses or their cognitions, each operating within its own domain, having attained enhancement.' For even of each individual [sense], the apprehension of all [objects] within its own domain is not observed; and [objects] beyond the senses, such as others' minds, are not apprehended [at all]. Thus, neither the sense organ nor sense-cognition apprehends everything — the first alternative is untenable.

body.text: nāpi dvitīyaḥ / tathā hi yadyapi tanmānasaṃ sarvārthaviṣayaṃ tathāpi na tasya svātantryeṇārthagrahaṇe vyāpāro 'sti / manaso bahirasvātantryāt / anyathāndhavadhirādyabhāvaprasaṅgaḥ / teṣāmapi manaso bhāvāt / pāratantrye cendriyajñānaparigṛhītārthaviṣayatvādatītānāgatadūrasūkṣmavyavahitaparacittāderarthasyendriyaparijñānāgocarasya manasā paricchedo na prāpnotīti kathaṃ sarvajñatā //
body.translated_text: Nor the second [alternative]. For, although the mental [cognition] has all objects as its domain, nevertheless it has no independent capacity to apprehend objects, because the mind lacks independence with respect to external [objects]. Otherwise, there would be the absurd consequence that there would be no blind, deaf, or other [disabled persons], since even they possess a mind. And if [the mind] is dependent [on the senses], then since it has as its domain the objects that have been grasped by sense-cognition, the mental determination of objects not within the range of sensory cognition — such as past, future, distant, subtle, hidden, and others' minds — is not attained. How then [could there be] omniscience?

body.text: na ca bhāvanābalajaṃ sarvārthagrāhīti tṛtīyaḥ pakṣaḥ / tathā hi tadbhāvanābalajamapi yadīndriyāśritamiti caturthaḥ pakṣaḥ, tadā so 'saṅgataḥ / indriyasya tajjñānasya ca niyataviṣayaviṣayatvapratipādanāt //
body.translated_text: Nor is the third alternative [tenable], namely that [cognition] born of the power of <s>bhāvanā</s> (meditative cultivation) apprehends all objects. For, if that which is born of the power of <s>bhāvanā</s> depends on the senses — this being the fourth alternative — then it is untenable, because it has been demonstrated that sense organs and their cognitions have delimited domains.

body.text: atha bhāvanābalena tathāvidhamutpannaṃ manovijñānaṃ sarvārthagrāhīti pañcamaḥ pakṣaḥ / tadānvarthatvāt pratyakṣaśabdasya tasya ca bhāvanābalāvalambino 'pyanakṣajatvāt nārthasākṣātkāritvamastīti pratipādanīyam / kiṃ ca svaviṣayasīmānamanatipatyaiva prakarṣo 'pi dṛśyate / na tu sarvaviṣayatveneti / kathaṃ tenāpi sakalārthajātādivedanam / yato na kasyacidabhyāse 'pyatīndriyārthadarśitvamupalabdham //
body.translated_text: Or if the fifth alternative [is proposed], namely that mental cognition produced in such a manner by the power of <s>bhāvanā</s> apprehends all objects — then, since the word '<s>pratyakṣa</s>' (perception) [etymologically] means 'in accordance with the [sense] object,' and since this [mental cognition], though supported by the power of <s>bhāvanā</s>, is not born of the senses, it must be demonstrated that it does not directly present the object. Moreover, enhancement too is observed only without exceeding the range of one's own objects, not in the form of [cognizing] all objects. How then could even that [bhāvanā-born cognition] know the entire range of objects and the like? For, even through practice, no one has been observed to see objects beyond the senses.

body.text: bṛhaṭṭīkā
body.translated_text: The <s>Bṛhaṭṭīkā</s> (Great Commentary) [says]:

children.translated_text: Even those men who are observed to possess exceptional intelligence, memory, and strength,
differ from one another only by small increments — they do not possess supersensory vision.
(Nibandh 9)

children.text: prājño 'pi ca naraḥ sūkṣmānarthān draṣṭuṃ kṣamo 'pi san /
children.translated_text: Even an intelligent man, though capable of discerning subtle matters,
does not transcend his own kind, nor does he surpass others [by a supersensory leap].
The perception that operates for one who dwells in a single room
has its capacity confined to that room alone, not extending to another room.
And those objects that are separated by vast distances — by lands, mountains, and oceans,
and those that are separated by different seasons, continents, and regions — who could perceive them while being right here?

body.text: atra varṣaḥ kālaviśeṣaḥ /
body.translated_text: Here, '<s>varṣa</s>' means a particular time-period.

children.translated_text: Thus, in the examination of the sciences, a great degree of excellence is observed,
but knowledge of another science is not established merely by that alone.
Having mastered grammar, one's intellect is drawn far into the distinction between correct and incorrect words,
but it is not thereby drawn into the determination of constellations, lunar days, and eclipses.
Even one greatly skilled in astronomy, regarding eclipses of the sun and moon and the like,
is not competent to know the correctness of initial word-forms and the like.
Likewise, even one possessing exceptional knowledge of the <s>Vedas</s>, <s>Itihāsas</s> (epics), and the like,
is not capable of directly perceiving heaven, deities, or <s>apūrva</s> (the unseen merit of ritual action).
One who, by jumping upward into the sky, travels a distance of ten arm-lengths,
is not able to go a <s>yojana</s> (league), even by a hundred repetitions of practice.
Therefore, even by knowledge that is excellent and far-reaching,
one can know only somewhat more, but not what is beyond the senses.

body.text: iti //
body.translated_text: Thus it is said.

body.text: pratyakṣasūtre tu kāśikākāraḥ paramatamāśaṅkyāha, tanna, avagataviṣayatvād bhāvanāyāḥ / na cākasmādavagaterūtpattiḥ saṃbhavati / sarvotpattimatāṃ kāraṇavattvāt / atha pramāṇāntarāvagataṃ bhāvyate / kiṃ bhāvanayā / tata eva tatsiddheḥ / kiṃ ca tatpramāṇam / na tāvadanumānaṃ dharmādharmayoḥ pūrvamagrahaṇena tadvayāptaliṅgasaṃvedanāsaṃbhavāt / jagadvaividhyārthāpatterapi hi kimapi kāraṇamastīti etāvadunnīyate / na tu kaścidviśeṣaḥ / na cānirdiṣṭaviśeṣaviṣayā bhāvanā bhavati / yogaśāstreṣvapi hi viśeṣā eva dhyeyatayopadiśyante /
body.translated_text: However, in the <s>Pratyakṣasūtra</s>, the author of the <s>Kāśikā</s>, raising the opponent's objection, says: 'That is not so, because <s>bhāvanā</s> (meditative cultivation) has a [previously] apprehended object as its domain. And the arising of cognition cannot occur without a cause, since everything that arises possesses a cause. Now, if what is cultivated was already apprehended by another <s>pramāṇa</s> (means of knowledge), then what is the use of <s>bhāvanā</s>? — since the result is already established by that very [<s>pramāṇa</s>]. Moreover, what is that <s>pramāṇa</s>? It is certainly not inference, because without prior apprehension of <s>dharma</s> (merit) and <s>adharma</s> (demerit), there can be no cognition of a mark pervaded by those two. Even from the inference of the duality of the world (<s>jagadvaividhya</s>), only this much is derived: that there exists some cause — but no specific determination. And <s>bhāvanā</s> cannot have an object whose specifics are unspecified. For even in the treatises on <s>Yoga</s>, only specific objects are taught as objects of meditation,

body.text: dhyeya ātmā prabhuryo 'sau hṛdi dīpa iva sthitaḥ /
body.translated_text: 'The self is to be meditated upon — the Lord who dwells in the heart like a lamp,'

body.text: ityādibhiḥ /
body.translated_text: and so forth.

body.text: āga(ma)mānāttarhi avagataṃ bhāvayiṣyate / yadi pramāṇāttadā tata evāvagateḥ / kiṃ bhāvanayā / hānopādānārthaṃ hi vastu jijñāsyate / te ca tata eva siddhe (#Nibandh 10#) iti vyarthā bhāvanā / kāruṇiko 'pi hi dharmāgamāneva śiṣyebhyo vyācakṣīta / na bhāvanābhedamanubhavet /
body.translated_text: If you say that what is apprehended through scripture (<s>āgama</s>) will be cultivated through <s>bhāvanā</s> — if it is already a valid means of knowledge, then apprehension is already obtained from that alone. What use is <s>bhāvanā</s>? For a thing is investigated for the purpose of adoption and avoidance, and if those are already established from that [scripture] alone, (Nibandh 10) then <s>bhāvanā</s> is purposeless. Even a compassionate teacher would simply expound the scriptures on <s>dharma</s> to the students — he would not prescribe the practice of meditative cultivation.

body.text: atha vipralambhabhūyiṣṭhatvādāgamānāṃ pramāṇamāgamo na veti vicikitsamāno bhāvanayā jijñāsate / tanna / tato 'pi tadasiddheḥ / bhāvanāvalapariniṣpannamapi jñānamanāśvasanīyārthameva / abhūtasyāpi bhāvyamānasyāparokṣārthavat prakāśanāt / yathā hi tairevoktam
body.translated_text: If you say that one who doubts whether scripture, being largely deceptive, is a valid means of knowledge or not, investigates through <s>bhāvanā</s> — that is not so, because even thereby the matter is not established. Even cognition brought to completion by the power of <s>bhāvanā</s> has an unreliable content, because even what is unreal, when cultivated, appears as if directly present. As they themselves have said:

children.translated_text: Therefore, whether real or unreal, whatever is intensely cultivated,
when <s>bhāvanā</s> reaches its completion, that appears vividly — like the fruit of a wish-fulfilling tree.

body.text: api ca bhāvanābalajamapramāṇam / gṛhītagrahaṇāt / yāvadeva hi gṛhītaṃ tāvadeva bhāvanayā viṣayīkriyate / mātrayāpyadhikaṃ na bhāvanā gocarayati / yogābhyāsāhitasaṃskārapāṭavanimittā hi smṛtireva bhāvaneti gīyate / sā ca na pramāṇamiti sthitameva / na ca taduttarakālaṃ sākṣātkārijñānamudetīti pramāṇamasti / indriyasannikarṣamantareṇārthasākṣātkārasya kvacidadarśanāt / yogināṃ dharmādharmayoraparokṣapratibhāsaṃ jñānaṃ nāsti, indriyasannikarṣābhāvādasmadādivat //
body.translated_text: Moreover, what arises from the power of <s>bhāvanā</s> is not a <s>pramāṇa</s> (valid cognition), because it is [merely] the apprehension of what was already apprehended. For <s>bhāvanā</s> makes its object precisely and only what was already apprehended — it does not bring even the slightest additional [content] into its scope. For what is celebrated as <s>bhāvanā</s> is merely memory (<s>smṛti</s>), caused by the sharpening of <s>saṃskāras</s> (latent impressions) through the practice of <s>Yoga</s>. And memory is established as not being a <s>pramāṇa</s>. Nor does any <s>pramāṇa</s> exist in the form of a directly-perceiving cognition that arises subsequent to it, because nowhere is direct perception of an object observed without sensory contact. The <s>yogins</s> do not possess a cognition in which <s>dharma</s> and <s>adharma</s> appear directly, due to the absence of sensory contact — just like us ordinary persons.

body.text: vācaspatistu kaṇikāyāmāha / satyaṃ śrutānumānagocaracāriṇī bhāvanā viśadābhajñānaheturiti nāvajānīmahe / kintu yadviṣayajātaṃ tadeva viśadapratipattigocaraḥ / na jātu rūpabhāvanāprakarṣo rasaviṣayavijñānavaiśadyāya kalpate /
body.translated_text: <s>Vācaspati</s> [<s>Miśra</s>], however, says in the <s>Kāṇikā</s>: 'It is true — we do not disregard the fact that <s>bhāvanā</s>, which operates in the domain of scripture and inference, is a cause of vivid cognition. However, the category of objects [of that vivid cognition] is exactly the same [category] that is the domain of vivid apprehension. Never does the excellence of cultivating form-objects serve to produce vividness of cognition concerning taste-objects.'

body.text: nanu na viṣayāntaravaiśadyahetubhāvaṃ bhāvanāyāḥ saṃgirāmahe / kintu śrutānumānaviṣayavaiśadyahetutāmeva / tadviṣayaśca samastavastunairātmyamiti tadbhāvanāprakarṣaḥ samastavastunairātmyaṃ viśadayan samastavastuviśadatāmantareṇa tadanupapatteḥ samastavastuvaiśadyamāvahatītyuktam /
body.translated_text: Objection: We do not maintain that <s>bhāvanā</s> causes vividness with respect to a different domain of objects. Rather, we maintain only that it causes vividness with respect to the very objects of scripture and inference. And the object of those is the selflessness (<s>nairātmya</s>) of all things. Therefore, the excellence of cultivating that — making vivid the selflessness of all things — necessarily brings about vividness regarding all things, since without vividness regarding all things, [the vividness of their selflessness] would be impossible. Thus it has been said.

body.text: satyamuktam / ayuktaṃ tu tat / tathā hi nāgamānumānagocaratvaṃ nirātmanāṃ vastubhedānāṃ paramārthasatām / nahi te eteṣāmanyanivṛttimātrāvagāhinī paramārthasatsvalakṣaṇaṃ gocarayitumarhataḥ / nāpi tadviṣayā bhāvanā / tadagrāhyamapi svalakṣaṇaṃ tadadhyavaseyatayā tadviṣaya iti tadyonirapi bhāvanā tadviṣayeti tatprakarṣastadvaiśadyaheturiti cet / na / tadadhyavaseyasyāpi paramārthasatvābhāvāt / tathā hi yadanumānena gṛhyate yaccādhyavasīyate te dve apyanyanivṛttī, na vastunī / svalakṣaṇāvagāhitve 'bhilāpasaṃsargayogyapratibhāsānupapatteḥ //
body.translated_text: Indeed, well said — but it is unjustified. For the individual entities that are selfless, which are ultimately real, are not within the domain of scripture and inference. For these [means of knowledge], which apprehend only the exclusion of what is other (<s>anyāpoha</s>), cannot bring within their scope the <s>svalakṣaṇa</s> (unique particular) that is ultimately real. Nor is <s>bhāvanā</s> directed at that [particular]. If you say that the <s>svalakṣaṇa</s>, though not apprehended by those [means], is their object insofar as it is determined (<s>adhyavasita</s>) by them, and so <s>bhāvanā</s> too, being derived from them, has that as its object, and its excellence is a cause of vividness regarding that — no, because even what is so determined lacks ultimate reality. For what is apprehended by inference and what is determined are both merely exclusions of what is other (<s>anyāpoha</s>) — not real things. [This is] because if they apprehended the <s>svalakṣaṇa</s>, the appearance as fit for verbal designation could not be accounted for.

body.text: mā bhūttayoḥ svalakṣaṇaṃ viṣayaḥ / tatprabhavabhāvanāprakarṣaparyantajanmanastu (#Nibandh 11#) viśadābhasya cetaso bhaviṣyati / kāminīvikalpaprabhavabhāvanāprakarṣādiva kāmāturasya kāminīsvalakṣaṇasākṣātkāraḥ / karikumbhakaṭhorakucakalaśahāriṇi hariṇaśāvalolalocane campakadalāvadātagātralate lāvaṇyasarasi nirantaralagnalalitadoḥkandalīmūla māliṅganamaṅgane preyasitare prayaccha / sañjīvaya jīviteśvari, patito 'smi tava caraṇanalinayoritivacanakāyaceṣṭayorupalabdheḥ / asti ca vikalpāvikalpayoḥ kathañcit samānaviṣayateti nātiprasaṅga iti cet / satyam / saṃbhavatyayamanubhavo na punarasyārthe prāmāṇyasaṃbhavaḥ / atadutpatteratadātmanastadavyabhicāraniyamāyogāt / atādātmyaṃ cārthasya vijñānādatirekāt / anatireke 'pi ca vijñānānāmanyonyasya bhedādatādātmyāt / ekasya vijñānasyetaravijñānavedanānupapatteḥ / vijñānasvalakṣaṇaikatvābhyupagame ca tannityamekamadvitīyaṃ brahmābhyasanīyamiti kṣaṇikanairātmyābhyāsābhyupagamo dattajalāñjaliḥ prasajyeta / tanna tādātmyāttasyāvyabhicāraḥ / nāpi tatkāryatvāt / bhāvanāprakarṣakāryaṃ khalvetanna viṣayakāryam / yadyucyeta pāramparyeṇa tatkāryamanumānavat / yathā hi vahnisvalakṣaṇāddhūmasvalakṣaṇam / tato dhūmānubhavastato dahana vikalpaḥ, tataścānumānamutpannamiti pāramparyeṇa vahnipratibandhāt prāpakaṃ ca vahnerdāhapākakāriṇaḥ tathedamapi anumānajanitabhāvanāprakarṣaparyantajaṃ pāramparyeṇārthaprasūta tayā tadavyabhicāraniyamāttatra pramāṇamiti / tat kimanumānena vahniṃ vyavasthāpya bhāvayato yadvahniviṣayamativiśadavijñānaṃ tatpramāṇamiti / omiti brubāṇasya parvatanitambārohaṇe satīndriyasannikarṣajanmano dahanavijñānasya bhāvanādhipatya viśadābhavijñānena saha saṃvādaniyamaprasaṅgaḥ / visaṃvādaśca bahulamupalabhyate / lakṣaṇayogini ca vyabhicārasaṃbhave tallakṣaṇameva bādhitamiti viśadābhamapi prātibhamiva saṃśayākrāntamapramāṇam / tadbhāvanāyā bhūtārthatvaṃ na tajjaviśadābha vijñānaprāmāṇyahetuḥ, vyabhicārāt / evañca prāsarpakasyeva saktukarkarīprāptimūlalābhamanorathaparamparāhito dvaviṇasaṃbhārasākṣātkārastathāgatasya nirātmakasamastavastusākṣātkāra ityāpatitam / sarvārthavastubhāvanāparikarmitacittasantānavartivijñānaṃ pratyālambanapratyayatvamarthamātrasya /
body.translated_text: Granted, let the <s>svalakṣaṇa</s> not be the object of those [means of knowledge]. But the vivid consciousness born at the culmination of the excellence of <s>bhāvanā</s> derived from them will have it as its object — just as a person consumed by desire, through the excellence of <s>bhāvanā</s> derived from conceptual imagination about a woman, has a direct perception of the woman's <s>svalakṣaṇa</s>. [As when one cries:] 'O beloved, dearer than life, whose pitcher-like breasts rival the frontal globes of an elephant in hardness, whose eyes are as restless as those of a young deer, whose body is a creeper pale as <s>campaka</s> petals, who is a lake of loveliness — with the beautiful vine of your arm eternally clinging at its root, embrace me! O mistress of my life, revive me! I have fallen at your lotus-feet!' — for such [vivid experience] is observed in both words, bodily gestures, and action. And since there is some commonality of object between conceptual and non-conceptual cognition, there is no overextension [of the argument]. Objection accepted — this experience is possible, but its validity with respect to the object is not possible. Because it does not arise from that [object], is not identical in nature with that, and therefore cannot have an invariable non-deviation from that. And the non-identity of the object with cognition follows from the [object's] being other than cognition. And even if there were no otherness, still, since cognitions differ from one another, there is non-identity [between any cognition and its object]. For one cognition cannot be experienced by another cognition. And if one were to accept the unity of the <s>svalakṣaṇa</s> of cognition, then what is to be cultivated would be the eternal, singular, non-dual <s>Brahman</s> — and the accepted practice of momentariness and selflessness (<s>kṣaṇika-nairātmya</s>) would have to be abandoned. Therefore, it is not the case that non-deviation [of <s>bhāvanā</s>-born cognition from its object] follows from identity [with the object]. Nor from being its effect. For this [vivid cognition] is the effect of the excellence of <s>bhāvanā</s>, not the effect of the object. If you say it is the effect of the object indirectly, like inference — for just as from the <s>svalakṣaṇa</s> of fire arises the <s>svalakṣaṇa</s> of smoke, from that the experience of smoke, from that the conceptual cognition of fire, and from that arises inference — so by indirect connection with fire, [inference] is valid regarding fire that burns and cooks; similarly, this [cognition] born at the culmination of the excellence of <s>bhāvanā</s> generated by inference, being indirectly derived from the object, through invariable non-deviation from it, is a <s>pramāṇa</s> regarding it — then is it the case that the extremely vivid cognition about fire, arising in one who, having ascertained fire through inference, then cultivates it, is a <s>pramāṇa</s>? If one says 'yes,' then when one actually climbs the mountainside and sensory contact arises, the consequent perceptual cognition of fire would have to be invariably concordant with the vivid cognition born under the dominion of <s>bhāvanā</s>. And discordance is frequently observed. And when deviation is possible in what possesses the defining mark, that very defining mark is contradicted — therefore, even a vivid appearance, like an intuitive flash, when beset by doubt, is not a <s>pramāṇa</s>. Thus, even if <s>bhāvanā</s> deals with real content, this is not a ground for the validity of the vivid cognition born from it, because of deviation. And so, just as the sequence of fantasies of the mendicant — rooted in the acquisition of a bag of barley flour, dreaming of ever-increasing wealth — culminates in the 'direct perception' of a pile of riches, so the <s>Tathāgata</s>'s 'direct perception' of all selfless things [is equally groundless]. This is what follows. The cognition occurring in a mental continuum refined by the cultivation of all objects and things takes merely the object as its <s>ālambanapratyaya</s> (object-condition).

body.text: tathā ca tadutpatteḥ tadavyabhicāraniyama iti cet / na / arthasya hyālambanapratyayatvavijñānaṃ pratīndriyāpekṣatvena vyāptam / taccāsmātsvaviruddhopalabdhyā (#Nibandh 12#) vyāvartamānamālambanapratyayatāmapyarthasya nivartayati / na khalvindhanaviśeṣo dhūmaheturiti vināpi dahanaṃ sahasreṇāpi saṃskārairdhūbhamādhate / tadādhāne vā samastakārya hetvanumānocchedaprasaṅgaḥ / bhāvanāyāśca bhūtārthāyā arthānapekṣāyā eva viśadavijñānajananasāmarthyamupalabdha kāmāturādivartinyā iti bhūtārthāpi tannirapekṣaiva samartheti nārthasyālambanapratyayatvaṃ śakyāvagamam / api ca ālambanapratyayā api ta evāsya kṣaṇā yujyante, ye tasya purastāttanā avyavadhānāstathā ca ta evāsya grāhyā na punaḥ pūrvatarāḥ / tatkālā anāgatāśceti na sarvaviṣayatā / atha dṛśyamānā dhātutrayaparyāpannāḥ prāṇabhṛto janmāntaraparivartopāttātītānāgataskandhakadambakopādānopādeyātmāna iti taddarśanaṃ dṛśyamānatādātmyena tadviśeṣaṇatayātītānāgatamapi gocarayati / na cāsmadādidarśanasyāpi tathātvaprasaṅgaḥ, rāgādimalāvṛtatvāt / tasya ca bhagavato nirmṛṣṭanikhilakleśopakleśamalaṃ vijñānamanāvaraṇaṃ paritaḥ pradyotamāna mālambanapratyayaṃ sarvākāraṃ gocarayet / tasya ca sākṣāt paramparayā ca kathañcit sarveṇa saṃbandhād deśkālaviprakīrṇavastumātraviśiṣṭasvabhāvatayā tathaiva gocarayet / na caitat sarvagrahaṇamantareṇeti sarvaviṣayamasya vijñānamanāvaraṇaṃ siddham /
body.translated_text: If you say that since it arises from that [object-condition], there is an invariable non-deviation from it — no. For the object-conditionality of the object with respect to cognition is pervaded by dependence on the senses. And that [sensory dependence], being excluded from the present case by the observation of something contradictory to it, (Nibandh 12) also excludes the object-conditionality of the object. For a particular kind of fuel is the cause of smoke — without fire, even a thousand <s>saṃskāras</s> (latent impressions) do not produce smoke. Or if they did, the consequence would be the destruction of all causal inferences. And since <s>bhāvanā</s>, even when dealing with real content, is observed to have the capacity to generate vivid cognition independently of the object — as in the case of one consumed by desire — even when dealing with real content, it is equally capable without the object. Therefore, the object-conditionality of the object cannot be ascertained. Moreover, the only moments that are justified as object-conditions for this [cognition] are those that are immediately preceding it without interruption — and those alone are its apprehended objects, not earlier ones. And those of the same time are future [at the moment of cognition] — therefore there is no all-encompassing scope. If you say that the visible beings, encompassed within the three time-periods (<s>dhātutraya</s>), possessing a self consisting of the aggregate-clusters (<s>skandha-kadambaka</s>) of past and future acquired through the cycle of rebirths, are such that their perception — by its identity with what is being perceived — also encompasses past and future as qualifications of them; and that this does not apply to our [ordinary] perception because it is obscured by the impurities of passion and the like; but that the cognition of the Blessed One, cleansed of all impurities of <s>kleśa</s> (afflictions) and <s>upakleśa</s> (secondary afflictions), being unobstructed and luminous in all directions, would encompass as object-condition every aspect — and since it is somehow connected with everything, either directly or indirectly, it would apprehend all objects scattered across space and time as having a nature qualified by all things; and that this cannot occur without the apprehension of everything — therefore his cognition, being unobstructed, is established as having all things as its object.

body.text:
tadanupapannam / vicārāsahatvāt / tathā hīyamālambanapratyayasya sarvaviśiṣṭātmatā bhāvikī na vā / bhāvikī cet / na tāvatsarvasminnālambanapratyaye caikā saṃbhavati / ekasyānekavṛttitvānupapatteḥ / nānā cet / ālambanapratyayāśca sarve ceti tattvam / tathā ca na saṃbandha iti na tadgrahaṇe sarvagrahaṇam / vikalpāropitatayā tvavikalpakaṃ samastavastuviṣayaṃ sarvatra pratīyata iti subhāṣitam / svālambanapratyayamātragocaramevāvikalpakaṃ samastavastuviśiṣṭālambanādhyavasāyajananam / tenādhyavasāyānugatavyāpāramavikalpakamapi samastavastuviṣayaṃ bhavati /
yadāha
body.translated_text: That is untenable, because it cannot withstand critical analysis. For this nature of the object-condition as qualified by everything is either intrinsic or not. If intrinsic, then first, a single [nature] cannot belong to every object-condition, since it is impossible for one thing to have multiple instantiations. If they are many, then 'the object-conditions are all [distinct]' — that is the truth. And in that case, there is no connection [between them], so the apprehension of one does not entail the apprehension of all. However, it is well said that non-conceptual cognition is experienced everywhere as having all things as its object through what is superimposed by conceptual thought. Non-conceptual cognition, having as its scope merely its own object-condition, generates a determination (<s>adhyavasāya</s>) whose support is qualified by all things. Therefore, even non-conceptual cognition, whose operation follows determination, has all things as its object.

body.text: vyavasyantīkṣaṇādeva sarvākārānmahādhiyaḥ /
body.translated_text: As it is said: 'Those of great intellect determine all aspects from a single moment.'

body.text: iti cet / atha katipayavastvālambanānubhavasya kutastya eṣa mahimā yataḥ samastavastvavasāya iti / rāgādyāvaraṇavigamāditi cet / tarhi yathāvad vastūni paśyet / na punarasmādapārthatvamasyeti / tadayuktaṃ vikalpanirmāṇakauśalamasya yujyeta / tattvāvarakatā hi sulabhamalānāṃ kleśādīnāṃ na punarvikalpanirmāṇapratibandhatā / tasmād bhāvanāprakarṣamātrajatvāt, arthāvyabhicāraniyamābhāvāt, viśadābhamapi saṃśayākrāntatvādapramāṇamapratyakṣaṃ ceti sāmpratam //
body.translated_text: If so — then whence comes this greatness of the experience resting upon only a few objects, such that it [claims to] determine all objects? If [you reply]: from the removal of the obscurations of <s>rāga</s> (attachment) and so forth — then it should perceive things as they truly are. And then there would be no incorrectness on this account. But that is untenable: what would be appropriate for it is skill in constructing <s>vikalpas</s> (conceptual constructions). For it is easily [shown] that the <s>kleśas</s> (afflictions) and so forth, which are stains, have the nature of obscuring reality; they do not, however, obstruct the construction of <s>vikalpas</s>. Therefore, since it arises merely from the culmination of <s>bhāvanā</s> (meditative cultivation), since there is no necessity of non-deviation from objects, and since even though it appears vivid it is pervaded by doubt — it is neither a <s>pramāṇa</s> (valid means of knowledge) nor <s>pratyakṣa</s> (perception). This is correct.

body.text:
(#Nibandh 13#)
yadapi sadarthaprakāśanaṃ buddheḥ svabhāvo 'sadarthatvaṃ cāgantukamiti, asati bādhake sadarthatvameveti, tadayuktam / anumitabhāvitavahniviṣayaviśadābhajñāna prāmāṇyaprasaṅgāt tadvidhasya kvacid bādhadarśanādaprāmāṇyamihāpi samānam / anyatrābhiniveśāt / tadiha yadi viśadābhavijñānahetutvaṃ bhāvanāyā viśeṣaṇatrayayogena sādhyate, tataḥ siddhasādhanam / bhavatu tathāgatastathābhūtavijñānavān / na tvetadvijñānamasya pratyakṣamapramāṇatvāt / tathā cāpakṣadharmatayā hetorasiddhatā / prasiddhadharmaṇo dharmiṇo 'jijñāsitaviśeṣatayā anumeyatvābhāvāt / atha pratyakṣavijñānahetutā bhāvanāyāḥ paraṃ pratyasiddhā sādhyate, tathā ca sati sādhyaviparyayavyāpterviruddhatā hetoḥ, viśeṣaṇatrayavatyā api bhāvanāyā viśadābhabhrāntavijñānajanakatvāt / dṛṣṭāntasya ca sādhyahīnatvāt / yadā ca bhūtārthabhāvanājanitatve 'pi nāsya prāmāṇyamabhūtārthatvāt, tadā yaducyate,
body.translated_text:
(#Nibandh 13#)
As for [the claim] that the illumination of real objects is the intrinsic nature of cognition, and unreality is adventitious, and that in the absence of a sublating cognition, reality alone [prevails] — that is untenable. Because the absurd consequence would follow that the vivid cognition whose object is fire that has been inferred and cultivated [in meditation] would be a <s>pramāṇa</s>; and since sublation of such [cognition] is observed in some cases, its being a non-<s>pramāṇa</s> applies here equally — [merely] due to attachment elsewhere. Therefore, if the <s>bhāvanā</s>'s being the cause of vivid cognition is to be proved with the threefold qualification, then it is <s>siddhasādhana</s> (proving what is already established). Let the <s>Tathāgata</s> possess such cognition — yet this cognition of his is not <s>pratyakṣa</s>, since it is not a <s>pramāṇa</s>. And thus, there is the failure of the <s>hetu</s> (reason) due to non-establishment as a property of the <s>pakṣa</s> (thesis). Since the <s>dharmin</s> (subject) whose properties are well-known, being of an unexamined particular nature, is not an object of inference. If, on the other hand, it is the <s>bhāvanā</s>'s being the cause of <s>pratyakṣa</s>-cognition that is being proved — which is unestablished for the opponent — then, since the <s>hetu</s> is pervaded by the opposite of the <s>sādhya</s> (probandum), the <s>hetu</s> is <s>viruddha</s> (contradictory), because even <s>bhāvanā</s> endowed with the threefold qualification produces vivid but erroneous cognition. And the <s>dṛṣṭānta</s> (example) is devoid of the <s>sādhya</s>. And when, even though [the cognition] is born from the cultivation of a real object, it is not a <s>pramāṇa</s> because its object is unreal — then as for the verse that states:

children.translated_text: "For a cognition whose intrinsic nature is a real object, free from defect,
There is no sublation by contraries, even with effort, due to its partiality [toward truth]."

body.text: iti / tadanupapannam / bhūtārthatve 'pi hi buddheḥ tatpakṣapātitā bhūtārthaiḥ pratipakṣairbādho na bhavet / abhūtārthā tviyaṃ sātmībhāva māpannāpyātmātmīyadṛṣṭiriva saṃbhavadbādhā / tasmāt pratipakṣavibṛddhimātram / na tvātyantikī vivṛddhiḥ saṃbhavati / yayā samūlakāṣaṃ kaṣitā doṣā na punarudbhaviṣyanti / ataevāsthirāśrayatve 'pi apunaryatnāpekṣatve 'pi asya nātyantikī niṣṭhā saṃbhavati / ātmātmīyadṛśa iva virodhipratyayasaṃbhavāt / tatsaṃbhavaścābhūtārthatvāt / śrutānumitaviṣayaṃ tu pratyakṣaṃ na saṃbhavatyeva / tayoḥ parokṣarūpāvagāhitvāt / pratyakṣasya ca tadviparītatvāt / tadgatabhūtābhūtārthānuvidhāyitvena svaviṣaye śrutānumānajñānāpekṣayā prāmāṇyānupapatteśva //
body.translated_text: That is untenable. For even though the cognition is of a real object, its partiality [toward truth] — [meaning] sublation by real-object contraries would not occur. But this [cognition], being of an unreal object, even though it has become assimilated [through practice], is like the view of self and mine — [for it] the possibility of sublation exists. Therefore, there is merely an increase of the antidote; but an absolute increase is not possible — by which the <s>doṣas</s> (faults) would be torn out root and branch, never to arise again. For this very reason, even though the support is not unstable, and even though renewed effort is not required, an absolute finality is not possible for this [cognition], because of the possibility of a contrary cognition, as with the view of self and mine. And that possibility [of a contrary cognition] is due to [its] being of an unreal object. But <s>pratyakṣa</s> whose object is what has been heard or inferred is simply impossible, since those two [hearing and inference] apprehend what is of a non-perceptual form, while <s>pratyakṣa</s> is of the opposite nature. Since [<s>pratyakṣa</s>] conforms to the real and unreal objects contained in those [hearing and inference], its being a <s>pramāṇa</s> with respect to its own object, in comparison with the cognitions born of <s>śruti</s> (scripture) and <s>anumāna</s> (inference), is untenable.

body.text:
tat siddhametat bhūtārthabhāvanāprakarṣaparyantajavijñānamapratyakṣamarthe 'prāmāṇyāt /
yadapramāṇaṃ tadapratyakṣamarthe /
yathā kāmāturasya kāminīvijñānam /
apramāṇaṃ ca tat /
nitāntaviśadābhatve sati bhāvanā (prakarṣa) jatvāt /
yannitāntaviśadābhatve sati bhāvanāprakarṣajaṃ vijñānaṃ tadapramāṇam /
body.translated_text:
Therefore, it is established that the cognition born at the culmination of the cultivation of a real object is not <s>pratyakṣa</s>, since it is not a <s>pramāṇa</s> with respect to its object.
That which is not a <s>pramāṇa</s> is not <s>pratyakṣa</s> with respect to its object —
just as the cognition of a woman by a man tormented by desire.
And that [cognition born of meditation] is not a <s>pramāṇa</s>,
because, while being extremely vivid, it is born from the culmination of <s>bhāvanā</s> (meditative cultivation).
That cognition which, while being extremely vivid, is born from the culmination of <s>bhāvanā</s> — that is not a <s>pramāṇa</s>.

body.text:
(#Nibandh 14#)
yathānumitabhāvitavahniviśadavijñānamiti / samānahetujatvaṃ samānarūpatayā vyāptam /
yadāha
body.translated_text:
(#Nibandh 14#)
Just as the vivid cognition of fire that has been inferred and cultivated [in meditation]. Being born from the same type of cause is pervaded by being of the same type [as the example].
As he states:

body.text: tadatadrūpiṇo bhāvāstadatadrūpahetujāḥ /
body.translated_text: "Things that are of such-and-such a form are born from causes of such-and-such a form;

body.text: iti / tadasya prāmāṇyaṃ nivartamānaṃ tulyahetujatvamapi nivartayati / na caiṣa bhūtārthabhāvanāprakarṣaparyantajo 'nindriyasannikṛṣṭānumitabhāvitavahnivaiśadye ca nirātmakasamastavastuvaiśadye ca viśiṣyate / na ca rāgādyāvaraṇaviraho viśeṣaḥ / na khalvete kambalādibadāvarakā vijñānasya / kiṃ tu tadākṣiptamanā vividhaviṣayabhedatṛṣṇādiparipluto na śaknoti bbāvayitumiti bhāvanādaramātra eva tadvirahopayogaḥ / asti cehāpi śiśirabharasaṃbhṛta jaḍimamantharatarakāyakāṇḍasyānumitavahnibhāvanābhiyoga iti na hetu bhedataḥ pratibandhasiddhiḥ / na caikapārthivāṇusamavāyikāraṇajanmabhirabhinnauṣṇyāpekṣaikavahnisaṃyogāsamavāyikāraṇairgandharasarūpasparśairnānāsvabhāvairvyabhicāraḥ / sāmarthyavaicitryādekatve 'pi pārthivasya paramāṇoḥ / tadvaicitryaṃ ca kāryavaicitryopalambhāt / tacca nityasamavetaṃ nityam, kāraṇasāmarthyaprakrameṇa ca pārthivāvayavini kārye jāyata iti avadātam / pariśiṣṭaṃ tu granthavyākhyānasamaye vyākhyāsyāmaḥ / tadāstāṃ tāvat //
body.translated_text: [and things] not of such-and-such a form [are born from causes] not of such-and-such a form." Thus, when this [cognition's] being a <s>pramāṇa</s> is negated, its being born from the same type of cause is also negated. And this [yogic cognition], born at the culmination of the cultivation of a real object, is not superior to the vividness [of the cognition] of inferred and cultivated fire that is not in contact with the sense-organs, nor to the vividness [of cognition] of all selfless objects. Nor is the removal of the obscurations of <s>rāga</s> (attachment) and so forth a distinguishing factor. For these [<s>rāga</s> etc.] are not obscurations of cognition like a blanket and so forth. Rather, the mind, drawn by them, flooded with craving for various object-distinctions, is unable to cultivate [meditation] — hence the removal of those [obscurations] is useful only for the enthusiasm of cultivation. And here too there exists the exertion of cultivating inferred fire by one whose bodily frame is sluggish and slow, weighed down by the mass of cold — therefore the invariable connection is not established from a difference in the <s>hetu</s>. Nor is there deviation through smells, tastes, colors, and touches — which are of various natures — born from the <s>samavāyikāraṇa</s> (inherent cause) of a single earth-atom and requiring a single fire-contact as their <s>asamavāyikāraṇa</s> (non-inherent cause) possessing undifferentiated heat — because of the diversity of capacities even in a single earth-atom. And that diversity [of capacities] is known from the observation of diversity in effects. And that [diversity], being eternally inherent, is permanent; and it arises in the earth-composed effect through the progression of causal capacity — this is well established. The remainder we shall explain at the time of commenting on the text. So let that be for now.
