body.text: trilocanastu nyāyaprakīrṇake prāha / iha kila duḥkhasamudayanirodhamārgākhyānyāryāṇāṃ satyāni catvāri / teṣāṃ satyānāṃ svarūpasākṣātkārijñānaṃ yogipratyakṣam / tatra duḥkhaṃ phalabhūtāḥ pañcopādānaskandhāḥ / tacca svarūpato jñātavyam / ta eva hetubhūtāḥ samudayaḥ / sa ca prahātavyaḥ / niḥkleśāvasthā cittasya nirodhaḥ / sa ca sākṣātkartavyaḥ / tadavasthāprāptiheturnairātmyakṣaṇikatvādyākāraścittaviśeṣo mārgaḥ / sa ca bhāvayitavya iti saugatamatam /
body.translated_text: Now, <s>Trilocana</s> states in the <s>Nyāyaprakīrṇaka</s>: Here, it is said, there are four truths of the <s>Āryas</s> (noble ones), called <s>duḥkha</s> (suffering), <s>samudaya</s> (origination), <s>nirodha</s> (cessation), and <s>mārga</s> (path). The cognition that directly apprehends the own-nature of those truths is <s>yogipratyakṣa</s> (yogic perception). Therein, <s>duḥkha</s> is the five <s>upādānaskandhas</s> (aggregates of clinging), which are results. And that is to be known in its own-nature. Those very [aggregates], as causes, are <s>samudaya</s>. And that is to be abandoned. The state of the mind free from <s>kleśas</s> (afflictions) is <s>nirodha</s>. And that is to be directly realized. The mental state that is the cause of attaining that condition — characterized by the aspects of <s>nairātmya</s> (selflessness), <s>kṣaṇikatva</s> (momentariness), and so forth — is the <s>mārga</s>. And that is to be cultivated. Such is the <s>Saugata</s> (Buddhist) doctrine.

body.text: atrocyate / mārgastāvat pramāṇapariśuddho na bhavatītyuktaṃ prāk / ato 'bhūtaviṣayasya vikalpasyābhyāsādasatyārthavijñānaṃ syānna saṃvādi / api ca pramāṇapariśuddhamārgavādo śākyaḥ pramāṇaṃ pṛṣṭaḥ san satvākhyaliṅgajaṃ vikalpaṃ brūyāt / tato yāvadvikalpena darśitarūpaṃ tatsarvamasat / śabdasaṃsṛṣṭatvāt / tasmiṃśca bhāvyamāne sattve bhāvakasya vikalpakasya bhāvanopahite viśadābhatve śabdasaṃsṛṣṭagrāhyanimittaṃ vikalpakatvaṃ nivartate / tadvyāvṛttau grāhyamapi śabdasaṃsṛṣṭaṃ nivartate / ato nirvikalpakamapi yogijñānaṃ nirviṣayaṃ prasaktam / yattu pāramārthikaṃ vastvātmakaṃ na (#Nibandh 15#) tatpramāṇapariśuddham / śuddhau vā kiṃ bhāvanayā / bhāvyasya sākṣādvijñātatvāt / na cānyasmin śabdasaṃsṛṣṭe bhāvyamāne sphuṭamanyadrūpaṃ bhavati / śokāturasyāpi niruddhendriyavyāpārasya tanayabhāvanāyāṃ mitrādipratibhāsaprasaṅgāt /
body.translated_text: To this we reply: The <s>mārga</s> (path), to begin with, is not purified by <s>pramāṇa</s> (valid means of knowledge) — this has been stated earlier. Therefore, from the repeated practice of a <s>vikalpa</s> (conceptual construction) whose object is unreal, there would arise a cognition of an unreal object — it would not be concordant [with reality]. Moreover, if a proponent of a path purified by <s>pramāṇa</s>, namely a <s>Śākya</s> (Buddhist), were asked what <s>pramāṇa</s> [establishes the path], he would cite the <s>vikalpa</s> born from the inferential mark called 'being' (<s>sattva</s>). From that, whatever form is shown by the <s>vikalpa</s>, all of that is unreal — because it is associated with words. And when that 'being' is cultivated, and the cultivator's <s>vikalpa</s> attains vividness enhanced by cultivation, the <s>vikalpatva</s> (conceptual character), whose apprehended cause is associated with words, ceases. When that [conceptuality] ceases, the apprehended object too, being associated with words, ceases. Therefore, even the non-conceptual (<s>nirvikalpaka</s>) yogic cognition is liable to be without an object. As for that which is ultimately real and of the nature of a thing — that is not purified by <s>pramāṇa</s>. Or if it is [already] purified, what need is there of <s>bhāvanā</s>? Since the object to be cultivated is directly known [already]. Nor does something else become vivid when something else — associated with words — is being cultivated. Otherwise, even for one tormented by grief, whose sense-faculties have ceased functioning, while cultivating [the image of] a son, the absurd consequence would follow that a friend and so forth would appear.

body.text: kṣaṇikatve bhāvye samāropite vāstavaṃ kṣaṇikatvameva yogivijñānapratibhāsīti cet / na / satyāsatyayorekatvābhāvātmake hi bhede 'satyabhāvane 'pi yadi satyapratibhāsaḥ, tarhi satyatanayābhyāse 'pi śabdasāmyādabhedinastanayasaṃjñakasya kasyacidaparasya svarūpapratibhāsaprasaṅgaḥ / tasmādabhūtaviṣayābhyāsaṃ nirvikalpakamapi saṃvādānna pramāṇamiti na sarvajñasiddhiḥ /
body.translated_text: If [the Buddhist objects:] when <s>kṣaṇikatva</s> (momentariness) is the object of cultivation, though superimposed, real momentariness itself appears in the yogic cognition — [we reply:] No. For in the distinction that consists in the absence of identity between the real and the unreal, even when the unreal is cultivated, if a real [object] were to appear, then even in the practice of [contemplating] a real son, due to the similarity of [the word] designation, the absurd consequence would follow that the own-form of someone else — who is non-different [in name], bearing the designation 'son' — would appear. Therefore, even a non-conceptual [cognition] born from the repeated cultivation of an unreal object is not a <s>pramāṇa</s>, since it does not accord [with reality]. Hence, the establishment of <s>sarvajñatva</s> (omniscience) is not achieved.

body.text: api ca bhāvyasya vastunaḥ punaḥ punaścetasi niveśanamabhyāsaḥ / sa ca brahmacaryeṇa tapasā sādaraṃ dīrghakālaṃ nirantaramāsevito dṛḍhabhūmirasphuṭākārasya vikalpasya sphuṭābhatvajanana iṣṭaḥ / sa kṣaṇikatvanairātmyavādinā draḍhayitumaśakyaḥ / tathā hi bhāvyagrāhī yādṛśo vikalpa utpannastādṛśa eva niranvayaṃ nirudhyate / tasmiṃśca niruddhe punaḥ punarutpadyamānaḥ pratyayastādṛśa evāpūrva utpadyate / tadanena paryāyeṇa kalpasahasre 'pi apūrvotpatteraviśeṣānna tajjanyaḥ saṃskāro 'bhyāsa utpadyate / etena viśiṣṭavijñānotpādo 'bhyāso vyākhyātaḥ / niranvayaniruddhaṃ hi pūrvapūrvavijñānaṃ kathamuttarottarāvasthāntaraṃ viśiṣṭaṃ janayet / sarvathā kramabhāvibhiḥ pratyayairavasthitameva rūpaṃ śakyaṃ saṃskartum / anavasthitaṃ tu svotpādavyayayogimātramityaviśiṣṭaṃ syāt / tasmāt pratyāvṛttibhāvyavastupratyayajaḥ saṃskāro vyutthānapratyayasaṃskāravirodhī yasyāsti tasyaivātmanaḥ prakṛṣṭo 'pi bhāvyasākṣātkāripratyayaheturitiyuktaṃ paśyāmaḥ / kiṃ ca cittamekāgraṃ vyavasthāpayituṃ vikṣepatyāgārthamabhyāso 'nuṣṭhīyate / na ca kṣaṇikavādināṃ vikṣiptaṃ cittamasti / pratyarthaniyatatayā sarvasya cittaikāgratvāt / tathā hi yadi sākāraṃ vikalpavijñānaṃ svapratibhāsaniyatatvāt ekāgrameva tat kathaṃ vikṣipyate / atha nirākāraṃ tathāpi vikalpakaṃ prati vikalpyaṃ bhinnameva / na tu sarvavikalpānāmekaṃ vikalpyamasti / tato nirākāramapi vijñānaṃ niyatālambanatvādekāgrameva, na vikṣiptam / sarvathā nāsti kṣaṇikavādināmekamanekārthamavasthitaṃ cittaṃ yadekāgraṃ kartumiṣyate / tadevamabhyāsānupapatterasarvajñavatyāṃ cittasantatau na ca vijñānaviśeṣaḥ sarvajñaḥ sidhyatīti //
body.translated_text: Moreover, <s>abhyāsa</s> (repeated practice) is the repeated installation of the object to be cultivated in the mind. And that [practice], when pursued with <s>brahmacarya</s> (celibacy), <s>tapas</s> (austerity), with care, for a long time, and without interruption, becomes firmly grounded — [and] is intended to produce vividness from a <s>vikalpa</s> whose form is indistinct. But one who propounds <s>kṣaṇikatva</s> (momentariness) and <s>nairātmya</s> (selflessness) cannot make it firm. For the <s>vikalpa</s> that apprehends the object of cultivation — exactly as it has arisen, so does it perish without any continuity. And when that has perished, the cognition that arises again and again is of exactly the same type — it arises as a new [cognition each time]. Therefore, by this process, even in a thousand <s>kalpas</s> (aeons), since there is no distinction from the [always] novel arising, no <s>saṃskāra</s> (dispositional imprint) born from that — which is <s>abhyāsa</s> — arises. By this, the [opponent's notion of] <s>abhyāsa</s> as the production of a distinguished cognition is refuted. For how can a prior cognition that has perished without any continuity produce a subsequent state that is distinguished? In every case, only an enduring form can be refined by successively arising cognitions. But what is non-enduring, being merely subject to its own arising and perishing, would remain undistinguished. Therefore, it is right, in our view, that only for one who possesses a self — in whom there exists a <s>saṃskāra</s> born from the repeated cognition of the object to be cultivated, opposing the <s>saṃskāras</s> of the waking state — can there be, even in a highly developed form, a cognition that is the cause of directly apprehending the object of cultivation. Furthermore, <s>abhyāsa</s> is undertaken for the purpose of making the mind one-pointed and abandoning distraction. But for the proponents of momentariness, there is no distracted mind — since every mind is one-pointed, being restricted to its own particular object. For if the <s>vikalpa</s>-cognition has form (<s>sākāra</s>), then, being restricted to its own appearance, it is already one-pointed — how is it distracted? If it is formless (<s>nirākāra</s>), even so, the object of conceptualization is distinct from the conceptualizer — there is no single object of conceptualization for all <s>vikalpas</s>. Therefore, even formless cognition, having a determined object, is already one-pointed, not distracted. In no way do the proponents of momentariness have a single, enduring mind attending to multiple objects that one wishes to make one-pointed. Thus, since <s>abhyāsa</s> is untenable, and since there is no distinguished cognition in a mental continuum that does not possess a [permanent] self — [therefore] the <s>sarvajña</s> (omniscient being), who is [supposedly] a distinguished cognition, is not established.

body.text: nyāyabhūṣaṇakārastvāha / sarvajñānānāṃ nirālambanatve saṃvedanamātratve ca yogītarapratyayayoḥ ko viśeṣaḥ / śuddhāśuddhatvamiti cet / bhavatu nāmaivam / tathāpi caturāryasatyādiviṣayatvamayuktam / na hi svātmamātravedanena caturāryasatyādikaṃ sākṣātkṛtamiti yuktamatiprasaṅgāt /
body.translated_text: Now the author of the <s>Nyāyabhūṣaṇa</s> says: If all cognitions of the <s>sarvajña</s> (omniscient being) are without object and consist merely in self-awareness, what distinguishes the yogic cognition from the cognitions of ordinary persons? If [you say] purity versus impurity — let it be so. Even then, [the claim of] having the four <s>Āryasatyas</s> (noble truths) and so forth as objects is untenable. For it is not reasonable that the four <s>Āryasatyas</s> and so forth are directly realized merely through self-awareness alone — otherwise there would be an absurd over-extension.

body.text:
(#Nibandh 16#)
tadākāratvena tadviṣayatvamiti cet / tat kimidānīṃ sautrāntikamatamabhyupagataṃ satyam / tathāpyatotānāgataviṣayatvaṃ katham / na hyasataḥ kaścidākāro 'sti / dṛṣṭaśrutānumitākāraśca yadi bhāvanābalataḥ spaṣṭa evāvabhāti, tathā ca satibhrāntameva yogipratyakṣaṃ syāt / avidyamānasya vidyamānākāratayā pratibhāsanāt, svapnavat / tathā(') visaṃvāditvānna bhrāntam / na / anumānajñānasya bhrāntatve 'pi avisaṃvāditvābhyupagamāt /
body.translated_text:
(#Nibandh 16#)
If [the Buddhist says:] because it has those [truths] as its aspect, it has those as its objects — then has the <s>Sautrāntika</s> position now been accepted as true? Even so, how can it have past and future objects? For what does not exist has no aspect whatsoever. And if an aspect that has been seen, heard, or inferred becomes vivid merely through the power of <s>bhāvanā</s> (cultivation), then <s>yogipratyakṣa</s> (yogic perception) would be simply erroneous — because of the appearance of what does not exist in the form of what does exist, like a dream. [If the Buddhist says:] it is not erroneous because it is non-discordant — [we reply:] No, because even <s>anumāna</s>-cognition (inferential cognition), though erroneous, is accepted as non-discordant.

body.text: atha bhrāntasyāpi saṃvāditvena prāmāṇyam / tathāpi pratyakṣalakṣaṇasyābhrāntatvaviśeṣaṇaṃ virudhyate / na cāvisaṃvāditvamapi tvanmate yuktam / yataḥ prāpyārthadarśakatvaṃ vā, pravṛttiviṣayopadarśakatvaṃ vā, avabhātādarthakriyāniṣpattirvā bhavatāmavisaṃvāditvamabhipretam / na caitadatītādyarthajñāne saṃbhavati / vartamānārthajñānasyāpi kṣaṇikatvapakṣe nopapadyata eva / tasmāt saugatānāṃ yogipratyakṣopavarṇanamayuktameveti //
body.translated_text: If [it is claimed that] even an erroneous [cognition], through its concordance, is a <s>pramāṇa</s> — even so, the qualification of non-erroneousness in the definition of <s>pratyakṣa</s> would be contradicted. Nor is non-discordance proper on your view. For your intended meaning of non-discordance is either: showing an object that leads to [successful] attainment, or: showing the object of purposeful activity, or: the accomplishment of <s>arthakriyā</s> (causal efficacy) following upon the appearance. But none of this is possible in the case of cognition of past and other [non-present] objects. And even for cognition of present objects, on the thesis of momentariness, it is simply untenable. Therefore, the description of <s>yogipratyakṣa</s> by the <s>Saugatas</s> (Buddhists) is indeed untenable.

body.text: kiṃ cedamapi vaktumucitam / yadyanumānapūrvakamartheṣu bhāvanābalajajñānamāśvāsabhājanaṃ, tadāstāṃ tāvadanumānapauruṣapratyāśā / pratyakṣeṇāpi cakṣurdahanādikaṃ gṛhītvā bhāvanāprakarṣaparyante jātaṃ sthirataraṃ tadākāravijñānaṃ syāt, yāvanna viparīta bhāvanābhiyogaparyantaḥ / astaṃ gataśca tadviṣayo 'vasthāntaraprāpto veti kathaṃ pramāṇopanītavastugocaratve 'pi saṃvādāśvāsaḥ / api ca yadā hālika eva havyāśanamanumāya bhāvanayā sphuṭayet, tadā na tadyogijñānaṃ paramārthaviṣayābhāvāditi pratyakṣāntaraprasaṅgaḥ /
body.translated_text: Is it proper to say even this? If knowledge born of the power of meditation (<s>bhāvanā</s>), preceded by inference, regarding objects is worthy of trust, then set aside the hope for the power of inference. Even having grasped [objects] such as the eye, fire, and the like through direct perception (<s>pratyakṣa</s>), the knowledge bearing their form, produced at the culmination of meditative cultivation, would remain more stable — until the culmination of cultivation of the contrary [view]. And [the object] may have ceased to exist or may have attained another state — so how can there be trust in correspondence, even when the [knowledge] concerns objects presented by a <s>pramāṇa</s> (means of valid knowledge)? Moreover, when a mere ploughman, having inferred fire, would make it vivid through meditation, then that would not be <s>yogipratyakṣa</s> (yogic perception), since it lacks a real object as its content — hence the absurd consequence of another [kind of] perception.

body.text: kiṃ ca tadyogijñānamindriyajñānādbhinnamabhinnaṃ vā / abhedapakṣe na yogijñānaṃ nāma pratyakṣeṇa bhinnamindriyajñānenaiva saṃgrahāt / na ca bhāvanopaskṛtasantānasya tathodayād bhedavyavasthā / rasāyanādisaṃskārāpekṣayāpi pratyakṣāntaravyavasthāprasaṅgāt / bhedapakṣe ca bhāvanāsaṃbhavaṃ jñānaṃ kṣaṇikasākṣātkāri / indriyajñānaṃ ca syairyagrāhīti sādhvī siddhiḥ / indriyajñānasyāpi tadavasthāyāmasthairyagrahaṇe kṛtaṃ yogijñānena / na ca tasyākasmikaḥ kṣaṇikatvāvabodhaḥ / bhāvanodbhūtavaiśadyasya hi tadbodhaḥ / na cendriyajñānasya bhāvanā / api tu manovijñāne / tāmantareṇāpi sākṣāt kriyālābhe ca bhāvanāvaiyarthyamiti kāraṇābhāvādeva sarvajñapratihatiḥ //
body.translated_text: Furthermore, is that yogic cognition different from or identical with sense-cognition? On the hypothesis of non-difference, there is no such thing as 'yogic cognition,' since it is subsumed under sense-cognition, which is not different from it. Nor can a distinction be established merely because [the cognition] arises differently in a mental continuum refined by meditation — for then the absurd consequence would follow that yet another [kind of] perception should be established with reference to refinements such as medicinal elixirs (<s>rasāyana</s>). On the hypothesis of difference, [yogic] cognition, born from meditation, directly perceives momentary [reality]; and sense-cognition grasps stability — this is a good proof. [But] if sense-cognition too, in that [yogic] state, does not grasp stability, then what need is there for yogic cognition? And its cognition of momentariness is not uncaused. For that cognition belongs to one whose clarity has arisen from meditation. And meditation does not belong to sense-cognition, but rather to mental cognition (<s>manovijñāna</s>). And if direct realization is obtained even without meditation, then meditation would be purposeless — thus, due to the absence of a cause, the refutation of omniscience is complete.

body.text: atrābhidhīyate / yattāvat sarvapadārthasaṃvedanasya kāraṇaṃ kimindriyajñānamityādi valgitaṃ tatra bhāvanābalajaṃ manovijñānameva sarvapadārthagrāhīti pañcama evāsmākaṃ pakṣaḥ / ataḥ pakṣāntarabhāvino doṣā anabhyupagamapratihatāḥ / yaccāsmadabhyupagate pañcame pakṣe dūṣaṇamuktam, anarthatvātpratyakṣaśabdasya, tasya ca bhāvanābalābalambinopya nakṣajatvānnārthasākṣātkāritvamastīti, tadasaṅgatam / tathā hi pratyakṣaśabdasya tāvadakṣāśritatvaṃ vyutpattinimittamarthasākṣātkāritvaṃ tu pravṛttinimittamiti pratipāditam / (#Nibandh 17#) na ca bhāvanābalāvalambino manovijñānasyānakṣāśritatve 'pyarthasākṣātkaraṇe kaścidasti śaktipratighātaḥ / yathā hi cakṣrurindriyaṃ svasāmarthyānatikrameṇa yogyadeśasthamarthamapekṣya svavijñānajanane pravartate, tathā sarvāvidyāparipanthibhūtārthabhāvanāsahitaṃ mana indriyamapi yogyadeśasthamarthaṃ prāpya svavijñānajanane pravartiṣyate / aprāpyakāritāyā ubhayoḥ sādhāraṇatvāt / arthavattāyāśca manaso 'pi tadānīmiṣṭatvāt / pṛthagjanasya tu na tādṛśī śaktiḥ, yato netraśrotravanmano 'pi tādṛṅmaryādayā yogyadeśasthamarthasahakāriṇamāsādya vedanamutpādayet, sarvāvidyonmūlakasya bhāvanāviśeṣasya sahakāriṇo 'bhāvāditi nātiprasaṅgaḥ / tadavasthāyāṃ tu śrutinayanayoriva manaso 'pi kiyaddūreṇa viṣayasannidhivyavasthitika eva pramātuṃ kṣamaḥ / kevalametāvaducyate / yāvattena śakyamadhigantuṃ svākārārpaṇasamartha sahakāri vastu tāvaditarajanāsādhāraṇaṃ truṭyadrūpatayā tasya gocarībhavatīti / ata evārthākāro vastuto na bhāvanāmātrajanita iti na visaṃvādaśaṅkāpi / bhāvanayā punastadīyasantāne netra ivāñjanaviśeṣeṇa śaktiratiśayavatī kācidarpitā yatparajanāsādhāraṇadarśanamasya / tasmādanakṣajatve 'pi manovijñānasyārthasākṣātkāritvaṃ sambhavati /
body.translated_text: To this we reply: As for the bluster that 'what is the cause of the cognition of all objects — is it sense-cognition?' and so forth — mental cognition born from the power of meditation is itself the grasper of all objects: this is precisely our fifth thesis. Therefore, the faults belonging to the other theses are repelled by non-acceptance [of those theses]. And as for the objection raised against our accepted fifth thesis — that the word <s>pratyakṣa</s> (perception) is meaningless [when applied to non-sensory cognition], and that [such cognition], being dependent on the power of meditation and not born from the senses (<s>akṣa</s>), does not directly perceive objects — that too is incoherent. For it has been established that the dependence on senses is merely the etymological ground of the word <s>pratyakṣa</s>, while direct apprehension of objects is the ground of its actual usage. And there is no obstruction to the capacity of mental cognition (<s>manovijñāna</s>), which depends on the power of meditation, to directly apprehend objects even though it does not depend on the senses. For just as the visual organ, without exceeding its own capacity, operates to generate its own cognition in dependence on an object situated in the appropriate range, so too the mental organ (<s>manas</s>), together with the meditation on reality that is the antidote to all ignorance (<s>avidyā</s>), upon reaching an object situated in the appropriate range, will operate to generate its own cognition — since non-contact causality is common to both. And since purposefulness of <s>manas</s> at that time is also accepted. But an ordinary person (<s>pṛthagjana</s>) does not have such capacity — so that, like the eye and ear, the mind too, reaching an object in the appropriate range as its cooperating condition within such limits, would produce cognition — because of the absence of the specific cooperating condition, namely the particular meditation that uproots all ignorance. Hence there is no overextension. In that [yogic] state, however, just as with hearing and sight, the mind too is capable of cognizing [only] with respect to objects present within a certain range. Only this much is said: whatever object is capable of imparting its own form, serving as a cooperating cause to the extent that [the yogin] can apprehend — that much, being inaccessible to other persons due to its evanescent nature, becomes the domain [of the yogin]. Therefore, the form of the object is not in reality produced by meditation alone — hence there is not even the suspicion of non-correspondence. Rather, by meditation, in his mental continuum, as if by a special collyrium upon the eye, a certain extraordinary capacity has been bestowed, by virtue of which his vision is inaccessible to other persons. Therefore, even though mental cognition is not born from the senses, direct apprehension of objects is possible.

body.text: nanu manaso bahirasvātantryam / anyathāndhabadhirādyabhāvaprasaṅgāt / uktaṃca yogināṃ dharmādharmayoraparokṣapratibhāsaṃ jñānaṃ nāsti / indriyasannikarṣābhāvādasmadādivaditi /
body.translated_text: Objection: the mind has no independence with respect to external [objects]. Otherwise, the absurd consequence would follow that there would be no blind or deaf persons and so forth. And it has been said: 'Yogins do not have cognition in which <s>dharma</s> (virtue) and <s>adharma</s> (vice) appear as non-remote — due to the absence of sense-contact, just as with us ordinary persons.'

body.text: api ca, arthasya hi ālambanapratyayatvamindriyāpekṣatvena vyāptam / taccāsmāt svaviruddhopalabdhyā vyāvartamānamālambanapratyayatāmapi tasya nivartayati / na khalvindhanaviśeṣo dhūmaheturiti vināpi dahanaṃ sahasreṇāpi saṃskārairdhūmamādhatte / tadādhāne samastakāryahetukānumānocchedaprasaṅgaḥ / na ca bhāvanābalena kasyacidatīndriyadarśitvaṃ sarvajñatvaṃ vā dṛṣṭamiti cet /
body.translated_text: Moreover, the object's being a supporting condition (<s>ālambanapratyaya</s>) is invariably concomitant with dependence on the senses. And that [invariable concomitance], being excluded from this [mental cognition] by the apprehension of what is incompatible with it, also negates the object's being a supporting condition for it. For just as a particular fuel is not the cause of smoke [directly] — even without fire, a thousand refinements will not produce smoke. If [one claims] it does produce [smoke without fire], the absurd consequence would be the destruction of all causal inferences. [Objection:] But it has not been observed that anyone has supersensory vision or omniscience through the power of meditation.

body.text: atrocyate / manaḥśabdena tāvadasmākamanakṣajaṃ vijñānamevābhipretam / na cāsminnandhabadhirādyabhāvaprasaṅgaḥ / sarvāvidyāpratipakṣabhūtārthabhāvanālakṣaṇasya sahakāriviśeṣasyāndhādīnāmabhāvāt / indriyasannikarṣābhāvāditi tvarthasākṣātkāritvamātrāpekṣayā sandigdhavyatirekitve anaikāntikī kāraṇānupalabdhiḥ / asmadvidhārthasākṣātkāritvāpekṣayā punaḥ siddhasādhanam //
body.translated_text: To this we reply: By the word '<s>manas</s>' (mind), we intend precisely cognition not born from the senses (<s>anakṣaja vijñāna</s>). And there is no absurd consequence of the absence of blind and deaf persons, etc. — because blind persons and the like lack the specific cooperating condition, namely meditation on reality that serves as the antidote to all ignorance. As for [the argument] 'due to the absence of sense-contact' — with respect to merely the direct apprehension of objects, this is a <s>kāraṇānupalabdhi</s> (non-apprehension of the cause) that is inconclusive (<s>anaikāntikī</s>), since the counter-example is of doubtful exclusion. With respect to the direct apprehension of objects by persons like us, however, it proves what is already established (<s>siddhasādhana</s>).

body.text: asmadādiviśeṣaṇaśūnyasyārthasākṣātkāritvamātrasyaivendriyādhīnatvadarśanādanaikāntikatvamasaṃbhavīti cet / yadyevamarthasākṣātkāritvamātrasyendriyavadālokādhīnatvamupalabdhamiti na santamase paśyeyurulūkādayaḥ / atha vyabhicāradarśanādālokasyāvyāpakatvam, vyabhicāraśaṅkayā tarhīndriyasyāpyavyāpakatvam / vyāptyā śaṅkā khaṇḍyata iti cet / śaṅkāsaṃbhavād vyāptirevāsaṃbhavinī / yadi hi prathamata eva vyāptiḥ, vyabhicāro 'pi na dṛśyeta /
body.translated_text: [Objection:] Since one observes that the mere direct apprehension of objects, without the qualifier 'by persons like us,' is dependent on the senses, it cannot be inconclusive. [Reply:] If so, then since one also observes that the mere direct apprehension of objects is dependent on light, just as it is on the senses, owls and the like should not see in darkness. If you say that light is not a pervader [of all perception] because a counter-example has been observed — then, by the suspicion of a counter-example, the senses too would not be a pervader. [Objection:] The suspicion is refuted by the invariable concomitance (<s>vyāpti</s>). [Reply:] Since the suspicion [itself] exists, the invariable concomitance itself is impossible. For if invariable concomitance existed in the first place, no counter-example would be observed either.

body.text:
(#Nibandh 18#)
tasmād vyabhicāradarśanaṃ vyāptiśaithilyādeva / sati ca vyāptiśaithilye śaṅkāpi nyāyādāpatantī kena pratihanyate / ulūkādīnāṃ bhinnajātīyatvādālokābhāve 'pyarthasākṣātkāritvamastviti cet / tarhi bhagavato 'pi bhūtārthabhāvanāprakarṣaparyantamahāpralayavāyunā nirastānādyavidyāvipakṣasya saṃsārakūpapatitebhyaḥ prāṇibhyo 'styevādbhutavaijātyamiti yuktamasyāvidyāpratipakṣabhāvanātiśayasahitātmakānantarapratyayādālambanapratyayācca sākṣādutpannasyendriyamantareṇārthasākṣātkāritvam / ataḥ kāraṇānupalabdhiḥ kāśikākārasya vyāpakaviruddhopalabdhiśca vācaspateḥ sandigdhavyatirekitvādanaikāntikī / sandigdhavyatirekitvaṃ tu dūṣaṇamasmadīśvaradūṣaṇe prasādhitam //
body.translated_text: Therefore, the observation of a counter-example is precisely due to the looseness of the invariable concomitance. And when there is looseness of the invariable concomitance, by what is the suspicion — which naturally arises by logic — refuted? [Objection:] Since owls and the like are of a different species, let their direct apprehension of objects exist even in the absence of light. [Reply:] Then the Blessed One too — whose beginningless ignorance has been swept away by the great storm at the culmination of meditation on reality, the opponent of all [forms of ignorance] — possesses a marvelous species-difference from beings fallen into the well of <s>saṃsāra</s> (cyclic existence). Therefore it is fitting that his cognition, directly arisen from the immediately preceding condition together with the extraordinary power of meditation that counteracts ignorance, and from the supporting condition [of the object], directly apprehends objects without the senses. Therefore, the <s>kāraṇānupalabdhi</s> (non-apprehension of the cause) of the <s>Kāśikā</s> author, and the <s>vyāpakaviruddhopalabdhi</s> (apprehension of the contradictory pervader) of <s>Vācaspati</s>, are inconclusive due to the doubtfulness of the counter-example's exclusion. And the doubtfulness of the counter-example's exclusion has been established as a defect in our [text on] the refutation of God (<s>Īśvara</s>).

body.text: tasmātsādhāraṇakarmanirjātānāmasmadādīnāmarthasākṣātkāritvamindriyāpekṣatvena vyāptamiti siddhasādhanam / prasiddhānumānasya ca na kṣatirdṛśyatvopādherdhūmādeḥ pratyakṣānupalambhato vyāptigrahaṇāvirodhāt / sāṃsārikāgocarārthasākṣātkāritvamātrāpekṣayā tu sandigdhavyatirekitvam / adṛśyasya pratyakṣānupalambhābhyāṃ kenacid vyāptigrahaṇāyogāt / viparyaye bādhakapramāṇasya cāsaṃbhavāditi / na catīndriyadarśitvaṃ sarvajñatvaṃ vādarśane 'pi niṣeddhuṃ śakyate, adṛśyānupalambhato niṣedhāyogāt / kāraṇānupalambhatastanniṣedha iti cet / kāraṇābhāvo 'pi adarśanamātrato na sidhyatīti tadavasthaḥ paribhavaḥ //
body.translated_text: Therefore, the statement that 'the direct apprehension of objects by persons like us, who are produced by ordinary <s>karma</s>, is pervaded by dependence on the senses' proves what is already established. And there is no damage to the well-known inference [from smoke to fire], since there is no contradiction in grasping the invariable concomitance through the perceptual non-apprehension of smoke as a visible entity with the condition of visibility. But with respect to the mere direct apprehension of objects not within the range of <s>saṃsāric</s> beings, the counter-example's exclusion is doubtful — since no one can grasp the invariable concomitance of what is invisible through perceptual non-apprehension [of either term]. And because there is no possibility of a countervailing <s>pramāṇa</s> in the contrary case. Nor can supersensory vision or omniscience be negated even when not observed, since negation is impossible from the non-apprehension of what is invisible. [Objection:] The negation follows from the non-apprehension of the cause. [Reply:] The absence of the cause too is not established merely from non-observation — hence the objection remains in the same predicament.

body.text: yadapi kāśikākāreṇābhihitam, atha pramāṇāntarāvagataṃ bhāvyate, ki bhāvanayā, tata eva tatsiddheriti / tadapyasaṃgatam / pramāṇāntaraṃ hyanumānam / na ca caturāryasatyasvarūpe vastutattve niścite sākṣātkāramantareṇa kleśajñeyāvaraṇakṣatiriti svārthamapi tāvad bhāvanā yuktimatī / tattvasākṣātkāriṇi ca cittasantāne sati śakyasākṣātkriyamidamityanye 'pi niścayānantaraṃ sākṣātkriyāyai pravartyante, tadupadiṣṭa svargasādhanaṃ cārthabhāvanayānusarantīti svargāpavargalakṣaṇaparārthasiddhaye ca bhāvanā saphaleti / anyathā tattvāsākṣātkāriṇo lokānatikrāntasya vacanamanādeyameva syāditi kva parārthavārtāpi / yacca kiṃ ca tatpramāṇamityādyārabhya tasmād bhūtamabhūtaṃ veti etatparyantena dharmādharmayoranumānāpravartanamuktam, tatra dharmādharmaśabdena kimabhipretam / yadi kṣaṇikanirātmakavastu tattvam, tadā tasya pratyakṣeṇāniścaye 'pi yathā viparyaye bādhakapramāṇabalena vyāptisaṃvedanaṃ tathā kṣaṇabhaṅgasādhanāvasare vyavasthāpitam / atha vastūnāṃ svargādisādhanatvamabhipretam, tadā tadviṣayaparijñānāprasādhane 'pi nāsmākaṃ kācit kṣatiḥ / saparikarasaṃsāranirvāṇaparijñānenaivopayuktasarvajñaprasādhanāt / yadāhuḥ
body.translated_text: As for what was said by the author of the <s>Kāśikā</s> — 'If what is meditated upon was [first] apprehended by another <s>pramāṇa</s>, then what is the use of meditation, since the thing is already established by that [other <s>pramāṇa</s>]?' — that too is incoherent. For the other <s>pramāṇa</s> is inference. And it is not the case that the destruction of the veils of affliction (<s>kleśāvaraṇa</s>) and the veils of the knowable (<s>jñeyāvaraṇa</s>) can occur without direct realization, even when the reality of the <s>Four Noble Truths</s> (<s>caturāryasatya</s>) has been ascertained. Therefore, meditation is reasonable even for one's own purpose. And when there exists a mental continuum that directly perceives reality, others too, upon being told 'this can be directly realized,' are motivated after that ascertainment to directly realize [it themselves]; and they also follow, through meditation on the relevant object, the means to heaven as taught by him — therefore meditation is fruitful for accomplishing the purpose of others, characterized by heaven and liberation (<s>svarga</s> and <s>apavarga</s>). Otherwise, the word of one who has not directly perceived reality and who has not transcended the ordinary world would simply not be acceptable — so where would even the talk of benefiting others arise? And as for what was said beginning with 'What kind of <s>pramāṇa</s> is that?' up to 'Therefore, whether it is real or unreal' — that inference does not operate with respect to <s>dharma</s> and <s>adharma</s> — what is meant by the words '<s>dharma</s>' and '<s>adharma</s>' there? If the reality of momentary and selfless things is meant, then even when perception has not ascertained it, just as in the case of the contrary [view], the apprehension of invariable concomitance by the force of a countervailing <s>pramāṇa</s> has been established in the context of proving momentary destruction. But if what is meant is that things are means to heaven and the like, then even if the knowledge of that subject-matter is not established, there is no damage to us — since omniscience is established precisely through the knowledge of <s>saṃsāra</s> and <s>nirvāṇa</s> together with their accessories. As they say:

body.text: heyopādeyatattvasyetyādi /
body.translated_text: 'Of what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted, the reality...' and so forth.

body.text: yadapi, api ca bhāvanābalajaṃ gṛhītagrahaṇādapramāṇamityuktam, tatra gṛhītaṃ nāma pratyakṣeṇānumānena vā / pramāṇāntarasyābhāvāt / na tāvat pratyakṣaṃ kṣaṇikatvādāvarvācīnasya (#Nibandh 19#) kasyacidasti / anumānena caikavyāvṛttiviśiṣṭe vastutattve 'vasite 'pi sarvātmanā spaṣṭavastutattvasākṣātkāri pratyakṣaṃ na gṛhītagrāhi, anumānena vastutattvāsparśanāt / na ca taduttarakālamityādi tu kāraṇānupalabdhidūṣaṇaprastāve prativyūḍhamiti /
body.translated_text: As for what was said — 'Moreover, [knowledge] born from the power of meditation is not a <s>pramāṇa</s>, because it grasps what is [already] grasped' — in that case, 'already grasped' means by perception or by inference, since there is no other <s>pramāṇa</s>. Not by perception, to begin with, since no modern person has perception of momentariness and the like. And even when the reality of things characterized by exclusion from all else (<s>ekavyāvṛtti</s>) has been ascertained by inference, perception that directly perceives the fully clear reality of things is not one that 'grasps what is already grasped,' since inference does not touch the reality of things. And [the objection] 'nor after that time...' and so forth has already been countered in the context of the refutation [based on] non-apprehension of the cause.

body.text: yadapi vācaspatinā satyamityādinā punaḥ punaruttarottaramāśaṅkaya tat kimanumānena vahni vyavasthāpyetyādinā bhāvanābalajasyānumānapūrvakatve visaṃvādamupadarśyopasaṃhṛtam, tanna bhāvanāyā bhūtārthatvaṃ tajjaviśadavijñānaprāmāṇyahetuḥ, vyabhicārāditi / tadasaṅgatam / tathā hyayaṃ vahniviṣayenumānapūrvakabhāvanābalataḥ spaṣṭavahnipratyayaḥ kiṃ vahnerapyutpannaḥ, tathābhūtabhāvanāmātrādeva vā /
body.translated_text: As for what <s>Vācaspati</s> concluded by repeatedly raising further and further objections beginning with 'True...' and then showing non-correspondence when [yogic cognition] born from the power of meditation is preceded by inference, [saying] 'Why should fire be established by inference?' and so forth — [we reply:] it is not the case that meditation's having a real object as its content is the cause of the validity of the vivid cognition born from it, because of deviation. For [consider:] this vivid cognition of fire, [produced] from the power of meditation preceded by inference about fire — is it produced [also] from the fire [itself], or from the mere meditation as such?

body.text: prathamapakṣe visaṃvādaśca bahulamupalabhyate iti yaduktaṃ taddurbhāṣitam / sākṣādarthādutpannasyāpi visaṃvādasaṃbhave 'nyasyāpi pratyakṣasya hastakatyāgaprasaṅgāt /
body.translated_text: On the first alternative, the statement that 'non-correspondence is frequently observed' is poorly spoken. For if non-correspondence is possible even for [cognition] produced directly from the object, the absurd consequence would follow that all other perception too should be abandoned.

body.text: dvitīyapakṣe tu bhāvanāprakarṣamātrajasyārthādanutpannasya bahulaṃ visaṃvādopalambhe 'pi bhāvanārthābhyāṃ sākṣādutpannasya yogipratyakṣasyāpi visaṃvādasaṃbhava iti sthavīyasī bhrāntiḥ /
body.translated_text: On the second alternative, however, even though frequent non-correspondence may be observed for [cognition] produced merely at the culmination of meditation and not produced from the object, it is a grave error [to conclude] that non-correspondence is possible for yogic perception that is produced directly from both the meditation and the object.

body.text: nanu yadīndriyaṃ vināpi bhāvanārthābhyāṃ yogijñānamutpadyate, tarhi parvate bhāvanāvahnibhyāṃ vahnijñānamutpadyatāmavisaṃvādi / visaṃvādaśca bahulamupalabhyata iti cet / na / sākṣādvahnerutpāde sati visaṃvādābhāvāt / kevalamutpāda eva durāpaḥ / na hi vayaṃ pramāṇadṛṣṭavastubhāvanāsahitaṃ manaindriyamarthasvarūpagrāhijñānaṃ janayatīti brūmaḥ, api tvasaddṛṣṭilakṣaṇāvidyāparipanthikṣaṇikanairātmyalakṣaṇasarvavastutattvabhāvanāsahitam / na ca vahnitvaṃ sarvavastutattvam, kiṃ tu kṣaṇikanairātmyameveti kṣaṇabhaṅgaprasādhanataḥ pratipāditamiti / kiṃ ca svamanīṣāparikalpitaḥ khalvayamanuimitabhāvitavahniviṣayaviśadaḥ pratyayaḥ / na punarasya loke saṃbhavaḥ / tathā hi niṣprayojanamanunmatto na kaścidbhāvayati / prayojanaṃ ca śiśirabharamantharakāyakāṇḍasyāpi dāhādimātrameva, taccānumitenaiva vahninā taddeśopasarpaṇāt sidhyati / anupasarpaṇe bhāvanāvaiyarthyam / purastāttu bhāvite parisphurati tadarthāpekṣayā bhrāntiḥ prāsarpakasyevetyādyupahāsyamapyasya kṣatātmano durnītipūtigavībhakṣaṇādhmātajaradgomāyorudgāra iva satāmasahyaḥ /
body.translated_text: If, objection: if yogic cognition arises from meditation and its object even without a sense faculty, then let cognition of fire, concordant [with reality], arise from meditation and fire on a mountain — and discordance is abundantly observed. Response: No, because when fire is directly produced there is no discordance. It is merely that [direct] production is difficult to achieve. For we do not say that the mental faculty (<s>manas</s>), combined with meditation on an object seen by a <s>pramāṇa</s> (valid cognition), generates cognition that grasps the intrinsic nature of the object; rather, [we say it arises] combined with meditation on the true nature of all things, characterized by momentariness and selflessness (<s>kṣaṇika-nairātmya</s>), which counteracts ignorance (<s>avidyā</s>) characterized by the false view (<s>asaddṛṣṭi</s>). And fire-nature is not the true nature of all things; rather, it is precisely momentariness and selflessness, as has been demonstrated in the proof of momentary destruction (<s>kṣaṇabhaṅga</s>). Moreover, this vivid cognition regarding fire that has been inferred and meditated upon is indeed fabricated by one's own intellect. Its occurrence in the world is impossible. For no one who is not insane meditates without purpose. And the purpose, even for one whose body is sluggish from the burden of cold, is merely burning and the like, and that is accomplished by approaching the vicinity where fire has been inferred. Without approaching, meditation is futile. But if one meditates beforehand and [fire] manifests vividly, it is an error relative to that purpose — like [the delusion] of one who crawls [toward a mirage]. These and other ridiculous [arguments] of this wounded soul are unbearable to the wise, like the belch of an old jackal bloated from eating the putrid flesh of a cow dead from bad policy.

body.text: yadapi tato 'nantaramāśaṅkayārthasyālambanapratyayatvamindriyāpekṣitvena vyāptamiti prasādhitam, tatpūrvameva pratyuktam / tathā bhāvanāyāścetyādyāśaṅkayārthasyālambanapratyayatvamaśakyāvagamamiti yaduktaṃ tadapyasambaddham /
body.translated_text: As for what was then established by way of the objection that the object's being an objective condition (<s>ālambanapratyaya</s>) is pervaded by dependence on a sense faculty — that has already been refuted above. And what was said by way of the objection beginning 'And of meditation...' — that the object's being an objective condition is impossible to ascertain — that too is incoherent.

body.text: cakṣurindriyasyāpyarthamantareṇa dvicandrakeśoṇḍukādau viśadabhrāntajñānajananasāmarthyamupalabdhamityarthasahitamapi kevalameva samartham / ato ghaṭāderapyālambanapratyayatvamaśakyāvagamamiti indriyapratyakṣamapi pratihataṃ syāditi / tathā, api (#Nibandh 20#) cālambanapratyayā api ta eva yujyanta ityādirna punarvikalpanirmāṇapratibandhateti paryanto vyarthaḥ / asmābhirevaṃvidhasya prastute 'nabhyupagatatvāt / ata eva tasmādbhāvanāprakarṣamātrajatvāt, arthāvyabhicāraniyamābhāvāt, viśadābhamapi saṃśayākrāntatvāt, apramāṇamapratyakṣaṃ ceti sāmpratamityupasaṃhāro 'pi dhikkāraḥ / sarveṣāmeva hetūnāmasiddhatvāt / bhāvanābalajasyārthādapyutpatterindriyapratyakṣavat / sadarthaprakāśanaṃ buddheḥ svabhāva ityādyasmākamapi manoharam / bhāvanāyāśca sāmānyena sphuṭābhajñānahetutvaṃ sādhyate / pramāṇopapannacaturāryasatyaviṣayaniṣṭhāyāṃ tu sāmarthyāt pratyakṣapramāṇahetutāpi sādhyate / ata eva kāminīpratibhāsasyāpramāṇatve 'pyapratyakṣatve 'pi sphuṭābhatvasya sādhyadharmasāmānyasya saṃbhavāt na viruddho hetuḥ / nāpi dṛṣṭāntasya sādhyaśūnyateti / na ca nairātmyadṛṣṭiḥ saṃbhavadbādhā, arthādutpatterabhūtārthatvābhāvāt /
body.translated_text: Even of the visual sense faculty, the capacity to generate vivid erroneous cognition of double moons, floating hairs, and the like without an [corresponding] object has been observed; thus [the faculty] is capable even when combined with an object, by itself alone. Therefore, the object's being an objective condition, even of a pot and the like, would be impossible to ascertain — and thus even sense perception (<s>indriyapratyakṣa</s>) would be blocked. Likewise, the passage beginning 'And the same objective conditions are appropriate...' through '...not a restriction on the construction of conceptual thought (<s>vikalpa</s>)' is pointless, since we do not accept such [a position] in the present context. For exactly this reason, the concluding summary — 'Therefore, because it arises merely from the intensity of meditation (<s>bhāvanāprakarṣa</s>), because there is no invariable non-deviation from the object, because even though vivid in appearance it is afflicted by doubt — it is neither a valid means of knowledge (<s>pramāṇa</s>) nor perception (<s>pratyakṣa</s>)' — is also a reproach [to itself], since all the reasons are unestablished. Because that which arises from the power of meditation also arises from the object, just like sense perception. 'The nature of cognition is to illuminate a real object' and so forth is delightful to us as well. And meditation in general is established as a cause of vivid cognition. But for meditation established in the realization of the Four Noble Truths (<s>caturāryasatya</s>), verified by valid cognition (<s>pramāṇa</s>), the status of being a cause of perceptual valid cognition is also established through its capacity. For exactly this reason, even though the appearance of a woman is not a valid cognition and not perception, the reason is not contradictory, since the general property of vividness, which is the general class of the property to be proved, is possible. Nor is the example devoid of the property to be proved. And the view of selflessness (<s>nairātmyadṛṣṭi</s>) does not involve possible invalidation (<s>bādhā</s>), because of the absence of unreality, since it arises from the object.

body.text: śrutānumitaviṣayaṃ pratyakṣaṃ na saṃbhavatotyapyayuktam / āgamānumānayordvividho viṣayaḥ grāhyo 'dhyavaseyaśca / tatra grāhyaḥ svākāraḥ, adhyavaseyastu pāramārthikavastusvalakṣaṇātmā / asya ca parokṣatve 'numānasāmagrīsaṃbhave 'numānaviṣayatvam, pratyakṣasāmagrīsaṃbhave ca krameṇa pratyakṣaviṣayatvaṃ dṛṣṭameva / tatsiddhamityādyupasaṃhāro 'pi paryākula eva / apramāṇatvāditi hetuśca prathamo 'siddhaḥ / bhāvanābalajasyārthādapyutpatteḥ, pramāṇaśaktisaṃbhavāt, indriyapratyakṣavat / bhāvanābalajatvāditi dvitīyastu sandigdhavyatirekitvādanaikāntikaḥ / tathā yathānumitabhāvitavahniviṣayaviśadajñānamiti dṛṣṭānto 'pyasaṃbhavīti pratipāditam / bhavatu vā, tathāpi yogijñānasya tena saha tulyahetutvamasiddham / taddhi pramāṇadṛṣṭavastubhāvanāmātrajam / yogijñānaṃ tu avidyāpratipakṣasarvavastutattvabhāvanāviṣayābhyāmutpannamiti mahāntamapi viśeṣamasau durmatiprapātapatito nāvagāhata ityupekṣaṇīyaḥ //
body.translated_text: That what is heard and inferred cannot become an object of perception is also unjustified. Scripture (<s>āgama</s>) and inference (<s>anumāna</s>) have two kinds of objects: the apprehended (<s>grāhya</s>) and the determined (<s>adhyavaseya</s>). Of these, the apprehended is its own form (<s>svākāra</s>), while the determined is the ultimately real particular (<s>svalakṣaṇa</s>) in nature. And when this [determined object] is beyond direct access, if the conditions for inference are present, it is an object of inference; and when the conditions for perception are present, it is observed to become gradually an object of perception. Therefore the concluding summary beginning 'That is established...' is also confused. And the first reason, 'because it is not a valid cognition,' is unestablished — because that which arises from the power of meditation also arises from the object, due to the possibility of the capacity for valid cognition, just like sense perception. The second [reason], 'because it arises from the power of meditation,' is inconclusive (<s>anaikāntika</s>) due to having a doubtful negative concomitance (<s>sandigdhavyatireka</s>). Likewise, it has been demonstrated that the example — 'like vivid cognition regarding fire that has been inferred and meditated upon' — is impossible. Or even granting that, the shared causal status of yogic cognition with that [example] is still unestablished. For that [fire-cognition] arises merely from meditation on an object seen by a valid cognition, whereas yogic cognition arises from the object and from meditation on the true nature of all things, which counteracts ignorance (<s>avidyā</s>). That person, fallen into the abyss of wrong views, fails to grasp even this great distinction — and so should be disregarded.

body.text: nyāyaprakīrṇe tu mārgastāvat pramāṇapariśuddho na bhavatītyuktaṃ yat, tat tatprasādhakapramāṇenaiva pratyuktam /
body.translated_text: As for what was said in the <s>Nyāyaprakīrṇa</s> — 'To begin with, the path is not purified by valid cognition' — that is refuted by the very valid cognition that establishes it.

body.text: yaccāpi cetyādyārabhya yogijñānaṃ nirviṣayaṃ prasaktamityuktam tatra keyaṃ nirviṣayatā nāma / kiṃ vikalpākāranivṛttau nirākāratā, arthākārādvisadṛśākāratā, atha tadākāratve 'pi tadvastusaṃsparśitā /
body.translated_text: And as for what was said beginning with 'And...' through 'yogic cognition is entailed to be without an object' — what is this 'objectlessness' supposed to mean? Is it formlessness (<s>nirākāratā</s>) upon the cessation of conceptual form? Or is it having a form dissimilar to the form of the object? Or is it, even while having that form, the lack of contact with that real object?

body.text:
na tāvatprathamaḥ pakṣaḥ kṣamaḥ / jñānasya nirākāratānupapatteḥ /
nāpi dvitīyaḥ / kāminyādibhāvanāyāstadākārasyaiva viśadasya darśanāt /
na ca tṛtīyaḥ / arthasamarpitākārasaṃsparśamapāsyānyasyārthasaṃsparśasyāyogāt /
tathā coktam
body.translated_text:
The first option is not viable, because it is impossible for cognition to be without form.
Nor the second, because in meditation on women and the like, it is observed that precisely that [corresponding] form becomes vivid.
Nor the third, because it is impossible to reject the contact with the object that has conferred its form and [then posit] contact with some other object.
Thus it has been stated:

body.text: arthena ghaṭayatyenāmityādi /
body.translated_text: 'It connects this [cognition] with the object...' and so forth.

body.text: tayoścaikatvenādhyavasāyād bāhya eva pravṛttinivṛttī, vyāvahārikasya sphuṭībhāvo 'pi bahirabhimatasya paryante vikalpopādeyakṣaṇasyaiva sphuṭasyodayaḥ / tāvataiva sa (#Nibandh 21#) viṣayastena sākṣātkṛta iti vyavahāraḥ kevalamarthādapyutpattau / anyathā vyabhicārādaprāmāṇyam / na ca vikalpopadarśitamapiḥ rūpamavastu jñānātmakatvāt / anātmakatve prakāśāyogāt / tadbhāvanaiva cārthabhāvanā, tatsphuṭībhāva eva bāhuasphuṭībhāvaḥ, prakārāntareṇa bāhyasparśāyogāt / etena yat pāramārthikamityādi na sarvajñasiddhiritiparyantaṃ pratyuktam /
body.translated_text: And because both [cognition and object] are determined as one, activity and cessation are directed toward the external alone. Even the becoming vivid of the conventional [object] — [which is] considered external — is ultimately the arising of a vivid moment that is the referent of conceptual appropriation (<s>vikalpopādeya</s>). By just that much, that object is directly realized by it — this is the convention — even when there is also arising from the object. Otherwise, there would be invalidity due to deviation. And the form presented by conceptual thought (<s>vikalpa</s>) is not unreal, since it is of the nature of cognition. If it were not of that nature, it could not be illuminated. And meditation on that [form] is itself meditation on the object; the becoming vivid of that is itself the becoming vivid of the external, because contact with the external is impossible by any other means. By this, what was said beginning 'That which is ultimate...' through 'there is no proof of omniscience' is refuted.

body.text: yaccāpi cetyādi na yuktaṃ paśyāma itiparyantena dūṣaṇamuktam, tadapyasaṃgatam / tathā hi yādṛśa eva bhāvyagrāhī pratyayaḥ prathamo niranvayo niruddhastādṛśa evāpara utpadyata iti niyamaniścayakāraṇaṃ na kiñcidasti caṇḍadevatāsparśādanyat, kṣaṇikatvāditi cet / nanu kṣaṇikatvaṃ sthāyitayā virudhyate na visadṛśotpādena, taddhi prācīnaṃ niranvayanirodhe yathā sadṛśakṣaṇāntaramārabhate tathā svahetugatasāmarthyayogāt kāryotpādānumeyād yadi viśeṣaleśaviśiṣṭaṃ kṣaṇāntaramutpādayati, tadā na kācit kṣatiḥ / na hi bhavata iva bhāvasyāpi kṣaṇikatāyāṃ pradveṣo nāma / tasmānna kṣaṇikatvottaraviśiṣṭakṣaṇajanakatvayorvirodha iti nāpārthako 'bhyāsaḥ /
body.translated_text: And the objection stated beginning 'And...' through 'we do not see it as justified' is also incoherent. For there is no cause for the certainty of the rule that 'a subsequent cognition arises of exactly the same kind as the first cognition that apprehends the object of meditation and has ceased without remainder' — other than the touch of a wrathful deity. If [one objects:] 'because of momentariness' — well, momentariness is contradicted by permanence, not by the arising of something dissimilar. For just as the previous [moment], upon cessation without remainder, initiates another similar moment, so too, if through the capacity present in its own cause — inferable from the production of effects — it produces a subsequent moment qualified by even the slightest distinction, there is no harm. For unlike you, we do not harbor hostility toward the momentariness of things. Therefore there is no contradiction between momentariness and the capacity to generate distinguished subsequent moments — and thus repeated practice (<s>abhyāsa</s>) is not purposeless.

body.text: yaccedaṃ kiñcetyādinā kṣaṇikatve cittamavikṣiptamāveditam, tadapyasādhu / nairātmyāditattvaparā(ṅ) mukhasya sarvasyaiva vikṣiptatvāt / bhāvanābalena tattvasākṣātkāriṇaḥ samāhitatvāt / atha ca tattvasākṣātkriyālābhāt grāhakākārāvagraha saṃbhavāt(ca) vyāvahārikamapi vikṣiptamasti cittam / yato mamaiva doṣakṣayo bhāvīti mārgāmyāsapravṛttirabhyāhateti / paramārthataḥ prāpyādīnāmabhāve 'pi tatsaṃkalpasyaivānādyavidyāprabhāvitasya sarvatra pravartakatvāt / ata eva mārgasatyābhyāsāt siddhaḥ sarvajñaḥ /
body.translated_text: And the claim beginning 'Whatever this...' that the mind is undistracted because of momentariness is also unsound — because everyone who turns away from the truth of selflessness (<s>nairātmya</s>) and the like has a distracted [mind]. Because one who directly realizes the truth through the power of meditation has a concentrated [mind]. And yet, because of obtaining direct realization of the truth and because of the possibility of apprehending the subjective aspect (<s>grāhakākāra</s>), there is also a conventionally distracted mind — from which [arises the thought]: 'My own defilements will diminish,' and the engagement in the practice of the path is unimpeded. Even though ultimately there is no attainer and so forth, it is because the volition (<s>saṃkalpa</s>) toward that [goal], empowered by beginningless ignorance (<s>avidyā</s>), functions as the activator everywhere. For exactly this reason, the <s>Sarvajña</s> (Omniscient One) is established through the practice of the truth of the path (<s>mārgasatya</s>).

body.text: nyāyabhūṣaṇasyāpi yogācārāpekṣayā dūṣaṇamaprastutam / bahirarthāmyupagamenaiva sādhanaprakramāt / yaccoktam tathāpyatītānāgataviṣayatvaṃ katham, na hyasataḥ kaścidākāro 'stīti, tadetat prastāvānavagāhanaphalam / upayuktasarvajñādhikāreṇa hi sarvakṣaṇikanirātmakavastubhāvanopakṣeṇaḥ, na sarvasarvajñāpekṣayā / tato 'tītānāgatamapratīyamānamapi na bādhakam / tāvataiva duḥkhanirodhasiddheḥ / parasmai ca kṣaṇikatvādini(ṣṭha)kasya deśanāvatārāt / na ca sarvasarvajñahastakatyāgaḥ / tathā hi caturāryasatyasākṣātkāraprāptau nirāvaraṇāntaḥ karaṇasya kāruṇyātiśayāt sarvākāraparārthaparatayā sakalagocaracāriṇi cetasi ciravirūḍhotsāhasya tādṛgupāyaviśeṣādhigamo bhaviṣyati, yamanutiṣṭhatastadutpattimantareṇāpi devatādhipatyāt satyasvapnavat / pratiparamāṇusarvaviṣayaṃ yathā deśakālākārapratyavasthānukāri sphuṭataraṃ jñānamudiyāt, tadā na tāvadvastuvyabhicārakṛtaṃ visaṃvāditvam, vastūnāmeva pratibhāsanāt / utpattisārūpyābhyāṃ vedyasthitiriti tu pṛthagjanāpekṣayā / yoginastu sārūpyamātreṇaiva grahaṇamiti nyāyaḥ /
body.translated_text: The refutation with respect to the <s>Yogācāra</s> position found in the <s>Nyāyabhūṣaṇa</s> is also irrelevant, since the line of proof proceeds on the basis of accepting external objects (<s>bahirarthā</s>). And what was said — 'Even so, how can there be cognition of past and future objects, for there is no form of what does not exist?' — this yields no fruit due to failure to grasp the context. For the omniscience section that has been employed concerns the meditation on the true nature of all things as momentary and selfless, not omniscience with respect to everything in every respect. Therefore past and future [objects], even though not [currently] apprehended, are not invalidating, since the cessation of suffering is accomplished by just that much. And the teaching of momentariness and the like is introduced for the sake of others. Nor is there abandonment of omniscience in every respect. For upon attaining the direct realization of the Four Noble Truths (<s>caturāryasatya</s>), one whose inner faculty is unveiled, through the surplus of compassion (<s>kāruṇya</s>), being intent on the welfare of others in all forms, with the mind ranging over all objects, having long-cultivated aspiration — such a one will attain that special means by which, even without the arising of [omniscient cognition], like a truthful dream, by a sovereignty over the divine — a cognition may arise, most vivid, encompassing all objects down to every atom, conforming to every place, time, and form. In that case, there is no discordant invalidity caused by deviation from reality, since it is real things themselves that appear. 'The ascertainment of the knowable through [both] origination and similarity of form' — that is with respect to ordinary beings. But for the yogin, apprehension through similarity of form alone is the principle.

body.text:
(#Nibandh 22#)
yad vārtikam
body.translated_text:
(Nibandhāvalī 22)
The <s>vārtika</s> (sub-commentary) states:

body.text:
aviśuddhadhiyaḥ prati /
grāhyagrāhakacinteyamacintyā yogināṃ gatiḥ // iti /
body.translated_text:
'For those of impure intellect,
this investigation of apprehended and apprehender [is relevant]; the way of yogins is inconceivable.'

body.text: tadevaṃ bhāvibhūtayorajanakayorapi yogijñāne sphuraṇamabādhyam / bhāvibhūtayostarhi yadi svarūpasya sphuraṇam, vartamānataiva syāt / atha svarūpasannihitaṃ jñānameva tadākāramiti nirālambanaṃ niyamena / tadapi nāsti / yasmādasannihite 'pyarthe bhāvanābalāt taddeśakālākārānukāri vijñānaṃ kathamanālambanam / tathātvenādhyavasāyācca, adhyavasitakālaviśiṣṭasyaiva satyasvapnavattasya prāpteḥ /
body.translated_text: Thus the manifestation in yogic cognition of future and past [objects], which are non-productive [of cognition in the ordinary way], is not invalidated. If, then, the manifestation is of the intrinsic nature of the future and past, they would be present. If, on the other hand, the cognition itself, present to the intrinsic nature, takes on that form — then it is necessarily without a support (<s>nirālambana</s>). That too is not the case. Because even when the object is not present, how can cognition that conforms to the place, time, and form of that [object], arising from the power of meditation, be without a support? And because of the determination 'as such,' because there is the attainment of [the object] qualified by the determined time, like a truthful dream.

body.text: yad bhāṣyam
body.translated_text: The <s>bhāṣya</s> (commentary) states:

children.text: yathā sa dṛṣṭaḥ śaradādikālayukta stathā tasya na bādhitatvam /
children.translated_text: Just as he was seen as connected with the autumn and other seasons, so there is no invalidation of that;

children.text: tatkālayuktastu na tena dṛṣṭa stathāpratītāvapi nāsti doṣaḥ //
children.translated_text: but as connected with that time he was not seen by that [perception] — even so, there is no fault in the non-apprehension.

body.text: jñānamātrasya tu tattvataḥ sphuraṇācca na vartamānatāprasaṅgaḥ saṅgataḥ / tathā kṣaṇikatvapakṣe 'pi ekatvādhyāropasāmarthyānna vyavahārikaṃ prati pramāṇasya kācit kṣatiriti śāstre prapañcitam /
body.translated_text: And because cognition alone truly manifests, there is no entailment of [the object's] being present — this is coherent. Likewise, even in the theory of momentariness (<s>kṣaṇikatva</s>), through the capacity of superimposing unity, there is no harm to the valid cognition with respect to the conventional — as has been elaborated in the treatise.

body.text: yadapi kiñcedamapi vaktumucitamityādyārabhya bhāvanābalajasyānumānapūrvakatve 'pi pratyakṣapūrvakatve 'pi vyabhicārābhidhānam, tadarthādapi bhāvanābalajasya sākṣādutpattisvīkārādapahastitam / yathendriyajasyāpi dvicandrādijñānasyārthādanutpatteraprāmāṇyam, arthendriyābhyāmutpattau tu prāmānyamevaṃ pramāṇapūrvakasyāpi bhāvanāmātrādutpannasyāprāmāṇyam, bhāvanārthābhyāmutpannasya tu prāmāṇyam /
body.translated_text: As for the charge of deviation stated beginning 'Even this is appropriate to say...' regarding yogic cognition born from the power of meditation, whether preceded by inference or preceded by perception — that is dismissed by accepting that what arises from the power of meditation also arises directly from the object. Just as, for sense-born cognition too, cognition of double moons and the like, when not arising from the object, is invalid, but when arising from both object and sense faculty it is precisely valid — so too, even for [cognition] preceded by valid cognition, when arising from meditation alone it is invalid, but when arising from both meditation and the object it is valid.

body.text: yadi yogijñānasyārthādutpattiḥ, pramāṇapūrvakatvāpekṣayā na kiñcatprayojanamiti ceta / na deśakālavastuviśeṣamapāsya sāmānyena sarvadikkālavartivastumātraṃ kṣaṇikanirātmakamityaniścaye mahāprayāsasādhyapuruṣāyuṣavyāpinyāṃ bhāvanāyāmeva pravṛtterabhāvāt / na ca hāliko havyāśanamanumāya sphuṭīkarotiyena pratyakṣāntaratvaprasaṅgaḥ / asāmarthyavaiyarthyābhyāṃ tadasaṃbhavapratipādanāt /
body.translated_text: If the cognition of the <s>yogin</s> arises from the object, and it is objected that there is no purpose with respect to its being preceded by a <s>pramāṇa</s> (valid means of knowledge) — no, because in the absence of certainty that, setting aside particular place, time, and object, everything existing in all directions and times is merely momentary and without a self in a general way, there would be no engagement in <s>bhāvanā</s> (contemplative cultivation), which requires great effort and spans a human lifetime. Nor does a ploughman, having inferred fire, make it vivid — so there is no absurd consequence of it becoming another kind of perception — because the impossibility of that has been demonstrated through [the arguments of] incapacity and purposelessness.

body.text: yadapyuktaṃ yogino jñānamindriyajñānādabhinnaṃ bhinnaṃ vā / tatra prathamapakṣe tāvanna vastudoṣaḥ / tādṛkpuruṣaviśeṣasya siddhatvāt / vyavasthādūṣaṇamapi nāsti / sādhyatayaiva tādṝgdaśāviśeṣasya lokātikrāntātiśayasya paramapuruṣārtharūpasya sādhanaviśeṣapratipādanāya pṛthagjanasādhāraṇendriyajñānād bhedena nirdeśāt / paramapuruṣārthaviṣayatvābhāvādeva ca rasāyanādisaṃskārajasyāpi jñānasya na pratyakṣāntaratā / bhedapakṣe 'pi na tāvat stharyetarasphuraṇakṛtopālambhasaṃbhavaḥ / indriyajñānenāpi vastu (#Nibandh 23#) sarvātmanā gṛhṇatā truṭyadrūpasyaiva grahaṇāt / adhyavasāyo hi pūrvaṃ durllabhaḥ idānīṃ tu bhāvanābalanirdalitāvidye cittasantāne so 'pīndriyajñānena janyata iti viśeṣaḥ /
body.translated_text: As to what was also said — that the cognition of the <s>yogin</s> is either identical with or different from sense-cognition: in the first alternative, there is no defect in the thesis, because such a special person is established. Nor is there any fault of [lack of] systematic distinction, because to demonstrate the special means [of attaining that state], it is described separately from the sense-cognition common to ordinary persons, precisely because that particular stage, which transcends the world and constitutes the supreme goal of human existence, is itself what is to be established. Moreover, because cognition that is purified by treatments such as <s>rasāyana</s> (elixirs) and the like lacks the nature of the supreme goal of human existence, it does not become another kind of perception. Even in the alternative of difference, there is no possibility of the objection based on the manifestation of permanence and impermanence, because even sense-cognition, when apprehending the object in its entirety, grasps only that which is momentary in nature. For <s>adhyavasāya</s> (determination) was previously difficult [to attain]; but now, in a mental continuum whose <s>avidyā</s> (ignorance) has been shattered by the force of <s>bhāvanā</s> (contemplative cultivation), that too is produced by sense-cognition — this is the distinction.

body.text:
nanu yogino manovijñānendriyajñānābhyāṃ paśyata ākāradvayasphuraṇaprasaṅga iti cet / satyam / satyajñānākārastāvad vastuno na bhinnadeśo 'nyatarabhrāntiprasaṅgāt / atastāvākārāvapratimau kayā gatyā spharata iti ko nirṇetuṃ kṣamaḥ /
yadāha
body.translated_text:
If it is objected that, for the <s>yogin</s> who perceives through both <s>manovijñāna</s> (mental cognition) and <s>indriyajñāna</s> (sense-cognition), there would be the absurd consequence of two aspects manifesting — true. The aspect of true cognition, to begin with, is not in a different location from the object, because otherwise there would be the absurd consequence of one of them being erroneous. Therefore, who is capable of determining in what manner those two incomparable aspects manifest?
As it has been said:

body.text: acintyā yogināṃ gatiriti /
body.translated_text: The ways of <s>yogins</s> are inconceivable.

body.text: sarvathā tu na yogijñānasya kṣatiriti siddham / tadevaṃ kāraṇānupalambhādapi na sarvajñatābhāvaḥ /
body.translated_text: In every respect, there is no damage to the cognition of the <s>yogin</s> — this is established. Thus, even from the non-apprehension of a cause [to negate it], the non-existence of omniscience does not follow.

body.text: nanu yadi nāma yuṣmadabhimatasyānumānasya na bādhakam, tathāpyastyevānumānaṃ bādhakam / tathā hi śakyamidamabhidhātum
body.translated_text: Now, even if the inference you accept is not subject to a defeater, still there does exist a defeating inference. For it can be stated thus:

body.text: sugato 'sarvajñaḥ /
body.translated_text: The <s>Sugata</s> (Buddha) is not omniscient,

body.text: jñeyatvāt, prameyatvāt, sattvāt, puruṣatvāt, vaktṛtvāt, indriyādimattvādityādi /
body.translated_text: because of being a knowable object, because of being a <s>prameya</s> (object of valid cognition), because of being existent, because of being a person, because of being a speaker, because of possessing sense-faculties, and so forth.

body.text: rathyāpuruṣavat /
body.translated_text: Like a man in the street.

body.text: tathā ca bṛhaṭṭīkā
body.translated_text: And thus [it is stated in] the <s>Bṛhaṭṭīkā</s> (Great Commentary):

children.translated_text: Who would posit him whose existence can be destroyed by reasons characterized by being knowable, being a <s>prameya</s>, being a real entity, and so forth?

children.text: nihantuṃ hetavaḥ śaktāḥ ko nu taṃ kalpayiṣyati //
children.translated_text: [verse end]

body.text: kārikāpi
body.translated_text: And also the verse:

children.translated_text: Who would posit him whose <s>prameyatva</s> (being an object of cognition) and the like, consistent with perception and other [<s>pramāṇas</s>],

children.text: sadbhāvavāraṇe śaktaṃ ko nu taṃ kalpayiṣyati //
children.translated_text: are capable of preventing [his] existence [as omniscient]?

body.text: atrocyate / kimete jñeyatvādayaḥ sarvajñatvena sākṣādviruddhāḥ paramparayā vā / aviruddhavidhāne pratiṣedhāyogāt / sa ca sākṣād virodha parasparaparihārasthitilakṣaṇo vā, bhāvābhāvavat; sahānavasthānalakṣaṇo vā, dahanatuhinavaditi /
body.translated_text: To this we reply: Are these [properties] such as being knowable and so forth directly contradictory to omniscience, or indirectly? Because what is not contradictory with something cannot negate it. And that direct contradiction is either characterized by mutual exclusion, like existence and non-existence; or characterized by non-co-occurrence, like fire and snow.

body.text: na tāvadādyaḥ pakṣaḥ / yadvyavacchedanāntarīyako yasya paricchedastayoreva parasparaparihārasthitilakṣaṇo virodhaḥ / na ca jñeyatvādi sarvajñatvavyavacchedena sthitam / kiṃ tarhi / ajñeyatvādivyavacchedena / tathā sarvajñatvamasarvajñatvavyavacchedena, na tu jñeyatvavyavacchedena /
body.translated_text: The first alternative does not hold. For the contradiction characterized by mutual exclusion obtains only between that by whose exclusion another is delimited. But being knowable and so forth do not exist by the exclusion of omniscience. Rather, [they exist] by the exclusion of being unknowable and so forth. Similarly, omniscience [exists] by the exclusion of non-omniscience, not by the exclusion of being knowable.

body.text: nāpi dvitīyo virodhaḥ / yasya hyavikalakāraṇasya bhavato yatsannidhānādabhāvastayoreva sahānavasthānalakṣaṇo virodhaḥ / na ca sarvajñatvaṃ prāk pravṛttamavikalakāraṇaṃ dṛṣṭaṃ yena paścājjñeyatvādisadbhāve nivartata iti syāt / tathātve sati deśādiniṣedya eva bhavenna tu sarvathoccheda iti /
body.translated_text: Nor does the second [type of] contradiction hold. For the contradiction characterized by non-co-occurrence obtains only between that which, when possessing all its causal conditions, ceases to exist upon the presence of the other. But omniscience is not observed to have previously arisen with complete causal conditions such that it would cease upon the presence of knowability and the like. And even if that were so, there would be negation with respect to [particular] place and so forth, not total annihilation.

body.text: na ca paramparayā virodhaḥ / sa hi bhavan niṣedhyasya sarvajñatvasya vyāpakaviruddhatvāt, kāraṇaviruddhatvāt, kāryaviruddhatvāt, svabhāvaviruddhakāryatvāt, (#Nibandh 24#) vyāpakaviruddhakāryatvāt, kāraṇaviruddhakāryatvāt, kāryaviruddhakāryatvāt, svabhāvaviruddhavyāptatvāt, vyāpakaviruddhavyāptatvāt, kāraṇaviruddhavyāptatvāt, kāryaviruddhavyāptatvād vā bhaved / tatra sarvajñatvasyāsattvāt, vyāpakakāraṇakāryāṇāmasiddhestadviruddhakāryavyāpyābhāvāt na prameyatvādayaḥ sarvajñatvena paramparayāpi viruddhāḥ /
body.translated_text: Nor is there indirect contradiction. For such [indirect contradiction] would have to be because [knowability and so forth] are contradictory to the <s>vyāpaka</s> (pervader) of the [property] to be negated — omniscience; or contradictory to its cause; or contradictory to its effect; or effects of something contradictory to its nature; or effects of something contradictory to its pervader; or effects of something contradictory to its cause; or effects of something contradictory to its effect; or pervaded by something contradictory to its nature; or pervaded by something contradictory to its pervader; or pervaded by something contradictory to its cause; or pervaded by something contradictory to its effect. Among these, since omniscience is not [established as] non-existent, and since the pervader, cause, and effect [of omniscience] are unestablished, and since there is no effect or pervasion of what is contradictory to them — <s>prameyatva</s> (being an object of cognition) and the like are not contradictory to omniscience even indirectly.

body.text: nanu vaktṛtvaṃ virudhyata eva sarvaviṣayanirvikalpajñānaviruddhavikalpakāryatvād vaktṛtvasya / naitad yuktam / savikalpāvikalpayoryugapadavṛttervikalpakatvena sarvajñasyāvirodhāt /
body.translated_text: Now, [it may be said that] being a speaker is indeed contradictory [to omniscience], because being a speaker is an effect of <s>vikalpa</s> (conceptual construction), which is contradictory to non-conceptual cognition having all objects as its domain. This is not correct, because since <s>savikalpa</s> (conceptual) and <s>avikalpa</s> (non-conceptual) [cognitions] do not operate simultaneously, there is no contradiction between being a conceptualizer and being omniscient.

body.text: kastarhi pṛthagjanādasya bheda iti cet / ucyate / yathā māyākāro nirmitāśvādiviṣayaṃ vijñānaṃ nirviṣayatvena niścinvannabhrāntaḥ, tadanyasmācca śreṣṭhaḥ, tathā bhagavānapi śuddhalaukikavikalpasammukhībhāve 'pi na bhrānto nāpi pṛthagjanasamāna iti / tataśca nirvikalpakasarvajñajñānavikalpayorvirodhābhāvād vaktṛtvaṃ sarvajñatvena sahāviruddhameva //
body.translated_text: If asked what then is the difference between [the omniscient one] and an ordinary person, we reply: Just as a magician, while ascertaining the cognition of illusory horses and the like as being without [real] objects, is not deluded and is superior to others [who are deluded by the illusion], so too the <s>Bhagavān</s> (Blessed One), even when confronted with pure mundane <s>vikalpas</s> (conceptual constructions), is not deluded and is not equal to an ordinary person. Therefore, since there is no contradiction between the non-conceptual omniscient cognition and <s>vikalpas</s>, being a speaker is entirely non-contradictory with omniscience.

body.text: etenaidapi nirastam yadāha kāśikākāraḥ, samādhervyutthāyopadekṣyata iti cet / na / vyutthitasya hyabhilāpinī pratītibhrāntabhāṣitamapramāṇaṃ bhavediti //
body.translated_text: By this, what the author of the <s>Kāśikā</s> says is also refuted — 'He will teach after emerging from <s>samādhi</s> (meditative absorption),' if so objected — no, because the conceptual cognition of one who has emerged [from samādhi], being of the nature of erroneous speech, would be a non-<s>pramāṇa</s> (invalid cognition).

body.text: yadapyuktaṃ bṛhaṭṭīkāyām
body.translated_text: As was also stated in the <s>Bṛhaṭṭīkā</s>:

children.translated_text: When he would teach some one thing, like an ordinary speaker,
that would be a song of one who knows only a part, not the utterance of an omniscient one.

body.text: tadapi nirastam, vikalpenaikasya kasyacidāmukhīkṛtvopadeśe 'pi nirvikalpena sarvamavabudhyamānasya vacanānāṃ sarvajñabhāṣitatvādeva //
body.translated_text: This too is refuted, because even when teaching by foregrounding some one thing through <s>vikalpa</s> (conceptual construction), his statements are indeed the utterances of an omniscient one, since he comprehends everything through non-conceptual [cognition].

body.text: yatpunaḥ kārikāyāmuktam
body.translated_text: And what was further said in the verse:

children.translated_text: From his mere presence, like a wish-fulfilling gem,
teachings issue forth at will, even from walls and the like.
Such statements indeed are fitting for one who has faith;
but because [the teachings] issue from walls and the like, we have no confidence in those teachings.
Are they perhaps promulgated by the <s>Buddha</s>,
or are they uttered by some invisible wicked beings such as <s>piśācas</s> (demons) for the purpose of deception?

body.text: bṛhaṭṭīkāyāmapi
body.translated_text: And also in the <s>Bṛhaṭṭīkā</s>:

children.translated_text: When he abides in <s>dhyāna-samādhi</s> (meditative absorption), stationed like a wish-fulfilling gem,
teachings issue forth at will, even from walls and the like.
Through them, people come to know all the matters they wish to investigate,
and they swiftly attain what is beneficial, each according to their capacity.
Such statements, when proclaimed, are fitting for one who has faith;
but we who lack faith seek reasoned arguments.
And in those [teachings] that issue from walls and the like, there would be no status of being taught by a reliable person,

children.text: viśvāsaśca na tāsu syātkenaitāḥ kīrtitā iti //
children.translated_text: and there would be no trust in them — by whom were these proclaimed?

children.text: kinnu buddhapraṇītāḥ syuḥ kiṃ vā brāhyaṇavañcakaiḥ /
children.translated_text: Are they perhaps authored by the <s>Buddha</s>, or are they taught by <s>brāhmaṇa</s>-deceivers,
playing [tricks], or by echoes from afar?
Or are they fabricated by invisible beings such as petty <s>piśācas</s> (demons) and the like?
Therefore, those who consider themselves wise should not place trust in them.

body.text: etadapyanabhyupagamenaiva nirastam / śuddhalaukikavikalpasaṃmukhībhāvenaiva tasya deśakatvābhyupagamāditi //
body.translated_text: This too is refuted simply by not accepting [that premise], since we accept that he teaches precisely through the confrontation of pure mundane <s>vikalpas</s> (conceptual constructions).

body.text: atha vā yathā cakrasyoparate 'pi daṇḍapreraṇāvyāpāre pūrvāvegavaśād bhramaṇam / evaṃ bhagavati pratyastamitasamastavikalpajāle 'pi sthite yadi pūrvapraṇidhānāhitasatatānābhogavāhinī deśanā syāttadā ko virodhaḥ / vivakṣābhāve kathaṃ vacanapravṛttiriti na vaktavyam / tadabhāve 'pi nidrāṇasya tattatpravyaktavacanasandarśanāt / vacanamātrasya vivakṣayā vyāpterabhāvāt / tasmād yathā pūrvābhyāsato jhaṭiti prabodhitasyāriṇā prahārādidānenānurūpa eva prakramaḥ śastroddharaṇādikaḥ, tathā sarvavedinopi sakalāḥ kalāḥ ityanākulam /
body.translated_text: Alternatively, just as a wheel continues spinning due to its prior momentum even after the application of the staff has ceased, so too if, even while the <s>Bhagavān</s> abides with the entire net of <s>vikalpas</s> having set, there were teachings flowing continuously and effortlessly due to prior aspiration (<s>praṇidhāna</s>) — what contradiction would there be? It should not be said 'how can speech proceed in the absence of the intention to speak,' because even in the case of a sleeping person, clearly articulated speech on various topics is observed, and because speech as such is not pervaded by intention to speak. Therefore, just as one who is suddenly awakened by an enemy, due to prior training, proceeds at once with an appropriate course of action such as drawing a weapon, so too all the arts of the omniscient one [proceed without difficulty] — this is unproblematic.

body.text: yadāhālaṅkāraḥ
body.translated_text: As the [author of the] <s>Alaṅkāra</s> says:

children.translated_text: By the mere proximity of an enemy, there proceed without conceptualization
the courses of action against that enemy, produced by anger, even beforehand.

body.text: yatpunaruktam piśācādikṛtaśaṅkayā nātrāśvāsaḥ satāṃ yukta iti / tadasaṅgatam, yataḥ
body.translated_text: As for what was further said — that the suspicion of [teachings] being produced by <s>piśācas</s> (demons) and the like makes confidence in them improper for the wise — that is incoherent, because:

children.translated_text: Incoherent speech, violence, and the display of contemptible meanings —
these are the work of playful <s>piśācas</s> and the like, [and] are not found in those [teachings].
The doctrine that is consistent with both <s>pramāṇas</s> (valid means of knowledge), in its entire domain,
whose refutation by the two <s>pramāṇas</s> is not seen even by [its most] minute [aspect] —
which, though entirely beyond the reach [of ordinary perception], has never been contradicted by prior or subsequent [cognitions],
and which, by virtue of the arising of qualities such as compassion, motivates all persons —
which teaches the antidote to the entire collection of <s>anuśayas</s> (latent afflictions),
and which breaks open the door-panels of the gate to the city of <s>nirvāṇa</s> —

children.text: taccet krīḍanaśīlānāṃ rakṣasāṃ vā vaco bhavet /
children.translated_text: if that were the speech of playful <s>rākṣasas</s> (demons),
then let them indeed be the Fully Awakened Ones, since all the characteristics [of a Buddha] are present in them.

body.text: na ca nāmni vivādaḥ / na ca nāmanivṛttau vastu nivartate / pratyuta vedasyaiva krīḍanaśīlapiśācādipraṇītatvaṃ yuktaṃ saṃbhāvayitum / yena gośavādiṣu yogeṣvagamyāgamanādayo 'satyasamudācārāḥ saṃprakāśitāḥ / lokaprasiddhiśca
body.translated_text: Nor is there a dispute about names. Nor does the thing cease when the name ceases. On the contrary, it is rather proper to suspect that the <s>Veda</s> itself is authored by playful <s>piśācas</s> (demons) and the like, since in rituals such as the <s>gośava</s> (cattle sacrifice), false practices such as sexual intercourse with forbidden persons are proclaimed. And the popular saying [goes]:

body.text: trayo vedasya kartāro munibhaṇḍaniśācarāḥ /
body.translated_text: The three authors of the <s>Veda</s> are a sage, a buffoon, and a night-wanderer (demon).

body.text: iti alamatinirbandhena //
body.translated_text: Enough of this obstinate argumentation.

body.text: nanu sarvajñatvaṃ vītarāgaditvena vyāptamiṣyate / tadviruddhaṃ ca rāgādiyogitvam, tatkāryaṃ ca vacanam / tadetad vyāpakaviruddhakāryabhūtaṃ vacanaṃ sarvajñābhāvaṃ sādhayati paramparayā viruddhatvāditi cet / na / rāgādīnāṃ vacasaśca kāryakāraṇabhāvāsiddheḥ / tathā hi vacanaviśeṣo rāgādikāryam, yo rāgeṇaiva janitaḥ, vacanamātraṃ vā /
body.translated_text: Now, if it is objected that omniscience is accepted as pervaded by freedom from attachment (<s>vītarāgatva</s>) and the like, and that attachment and the like are contradictory to that, and that speech is an effect of that [attachment], and therefore this speech, being an effect contradictory to the pervader [of omniscience], establishes the absence of omniscience through indirect contradiction — no, because the cause-effect relation between attachment and the like and speech is not established. For a particular [kind of] speech is an effect of attachment — namely, that which is produced by attachment alone — or [it is] mere speech [in general].
