body.text: tatra na tāvat prathamaḥ pakṣaḥ / tādṛśasya vacanasya niścayopāyāsaṃbhavāt / asabhyamaithunācāraprakāśakaṃ vacanaṃ tatkāryamiti cet / na / abhiprāyasya durlakṣyatvāt / virakto 'pi raktavacceṣṭate, rakto 'pi viraktavadityabhiprāyo durbodhaḥ / tataśca viśiṣṭavyavahārasya sāṃkaryeṇa na tatraikāntena rāgānumānaṃ yujyate / nāpi vacanamātraṃ rāgādikāryam / asaṃmukhībhūtarāgādayo 'pi hi svābhimatadevatāstutividhāne mātrādigurujanasaṃbhāṣaṇādau ca vacanamātramuccārayantaḥ samupalabhyante / na ca yadyadabhāve bhavati tasya tatkāryatocyate, atiprasaṅgāt / rāgādiyogyatā tarhi vacasaḥ kāraṇam, tayā vinopalakhaṇḍalādau vacanasyādarśanāditi cenna / karaṇaguṇavaktukāmate hi vacanasya hetuḥ / tadabhāvādevopalakhaṇḍalādau nivartate, na rāgādiyogyatāyā abhāvāt / yadi kāraṇaguṇādisakalatadanyakāraṇabhāve 'pi rāgādi yogyatābhāvānnotpadyate vacanamiti sidhyettasyāḥ kāraṇatvam / upalakhaṇḍalādau tu vaktukāmatā nāsti / tatkathaṃ tatkāraṇatvaṃ vacasāmiti / evaṃ tarhi vaktukāmataiva rāgo 'stu / iṣṭatvānna kiñcid bādhitaṃ syāt, nāmni vivādābhāvāt / paramārthataḥ punarnityasukhātmātmīyadarśanākṣiptaṃ sāśravaviṣayaṃ cetaso 'bhiṣvaṅgaṃ rāgamāhuḥ /
body.translated_text: Of these, the first position [is untenable]. Because there is no means of ascertaining such a statement [as being produced by passion]. If [you say] a statement that reveals unchaste sexual conduct is its [passion's] effect — no, because the intention is difficult to discern. Even one who is dispassionate may behave like one with passion, and one with passion may behave like one without it — thus the intention is hard to understand. Consequently, due to the intermixture of specialized behavior, the inference of passion cannot be made there with certainty. Nor is mere speech an effect of passion and the like. For even those in whom passion and such have not become active are observed uttering mere speech in composing hymns to their favored deity, in conversing with their mother and other elders, and so forth. And one cannot say that whatever occurs in the absence of [something] is its effect, because of over-extension. If [you say] the capacity for passion is the cause of speech, since speech is not observed in [inanimate things like] stones, pots, etc. without that [capacity] — no, because the cause of speech is the desire to speak, [which requires] the quality of being an instrument. Speech ceases in stones, pots, etc. precisely because of the absence of that [desire to speak], not because of the absence of the capacity for passion. If speech does not arise even when all other causes — instrumental qualities, etc. — are present, due solely to the absence of the capacity for passion, then its causality would be established. But in stones, pots, etc. there is no desire to speak — so how can they [prove] the causality of that [passion-capacity] for speech? If so, then let the desire to speak itself be passion. Since [this is] what is desired [by us], nothing would be refuted, as there is no dispute about names. But in the ultimate sense, they call passion the attachment of the mind toward objects that are conditioned (<s>sāśrava</s>), [an attachment] driven by the view of a permanent, blissful self and 'mine.'

body.text: niṣpannasarvasampattervivakṣāpi na yujyata iti cet / adoṣo 'yam, parārthatvādvivakṣāyāḥ / vītarāge 'rthāsaṅgābhāvāt kathaṃ parārthāpi pravṛttiriti cet / na / āsaṅgamantareṇa karuṇayāpi pravṛtteḥ /
body.translated_text: If [you object that] for one in whom all attainments are accomplished, even the desire to speak is not fitting — this is no fault, because the desire to speak is for the benefit of others. If [you ask] how can there be activity even for others' benefit in one free from passion, since there is no attachment to objects — no, because activity can proceed from compassion even without attachment.

body.text: saiva rāga iti cet / iṣṭatvādadoṣaḥ /
body.translated_text: If [you say] that very [compassion] is passion — since [this is] what is desired [by us], there is no fault.

body.text: rāgasya tu svarūpamuktam /
body.translated_text: But the true nature of passion has [already] been stated.

body.text: kāruṇikasyāpi niṣphalārambho na yukta iti cet / na / parārthasyaiva phalatvāt / iṣṭalakṣaṇatvāt phalasyeti yatkiñcidetat /
body.translated_text: If [you say] a futile undertaking is not fitting even for a compassionate one — no, because the benefit of others is itself the fruit. [The objection that] the fruit has the character of what is desired — this amounts to nothing.

body.text:
(#Nibandh 27#)
nanu nirvikalpasya bhagavataḥ kathaṃ tasyāmavasthāyāṃ karuṇāsaṃbhavaḥ / duḥkhavikalpaprabhavā hi karuṇetyanvayavyatirekābhyāmanyatvena niścitam /
body.translated_text: [Nibandh 27] But [you object:] for the Blessed One who is free from conceptual thought (<s>nirvikalpa</s>), how can compassion be possible in that state? For it has been ascertained through positive and negative concomitance that compassion arises from the conceptualization of suffering [in others], and it is something distinct [from mere thought].

body.text: tataśca kāraṇābhāvāt kathaṃ kāryasaṃbhava iti cet / na / yathā kumbhakāranivṛttāvapi svasantānamātrabhāvinī ghaṭādisthitistathotthāpakavikalpābhāve 'pi sama(na) ntarapratyayabalādanālambanakaruṇāpravṝtteravāryatvāt / yadāhurguravaḥ
body.translated_text: If [you ask] how can the effect exist when the cause is absent — no, because just as pots and such persist through a mere continuation of their own series even after the potter has ceased [working], so too, even in the absence of the initiating conceptual thought, the flow of objectless compassion (<s>anālambana-karuṇā</s>) cannot be arrested due to the force of the immediately preceding condition. As the masters say:

children.translated_text: 'Even though aided by practice, one [who has attained] becomes firm like the hardness [of a forged metal],
And even in that relaxation, the intense effort for the removal of suffering [of others persists].

children.text: utpāde tu phalasya hetuniyamo no tu prabandhasthitau
children.translated_text: There is a restriction of the cause in the origination of the fruit, but not in the continuity of the stream;
Therefore, to him in whom friendliness and the like shine forth even after the cessation of the perception of suffering — homage to him!'

body.text: etenaitadapi nirastaṃ yadāha kārikāyām
body.translated_text: By this, what is said in the [opponent's] verse is also refuted:

children.translated_text: 'And for this one, who is free from passion and the like, and who is established as inactive,
The teaching would be composed by someone else, since [he himself] is devoid of reflective awareness.'

body.text: nanu yadi nāmaivaṃ vaktṛtvaṃ sarvajñatvena sahāviruddhaṃ dehendriyabuddhyādiyogitvaṃ tu viruddhameva / sarvajñatāvyāpakavītarāgatvaviruddharāgādikāraṇatvāddehādīnām /
body.translated_text: But [you object:] even if speaking is thus not inconsistent with omniscience, having a body, sense organs, intellect, and the like is indeed inconsistent — because the body and such are the cause of passion and the like, which is contradictory to freedom from passion (<s>vītarāgatva</s>), which pervades omniscience.

body.text: tataśca pratiṣedhyavyāpakaviruddhakāraṇopalambhāt sarvajñābhāva iti cet / ucyate / dehādīnāṃ hetutve 'pi naiṣāṃ kevalānāṃ sahakārimātrāṇāmātmābhiniveśalakṣaṇopādānakāraṇavikalānāṃ rāgādijanakatvamityagamakā eva dehādayaḥ sarvajñābhāvasya / tasmāj jñeyatvādīnāmapyasāmarthyānna paraparikalpitānumānato 'pi sarvajñābhāvaḥ /
body.translated_text: If [you conclude] therefore, since we perceive the cause that contradicts the pervader of [what is to be] negated, there is no omniscient being — [we] reply: even though the body and such are causes, they alone, as mere auxiliary causes lacking the appropriating cause characterized by self-attachment, cannot generate passion and the like. Therefore, the body and such are non-probative of the absence of an omniscient being. Hence, even from the inference devised by others, the absence of an omniscient being [does not follow] due to the incapacity of [reasons such as] 'being an object of knowledge' and the like.

body.text: nāpi svavikalpitaṃ śābdādikaṃ bhagavato bādhakam / tathā hi yadyapi teṣāṃ sati prāmāṇye 'numāna evāntarbhāvaḥ, anantarbhāve cāprāmāṇyameveti sthūlaṃ dūṣaṇamasti, tathāpi tatprāmāṇyamabhyupagamyāpi brūmaḥ / yattāvat pauruṣeyavacanaṃ tadapramāṇameva bhavatām / na ca vaidikaṃ kiñcidvacanaṃ sarvanarāsarvajñatvapratipādaka mupalabhyate / pratyuta nimittanāmni śākhāntare sphuṭatarameva sarvajñaḥ pratipāditaḥ / tathā hi
body.translated_text: Nor is the Blessed One refuted by the <s>śabda</s> (verbal testimony) and other [means of knowledge] devised by you [opponents]. For although — if they are valid — they would be subsumed under inference, and if not subsumed, they would simply be invalid — this is a coarse refutation — nevertheless, accepting their validity for the sake of argument, we say: whatever is human speech (<s>pauruṣeya-vacana</s>) is indeed non-<s>pramāṇa</s> for you. And no Vedic statement whatsoever is found that establishes the non-omniscience of all men. Rather, in a different branch [of the <s>Veda</s>], in the section on omens (<s>nimitta</s>), the omniscient one is quite clearly established. For:

body.text: sa vetti viśvaṃ na ca tasya vettā
body.translated_text: 'He knows the universe, but no one knows him' —

body.text: ityādinā ca sarvajño vede pratipāditaḥ //
body.translated_text: By this and similar [passages], the omniscient one is established in the <s>Veda</s>.

body.text: nāpyupamānāttadabhāvaḥ sidhyati / tathā hi smaryamāṇameva gavādivastu purovartigavayādisādṛśyopādhi gavādyupādhi vā sādṛśyamupamānena pratīyata iti sthitiḥ / na ca sarvajñasantānavartīni cetāṃsi kenacit sarvajñenānubhūtāni yataḥ smaraṇena viṣayīkriyeran, paracittavitterayogāt //
body.translated_text: Nor is the absence of [the omniscient one] established through <s>upamāna</s> (analogy). For the established [view] is that what is cognized through <s>upamāna</s> is the similarity conditioned by the resemblance of the <s>gavaya</s> (wild ox) etc. present [before one] to a <s>go</s> (cow) etc. recalled [in memory], or [conditioned by] the <s>go</s>-predicate [applied to] the resemblance. And the mental states occurring in the continuum of an omniscient being have not been experienced by any omniscient being [known to us] such that they could be made objects of recollection — since cognizing another's mind is impossible [for ordinary persons].

body.text:
(#Nibandh 28#)
yat punaruktaṃ kumārilena
body.translated_text: [Nibandh 28] Furthermore, what <s>Kumārila</s> has said —

children.translated_text: 'Having seen that all present-day men are non-omniscient,
The certainty of non-omniscience of the rest [follows] by analogy with their resemblance.'

body.text: tadapyayuktam, adhunātanasarvanarāsarvajñatvāniścayāt / niścaye cātmanyeva sarvajñatvābhyupagamaprasaṅgāt /
body.translated_text: This too is untenable, because there is no certainty of the non-omniscience of all present-day men. And if there were such certainty, the absurd consequence of accepting omniscience in oneself [would follow].

body.text: nāpyarthāpattirbādhikā / yato dṛṣṭaḥ śruto vārtho 'nyathā nopapadyata iti adṛṣṭārthaṃparikalpanamarthāpattirucyate / na cāsarvajñatvamantareṇa sarvanareṣu kaścidartho dṛṣṭaḥ śruto vā nopapadyate yatastadarthāpattyā parikalpyeta / nanu saṃsārasya tāvadanāditvaṃ pramāṇena pratītam / tacca na sarvajñena jñāyate, tajjñānāvadheḥ parastādasattve 'nāditākṣatiprasaṅgāt, tadanyathānupapadyamānaṃ sarvabhāvānāmanāditvaṃ sarvajñābhāvaṃ sādhayatīti cet /
body.translated_text: Nor is <s>arthāpatti</s> (presumption) a refuter [of omniscience]. For <s>arthāpatti</s> is said to be the postulation of an unseen fact [when] a seen or heard fact cannot be explained otherwise. And there is no fact, seen or heard, regarding all men that cannot be explained except through non-omniscience, such that non-omniscience could be postulated through it. [You object:] But at least the beginninglessness of <s>saṃsāra</s> is cognized by a <s>pramāṇa</s>; and that cannot be known by an omniscient being, because if [time] before the limit of that knowledge were non-existent, the beginninglessness would be violated; and this — the beginninglessness of all things, which cannot be explained otherwise — establishes the absence of an omniscient being.

body.text: ucyate / upayuktasarvajñāpekṣayā tāvadidamadūṣaṇam / tasyānāditvājñāne 'pi upayuktasarvajñatvāvyāhateḥ / sarvasarvajñasyāpyabhāve sādhye 'samartheyamarthāpattiḥ / tathā hi yathā saṃsārasyānāditve pūrvapūrvavastusattāyā anavadhitvaṃ tathā sarvajñajñānasyāpi pūrvapūrvavastusattāvyāpakatvenānavadhiprasaratā iti / ajñātasyaikasyāpi vastuno 'navasthiteḥ / satyapi sarvajñe 'nāditvamupapadyamānaṃ na sarvajñābhāvamākṣipati / tataścārthāpattirapi na sarvajñasya bādhikā /
body.translated_text: [We] reply: With respect to a 'useful omniscient' (<s>upayukta-sarvajña</s>), this is no refutation, because even without knowledge of [absolute] beginninglessness, 'useful omniscience' is not contradicted. And if the absence of even an 'all-knowing omniscient' is what is to be proved, this <s>arthāpatti</s> is powerless. For just as the beginninglessness of <s>saṃsāra</s> implies the limitlessness of the existence of successive prior things, so too the knowledge of the omniscient, pervading the existence of each successive prior thing, has limitless extent. Since even one thing unknown [to the omniscient] has not been established. Beginninglessness is possible even when an omniscient being exists, so it does not entail the absence of an omniscient being. Therefore, <s>arthāpatti</s> too does not refute the omniscient being.

body.text: na cābhāvapramāṇabādhyaḥ sarvajñaḥ / pramāṇapañcakanivṛttirabhāvapramāṇamiṣyate / tatra nivṛttiriti prasajyavṛttyā pramāṇānutpattimātramabhipretam, atha vā paryudāsavṛttyā vastvantaram, vastvantaramapi jaḍarūpaṃ jñānarūpaṃ vā, jñānamapi jñānamātram, ekajñānasaṃsargivastujñānaṃ veti vikalpāḥ /
body.translated_text: Nor is the omniscient being refuted by the <s>pramāṇa</s> of non-perception (<s>abhāva</s>). What is accepted [by you] as the <s>pramāṇa</s> of non-existence is the cessation of the group of five <s>pramāṇas</s>. Now, 'cessation' here means — in the <s>prasajya</s> (implicative negation) reading — merely the non-arising of a <s>pramāṇa</s>; or, in the <s>paryudāsa</s> (exclusion) reading — some other entity. And that other entity is either of inert nature or of the nature of knowledge; and if knowledge, [it is] either mere knowledge, or knowledge of a thing connected with a single cognition — these are the alternatives.

body.text: tatra na tāvannivṛttimātrabhāvapramāṇamupapadyate / tatkhalu nikhilaśaktivikalatayā na kiñcit / yacca na kiñcit tatkathaṃ prameyaṃ paricchindyāt, tadviṣayaṃ vā vijñānaṃ janayet, pratītaṃ vā tatkathamiti sarvamandhakāranartanam / yathoktam
body.translated_text: Of these, the position that non-existence-<s>pramāṇa</s> is mere cessation is untenable. For that, being devoid of all capacity, is nothing at all. And how could what is nothing at all delimit an object of knowledge, or generate a cognition having it as its object? And how is it cognized? — thus everything is a dance of darkness. As it has been said:

body.text: na hyabhāvaḥ kasyacitpratipattiḥ pratipattiheturvā / tasyāpi vā kathaṃ pratipattiriti /
body.translated_text: 'For non-existence is not the cognition of anything, nor the cause of cognition. And how could there be cognition of it?' —

body.text: nāpi vastvantaratāpakṣe jaḍarūpaḥ pramāṇābhāvaḥ saṃgacchate, tasya prameyaparicchedāyogāt / paricchedasya jñānadharmatvāt / nāpi jñānamātrasvabhāvo 'bhāvaḥ / deśakālasvabhāvaviprakṛṣṭasyāpi tato 'bhāvaprasaṅgāt / tadapekṣayāpi vijñānamātratvāt tasya / athaikajñānasaṃsargisvabhāvo 'numanyate, tadā kṣatamabhāvapramāṇapratyāśayā, adhyakṣaviśeṣasyaivābhāvapramāṇanāmakaraṇāt / tasya cāsmābhirdṛśyānupalambhākhyasādhanatvena svīkṛtatvāt / dṛśyānupalambhaśca bhagavadabhāvasādhane 'samartha iti pūrvamevāveditam /
body.translated_text: Nor does non-existence-<s>pramāṇa</s> in the form of a real entity of inert nature make sense, because it cannot delimit an object of knowledge, since delimitation is a property of knowledge. Nor is non-existence of the nature of mere knowledge, because even what is remote in place, time, and nature would absurdly become its non-existence, since even with respect to that [remote thing], it [the knowledge] would be mere knowledge. If non-existence of the nature connected with a single cognition is accepted, then the hope placed in non-existence-<s>pramāṇa</s> is dashed, because it is just a particular type of direct perception that is given the name 'non-existence-<s>pramāṇa</s>.' And that has been accepted by us as having the probative force called 'non-apprehension of what is fit to be perceived' (<s>dṛśyānupalambha</s>). And the non-apprehension of what is fit to be perceived is incapable of proving the absence of the Blessed One — this has already been shown.

body.text:
(#Nibandh 29#)
kiṃ ca, kaḥ punarayaṃ pramāṇābhāvo 'bhimato bhavatām / svapramāṇagaṇanivṛttiratha sarvaprāṇigaṇapramāṇanivṛttiḥ / tatra svapramāṇagaṇanivṛttirvyabhicāriṇī, tasyāṃ satyāmapi vyavahitasyārthasyāna pahnavatvāt / parapramāṇanivṛttistvasarvavido 'siddhā /
yadāha
body.translated_text: [Nibandh 29] Moreover, what exactly is this 'non-existence of <s>pramāṇa</s>' accepted by you? Is it the cessation of your own group of <s>pramāṇas</s>, or the cessation of the <s>pramāṇas</s> of all living beings? Of these, the cessation of one's own group of <s>pramāṇas</s> is deviant [i.e., non-conclusive], because even when it obtains, a distant object cannot be denied. And the cessation of others' <s>pramāṇas</s> is unestablished for the omniscient one. As [<s>Dharmakīrti</s>] says:

children.translated_text: 'The non-perception by all is doubtful; non-perception by oneself is deviant [non-conclusive];
Because of the reality [of something] even when unseen — like the <s>dūrvā</s> grass in the caves of the <s>Vindhya</s> mountains.'

body.text: tadevaṃ nābhāvapramāṇato 'pi sarvajñaniṣedha iti sthitam //
body.translated_text: Thus it is established that even from the non-existence-<s>pramāṇa</s>, there is no negation of the omniscient being.

body.text:
nanu tathāpi sadvyavahārārthaṃ sādhakamapyasya na vidyate /
tathā hi sarvavido 'tīndriyatvāt na tāvadasmadādipratyakṣamasya sādhakam / yathā cāsmābhirasau nopalabhyate tathāsmajjātīyairapyapratyakṣasvabhāvaniyamāt / na cāyaṃ kālāntare 'bhūditi ca kalpanā yujyate / yathā hi kālatvādidānīntanakālavaditi anenānumānena nirākartuṃ śakyate, na tathā sādhayitum /
body.translated_text: But [you object:] even so, there is no positive means of establishing [the omniscient being] for the purpose of valid conduct. For since the omniscient being is beyond the senses, our perception and the like cannot be its means of proof. And just as he is not perceived by us, so too by those of our kind — due to the invariable rule of being imperceptible in nature. Nor is the supposition that 'he existed at another time' fitting, because just as [one can argue] 'since it is a time, [it is] like the present time' — by this inference [non-existence] can be negated, but [existence] cannot likewise be proved.

body.text: kārikā
body.translated_text: Verse:

children.translated_text: 'The supposition of an omniscient being by some, or the uncreated nature of the <s>Veda</s> —
Since [both] are equally supposed, this is to be considered:'
'An omniscient being is not seen by us and our like at present;
Like negation, the supposition "he did not exist" is possible.' Thus [says the opponent].

body.text: nāpyanumānataḥ sarvajñasiddhiḥ / tatpratibaddhaliṅgāniścayāt /
body.translated_text: Nor is the establishment of the omniscient being [possible] through inference, because there is no certainty of a mark (<s>liṅga</s>) invariably connected with it.

body.text: kiṃ ca sarvajñasattāsādhane sarvo hetuḥ trayīṃ doṣajātiṃ nātivartate asiddhatvaṃ viruddhatvamanaikāntikatvaṃ ceti / tathā hi sarvajñe dharmiṇi kriyamāṇe na taddharmo hetuḥ siddhaḥ / tasyaiva dharmiṇaḥ sādhyatvenāsiddhatvāt / siddhau vā vaiyarthyaprasaṅgāt / asarvajñe dharmiṇi na sarvajñasiddhiḥ / hetoḥ sarvajñaviparītasādhanatvena viruddhatvāt / nāpi sarvajñāsarvajñadharmo hetuḥ / tasyānaikāntikatvāt / tasmānnānumānato 'pi sarvajñasiddhiḥ /
body.translated_text: Moreover, every logical reason (<s>hetu</s>) in proving the existence of an omniscient being does not transcend the threefold class of faults: being unestablished (<s>asiddha</s>), being contradictory (<s>viruddha</s>), and being inconclusive (<s>anaikāntika</s>). For: when the omniscient being is made the subject (<s>dharmin</s>), no property [used as] a reason is established as belonging to it — because the very subject is unestablished, being what is to be proved; or if it is [already] established, the absurd consequence of purposelessness [of the proof] arises. When a non-omniscient being is the subject, the establishment of an omniscient being [does not follow] — because the reason would be contradictory, proving the opposite of omniscience. Nor can a property belonging to both omniscient and non-omniscient beings be a reason — because it would be inconclusive. Therefore, the omniscient being is not established through inference either.

body.text: kārikā
body.translated_text: Verse:

body.text: dṛṣṭo na caikadeśo 'sti liṅgaṃ yo vānumāpayet / iti //
body.translated_text: 'There is no observed [invariable connection], nor any partial [reason] that could inferentially indicate [omniscience].' Thus [says the opponent].

body.text: nāpyāgamagamyaḥ / āgamo hi dvividhaḥ pauruṣeyo nityaśca / tatra pauruṣeyopyāgamaḥ tadīyo vā tatra pramāṇam, narāntarapraṇīto vā / na tāvattadīyaḥ / anyo 'nyasaṃśrayāpatteḥ / tathā hyāgamasya sarvajñoktatve prāmāṇyam / asya ca prāmāṇye satyasmāt sarvajñasiddhiriti / narāntarapraṇītastu pramāṇatvenānabhimata evetyato 'pi na sarvajñasiddhiḥ //
body.translated_text: Nor is [the omniscient being] knowable through scripture (<s>āgama</s>). For scripture is of two kinds: human-authored (<s>pauruṣeya</s>) and eternal. Of these, the human-authored scripture — is the <s>pramāṇa</s> there [the omniscient being's] own, or one composed by another person? Not his own [scripture], because of the fault of mutual dependence. For: the scripture's authority [depends on] its being spoken by an omniscient being, and the establishment of the omniscient being [depends on] the authority of that [scripture]. And scripture composed by another person is not accepted as a <s>pramāṇa</s> [by you] — therefore, even from this [source], the omniscient being is not established.

body.text:
(#Nibandh 30#)
kiṃ ca sarvajñapraṇītādvacanāt sarvajñasiddhau kimaparāddhaṃ svavacanena yenāto 'pyasau na gamyeta / nāpi nityāgamagamyaḥ sarvajñaḥ, tathāvidhasya sarvajñapratipādakasya nityāgamasyābhāvāt / yaccopaniṣadādau sarvajñapratipādakavākyaṃ tasyānyārthatvaṃ draṣṭavyam / na ca nityavākyasyānityasarvajñatvapratipādakatvam, nirviṣayatvaprasaṅgāt /
body.translated_text: Furthermore, if omniscience is established from the words of an omniscient being, what fault has his own statement committed that omniscience should not be known from it? Nor is the omniscient being known through an eternal scripture, since there is no such eternal scripture that establishes an omniscient being. And as for the statement in the <s>Upaniṣads</s> and elsewhere that establishes an omniscient being, a different interpretation must be seen. Moreover, an eternal statement cannot establish a non-eternal omniscient being, since it would be without an object.

body.text: kiṃ ca yadyaṅgīkṛto nityāgamaḥ, kiṃ sarvajñakalpanayā, nitya evāgamo dharme pramāṇaṃ bhaviṣyati /
body.translated_text: Furthermore, if an eternal scripture is accepted, what need is there for postulating an omniscient being? The eternal scripture itself will be the <s>pramāṇa</s> (means of valid knowledge) regarding <s>dharma</s>.

body.text: kārikā
body.translated_text: Verse:

children.translated_text: The omniscient being cannot be established through scripture, nor scripture through him, because of mutual dependence.
How can the validity of a scripture composed by another person be established?

children.text: na cāpyevaṃ paro nityaḥ śakyo labdhumihāgamaḥ /
children.translated_text: Nor can an eternal scripture beyond this be obtained in this way.
If one is found, it would be mere <s>arthavāda</s> (eulogy); for the other view, it would mean non-eternality.

body.text:
āgamasya ca nityatve siddhe tatkalpanā vṛthā /
yatastaṃ pratipatsyante dharmameva tato narāḥ /
body.translated_text: And if the eternality of scripture is established, then the postulation of an omniscient being is futile; for from that, people will understand <s>dharma</s> itself directly.

body.text: bṛhaṭṭīkāpi
body.translated_text: The <s>Bṛhaṭṭīkā</s> (Great Commentary) also states:

body.text: na cāgamavidhiḥ kaścinnityaḥ sarvajñabodhakaḥ /
body.translated_text: "There is no eternal scriptural injunction that reveals an omniscient being" —

body.text: ityādi saptacatvāriṃśat ślokāḥ saprapañcametamarthaṃ pratipādayanti / tadevamāgamato 'pi na sarvajñasiddhiḥ /
body.translated_text: thus forty-seven verses with elaboration establish this very point. Therefore, even from scripture, omniscience is not established.

body.text: nāpyupamānapramāṇasamadhigamyaḥ / upamānaṃ hi sadṛśagrahaṇanāntarīyakapravṛttika masannikṛṣṭārthagocaram / yathā gavayagrahaṇadvāreṇa goḥ smaraṇam / na ca sarvajñasadṛśaḥ kaścidasti /
body.translated_text: Nor is the omniscient being cognizable through the <s>pramāṇa</s> of <s>upamāna</s> (analogy). For <s>upamāna</s> operates necessarily through the apprehension of similarity and has as its object something not in proximity — as, for example, the recollection of a cow through the apprehension of a <s>gavaya</s> (wild ox). But there is no one similar to an omniscient being.

body.text: kārikā
body.translated_text: Verse:

children.translated_text: If we were to see someone similar to an omniscient being now,
then we could know the omniscient being through <s>upamāna</s> (analogy).

body.text: nāpyarthāpattitaḥ sarvajñasiddhiḥ / dṛṣṭaḥ śruto vārtho 'nyathā nopapadyate iti adṝṣṭārthaparikalpanamarthāpattilakṣaṇam / na cātra pramāṇapratītaṃ kiñcid vastvasti yatsarvajñamantareṇānupapadyamānaṃ tatsattāmupanayet / tannārthāpattirapi sarvajñasādhanī /
body.translated_text: Nor is omniscience established through <s>arthāpatti</s> (presumption). The definition of <s>arthāpatti</s> is: the postulation of an unseen matter when a seen or heard matter cannot be explained otherwise. But here there is no real entity cognized by a <s>pramāṇa</s> which, being inexplicable without an omniscient being, would lead one to posit his existence. Therefore <s>arthāpatti</s> too does not establish omniscience.

body.text: na ca pramāṇapañcakābhāvasvabhāvādabhāvapramāṇādasya siddhiḥ, vastvabhāvasādhanatvādasya / pratyutāyamevāsyābhāvaṃ sādhayatīti pratipāditam / yadapīdaṃ kārikābṛhaṭṭīkayorekaṣaṣṭyā ślokaiḥ sarvajñasiddhaye bauddhasya sādhanamāśaṅkaya dūṣitaṃ tadapi ghṛṇākaramiti granthavistarabhayānna likhitam /
body.translated_text: Nor is omniscience established through the <s>pramāṇa</s> of <s>abhāva</s> (non-existence), whose nature is the absence of the five <s>pramāṇas</s>, since its function is to establish the non-existence of a real entity. On the contrary, it has been demonstrated that this very <s>abhāva-pramāṇa</s> establishes the non-existence of omniscience. As for the refutation — in sixty-one verses of the <s>Kārikā</s> and <s>Bṛhaṭṭīkā</s> — of the Buddhist's proof for establishing omniscience, which was raised as an objection, that too is repugnant, and out of fear of expanding the text it has not been recorded here.

body.text:
(#Nibandh 31#)
tathā hyetāni kila saugataiḥ sarvajñasādhanāya sādhanānyabhidhīyante
sarvajño 'stīti satyam,
body.translated_text: For it is said that the following proofs are offered by the Buddhists for establishing an omniscient being: 'An omniscient being exists — this is true,

body.text: sarvajñoktatvāt, dharmābhyupadeśakatvāt, buddhaḥ sarvajña iti cirapravṛttadṛḍhasmṛteḥ, prathamataramaśeṣaśiṣyajanavargasyānekavidhacittacaittādiparijñānāt, sakalapadārtharāśitattvopadeśāditi //
body.translated_text: because of being stated by an omniscient being, because of being a teacher of <s>dharma</s>, because of the firm and long-standing tradition that the <s>Buddha</s> is omniscient, because of the initial comprehension of the manifold mental states and mental factors of the entire multitude of disciples, and because of the teaching of the true nature of the totality of all entities.'

body.text: tasmāt sthitametat nātīndriyadarśī sākṣādasti, api tu nityavacanadvāreṇaiva tasya darśanamiti / tadevaṃ sarvathā sarvajñasādhakapramāṇāsabhavādayukto bauddhānāṃ sarvajñe sadvyavahāra iti //
body.translated_text: Therefore this stands: there is no direct perceiver of the supersensuous; rather, its perception is only through the medium of eternal words. Thus, since there is in every way no <s>pramāṇa</s> establishing omniscience, the Buddhists' positive usage regarding an omniscient being is unjustified.

body.text: atrocyate / anumānādanyato 'siddhau siddhasādhanam / anumānādapītyasiddham, anumānasya pūrvamuktatvāt / tatpratibaddhaliṅgāniścayādityādidūṣaṇaprabandho 'pi prativyūḍha ityupayuktasarvajñastāvat trailokyālokaḥ siddhaḥ /
body.translated_text: To this we reply: That omniscience is not established from anything other than inference is a case of proving what is already established. That it is not established even from inference — this is itself unestablished, since inference has already been stated. The series of objections beginning with 'because of the uncertainty of the logical mark connected with it' has also been refuted. Therefore, the omniscient being useful [for our purposes], the Light of the Three Worlds, is established.

body.text: sarvasarvajñapakṣe 'pīdaṃ sādhanam /
body.translated_text: Even for the thesis that everyone is omniscient, this proof applies:

body.text: yatpramāṇasaṃvādiniścitārthavacanaṃ tatsākṣātparamparā(vā) tadarthasākṣātkārijñānapūrvakam /
body.translated_text: Whatever is a statement of a matter ascertained in accordance with a <s>pramāṇa</s> (valid means), that is preceded — directly or indirectly — by a cognition that directly perceives that object.

body.text: yathā dahano dāhaka iti vacanam /
body.translated_text: For example, the statement 'fire is capable of burning.'

body.text: pramāṇasaṃvādi niścitārthavacanaṃ cedam /
body.translated_text: And this [statement of the <s>Buddha</s>] is a statement of a matter ascertained in accordance with a <s>pramāṇa</s>.

body.text: kṣaṇikāḥ sarvajñasaṃskārā ityarthataḥ kāryahetuḥ / nāsyāsiddhiḥ, sarvabhāvakṣaṇabhaṅgaprasādhanādasya vacanasya satyārthatvāt / nāpi virodhaḥ, sapakṣe bhāvāt / na cānaikāntikaḥ, vacanamātrasya saṃśayaviparyāsapūrvakatve 'pi pramāṇaniścitārthavacanasya sākṣātpāramparyeṇa tadarthasākṣātkārijñānapūrvakatvāt / anyathā niyamena pramāṇasaṃvādāyogāt //
body.translated_text: Since all <s>saṃskāras</s> (mental formations) are momentary — this, in substance, is a <s>kāryahetu</s> (reason based on effect). There is no non-establishment of it, since this statement has a true content, as established by the proof that all entities are momentary. Nor is there contradiction, since the reason is present in the <s>sapakṣa</s> (similar instances). Nor is it inconclusive, because although a mere statement may be preceded by doubt or error, a statement of a matter ascertained by a <s>pramāṇa</s> is preceded — directly or indirectly — by a cognition that directly perceives that object; otherwise, agreement with the <s>pramāṇa</s> would invariably not obtain.

body.text: ayaṃ ca bhāṣyakārīyaḥ sarvasarvajñaprasādhakaprayogaḥ paṇḍitajitāribhiḥ prapañcita iti tata eva pracayato 'badhārya iti /
body.translated_text: And this proof, which establishes that everyone [who makes such statements] is omniscient, belongs to the <s>Bhāṣyakāra</s> (Commentator) and has been elaborated by the learned <s>Jitāri</s>; therefore it should be understood from that text in full.

body.text:
daurvāraprativādivikramamanādṛtya pramāprauḍhitaḥ
sarvajño jagadekacakṣurudagādeṣa prabhāvo 'tra ca / saṃbuddhasthitimedinīkulagirerasmadguroḥ kintvayaṃ
saṃkṣepo mama ratnakīrtikṛtinastadvistaratrāsinaḥ //
body.translated_text: Disregarding the irresistible prowess of opponents, the omniscient one — the sole eye of the world — arose, firmly established in truth, and herein lies his power. But this is merely a summary by me, <s>Ratnakīrti</s>, who is afraid of the full elaboration, regarding the king-of-mountains foundation of the established <s>Saṃbuddha</s> (Fully Awakened One), our teacher.

children.translated_text: May the world attain well-being from this! May <s>Rati</s> and <s>Manmatha</s> (the god of love) delight as they wish!
And may <s>Mañjuvajra</s> at the end grant the fruit of goodness at his feet!
May I become <s>Mañjuvajra</s>, or <s>Mañjughoṣa</s>, or <s>Mañjuvāk</s>,
or <s>Mañjuśrī</s>, or the splendid <s>Mañjukumāra</s>, the upholder of the <s>Jinas</s> (Victorious Ones)!

body.text: // sarvajñasiddhiḥsamāptā //
body.translated_text: Thus the <s>Sarvajñasiddhi</s> (Proof of Omniscience) is completed.
Section 2:

body.text: // īśvarasādhanadūṣaṇam //
body.translated_text: Refutation of the Proof of <s>Īśvara</s> (God).

body.text: oṃ namastārāyai /
body.translated_text: Oṃ, homage to <s>Tārā</s>!

children.translated_text: Being a repository of jewels of well-spoken words, this surpasses the ocean of jewels.
Something is extracted and written here to call to mind the ocean of the teacher's words.
This style is a treasure of nectar for the wise who abide in the middle path;

children.text: vidveṣiṇi viṣajvālā kiñcijjñe tu na kiñcana //
children.translated_text: for the hostile it is a flame of poison; for the half-learned it is nothing at all.

body.text: ihaite naiyāyikādayo vivādapadasya kṣitidharādeḥ svarūpopādānopakaraṇasaṃpradānaprayojanavibhāgapravīṇaṃ sarvajñatādiguṇaviśiṣṭaṃ puruṣaviśeṣamicchanti / yadāhuḥ
body.translated_text: Here these <s>Naiyāyikas</s> (logicians) and others posit a special being (<s>puruṣaviśeṣa</s>) — distinguished by qualities such as omniscience — who is skilled in the intrinsic nature, material cause, instrumental cause, giving, and purposive distinction of the objects of dispute such as the earth and the like. As they say:

children.translated_text: "He is one, omnipresent, all-knowing, the sole support of intelligence, eternal, called <s>Īśvara</s> (God),
accepted as the authority and creator of the world, to be sought by those desiring heaven and liberation."

body.text: sa ca kathaṃ sidhyatīti paryanuyuktāḥ sādhanamidamācakṣate /
body.translated_text: When asked how he is established, they state this proof:

body.text: vivādādhyāsitaṃ buddhimaddhetukam /
body.translated_text: The object of dispute has an intelligent cause,

body.text: kāryatvāt /
body.translated_text: because it is an effect.

body.text: yat kāryaṃ tadbuddhimaddhetukam / yathā ghaṭaḥ /
body.translated_text: Whatever is an effect has an intelligent cause — for example, a pot.

body.text: kāryaṃ cedam /
body.translated_text: And this [world] is an effect.

body.text: tasmād buddhimaddhetukamiti /
body.translated_text: Therefore it has an intelligent cause.

body.text: hetoḥ parokṣārthapratipādakatvamanubhūteṣu hetvābhāseṣu na śakyamāvedayitum / hetvābhāsāśca pañca / yathoktam
body.translated_text: The capacity of a reason to establish an imperceptible object cannot be demonstrated when the pseudo-reasons have been experienced. And there are five pseudo-reasons. As stated:

body.text: savyabhicāraviruddhaprakaraṇasamasādhyasamātītakālā iti /
body.translated_text: "The deviant, the contradictory, the unestablished-as-reason, the equal-to-what-is-to-be-proved, and the past-its-time."

body.text: tatra na tāvadayaṃ sādhyasamo hetuḥ / asiddho hi sādhyasamaḥ kathyate / sa ca saṃkṣepato vibhajyamāno dvidhā vyavatiṣṭhate / āśrayāsiddhatvād vāsiddho yathā surabhi gaganāravindamaravindatvāditi / satyapi cāśraye pramāṇena saṃbandhāsiddherasiddho (#Nibandh 33#) yathā anityaḥ śabdaḥ sāvayavatvāditi / na cābhyāṃ prakārābhyāṃ prastutasya hetorasiddhirasti / kṣmāruhādau dharmiṇi pramāṇasamadhigate kāryatvasya sādhanasya pramāṇapratītatvāt / cirotpannaparvatādau ca dharmiṇi kāryatvaṃ sāvayavatvena hetunā boddhavyam / tad yathā
body.translated_text: Now, firstly, this reason is not <s>sādhyasama</s> (equal to what is to be proved). For what is called <s>sādhyasama</s> is unestablished. And that, when briefly analyzed, is of two kinds: unestablished because the locus is unestablished — as in 'the sky-lotus is fragrant, because it is a lotus'; or unestablished because the relation is not established by a <s>pramāṇa</s> even though the locus exists — as in 'sound is impermanent, because it has parts.' But the present reason is not unestablished in either of these ways, since effecthood, the proving property, is established by a <s>pramāṇa</s> in the <s>dharmin</s> (subject), namely trees and the like, which are cognized by <s>pramāṇa</s>. And in subjects such as mountains that originated long ago, effecthood should be understood through the reason of having parts. Thus:

body.text: vivādapadaṃ kāryam /
body.translated_text: The object of dispute is an effect,

body.text: sāvayavatvāt /
body.translated_text: because it has parts.

body.text: yatsāvayavaṃ tat kāryam / yathā vastram /
body.translated_text: Whatever has parts is an effect — for example, a cloth.

body.text: tathā cedam /
body.translated_text: And this is likewise.

body.text: tasmāt kāryamiti /
body.translated_text: Therefore it is an effect.

body.text: nanu sāvayavatvena hetunā dravyāṇāmeva kāryatvaṃ sidhyati / na tu tatsamavetānāṃ guṇakarmādīnām / teṣāmavayavasaṃbandhābhāvāditi cet / satyam / teṣāṃ kāryaguṇāditvena hetvantareṇa kāryatvamadhigantavyam / tathā hi
body.translated_text: Objection: By the reason of having parts, the effecthood of only substances is established, not of qualities, actions, and the like that inhere in them, since they lack the relation of parts. Reply: True. Their effecthood must be understood through another reason, namely their being effect-qualities and the like. Thus:

body.text: janmabhājo vivādādhyāsitanityetarasamavāyino guṇādayaḥ /
body.translated_text: The qualities and the like that are the objects of dispute, which are non-eternal and inhere in things subject to origination, are subject to origination,

body.text: kāryaguṇāditvāt /
body.translated_text: because they are effect-qualities and the like.

body.text: yo yaḥ kāryaguṇādiḥ sa sarvastathā, yathā ghaṭādirūpādiḥ /
body.translated_text: Whatever is an effect-quality and the like is always so — for example, the color and the like of a pot.

body.text: tathā caite /
body.translated_text: And these are likewise.

body.text: tasmājjanmabhājaḥ / iti /
body.translated_text: Therefore they are subject to origination.

body.text: kāryatvaṃ ca na svakāraṇasamavāyaḥ, sāmānyaviśeṣo vā boddhavyaḥ, yenāsya pradhvaṃsāvyāpakatvād bhāgāsiddhatā syāt, kiṃ tu kāraṇādhīnasvarūpamātram / tacca śabdādiṣviva pradhvaṃsādāvapi pratyakṣeṇādhigatamiti na tāvadayamasiddho hetuḥ / nāpi viruddhaḥ / tathā hi yo vipakṣa eva vartate sa khalu sādhyaviparyayavyāpteḥ sādhyaviruddhaṃ sādhayan viruddho 'bhidhīyate / yathā nityaḥ śabdaḥ kṛtakatvāditi / na cāyaṃ tathā, prasiddhakartṛkeṣu ghaṭādiṣu sapakṣeṣu sadbhāvadarśanāt /
body.translated_text: And effecthood should not be understood as co-inherence in one's own cause, or as a universal or a particular, for then there would be the fault of partial non-establishment due to its non-applicability to destruction; rather, it is merely the dependence of one's own nature on a cause. And that is ascertained by perception even in destruction and the like, just as in sound and the like. Therefore this is not an unestablished reason. Nor is it contradictory. For indeed, one that is present only in the dissimilar instances is called contradictory, since, being pervaded by the opposite of what is to be proved, it proves what is opposed to what is to be proved — as in 'sound is permanent, because it is produced.' But this reason is not like that, since its presence is observed in the similar instances, namely pots and the like, which have a known maker.

body.text: nanu buddhimatpūrvakatve sādhye siddhasādhanam / abhimataṃ hi pareṣāmapi karmajatvaṃ kāryajātasya, karmaṇaśca cetanātmakatvāt, cetanāhetukatvādvā / taddhetukatvaṃ ca jagataḥ / sarvajñapūrvakatve tu sādhye vyāptiḥ svapne 'pi nopalabddhā / dṛṣṭāntaśca sādhyahīnaḥ, kulālādīnāmasarvajñatvāt / viruddhatā ca hetorasarvajñapūrvakatvenaiva kumbhādau kāryatvasya vyāpterupalabdheḥ / na copalabdhimatpūrvakatvamātraṃ sādhanaviṣayaḥ, tadviśeṣasya tu sarvajñapūrvakatvasyātadviṣayasyāpi tataḥ siddhiriti sāmpratam / tathā hi yadyasau viśeṣo na sādhanaviṣayaḥ kathamatastatsiddhiḥ, siddhaṃ vā kathamaviṣayaḥ, viṣayaścet kathamananvayadoṣaṃ na spṛśediti cet /
body.translated_text: Objection: When 'having an intelligent prior cause' is what is to be proved, this is a case of proving what is already established. For even the opponents accept that the class of effects is produced by <s>karma</s> (action), and <s>karma</s> is of the nature of consciousness or caused by consciousness. And the world is caused by that. But when 'having an omniscient prior cause' is what is to be proved, the pervasion has not been apprehended even in a dream. And the example is devoid of the <s>sādhya</s> (property to be proved), since potters and the like are not omniscient. Moreover, the reason is contradictory, since the pervasion of effecthood with having a non-omniscient prior cause is indeed apprehended in pots and the like. And it is not the case that the mere having of a cognizing prior cause is the subject of the proof, while the particular — namely having an omniscient prior cause — which is not its subject, is also established from that. Reply: To this we say —

body.text: ucyate / sāmānyamātravyāptāvapi antarbhāvitaviśeṣasya sāmānyasya pakṣadharmatāvaśena sādhyadharmiṇyanumānāt viśeṣaviṣayamanumānaṃ bhavatyeva / itarathā sarvānumānocchedaprasaṅgāt / (#Nibandh 34#) tathā hi vahnayanumānamapi na sāmānyamātraviṣayam, tasya prāgeva siddhatvāt / nāpi tadviśiṣṭagirigocaram vahnitvasāmānyasya tatsambandhābhāvena tadviśeṣaṇatvānupapatteḥ / itarathā gotvasamavāyādiva gāvaḥ śābaleyādayaḥ parvato 'pi vahnitvasamavāyād vahniḥ prasajyeta / astyeva girervahnitvena saṃyuktasamavāyaḥ saṃbandha iti cet / tarhi nāpratipadya parvatasaṃyuktaṃ vahniviśeṣamasau śakyapratipattiriti vahniviśeṣasyāpyananumānam / tathā cānanvayadoṣaprasaṅgaḥ / indriyānumāne 'pyayameva nyāyo draṣṭavyaḥ, yathendriyalakṣaṇakaraṇaviśeṣasiddhiḥ / tathā hi tatrāpi nendriyakaraṇikā kācit kriyopalabdhā / na khalu cchidādyāḥ kriyā indriyasādhanā, vraścanādīnāmanindriyatvāt / na ca vraścanādisādhanā saṃbhavati rūpādiparicchittilakṣaṇā kriyā / tasmād yathā kriyātvasāmānyasya karaṇamātrādhīnatvavyāptatve pakṣadharmatāvaśādindriyalakṣaṇakaraṇaviśeṣasiddhistathehāpi satyapi kāryatvasyopādānopakaraṇasaṃpradānaprayojanajñakartṛmātravyāptatve 'pi vivādādhyāsiteṣu pakṣadharmatāvaśādupādānādyabhijñasāmānyasyākṣiptaviśeṣasyaiva siddhiḥ / anyathā sāmānyasyāpi vyāpakābhimatasya na siddhiḥ syāt, nirviśeṣasyāsaṃbhavadviśeṣasya vā tasyānupapatteḥ / asarvajñasya cātrādṛṣṭādibhedavijñānarahitasyādhiṣṭhātṛbhāvāsaṃbhavāt sarvajñātmaka eva viśeṣo balādāpatati /
body.translated_text: It is replied: Even when the pervasion extends only to the general property (<s>sāmānya</s>), the inference yields a specific conclusion (<s>viśeṣa</s>), because by the force of the property-of-the-subject (<s>pakṣadharmatā</s>), the general property in which the specific is subsumed is inferred to apply to the subject under debate. Otherwise there would be the consequence of the destruction of all inference. For the inference of fire too is not directed at the mere generality, since that is already established beforehand. Nor is it directed at fire as qualified by the specific mountain, because the generality of fire-ness, having no connection with that [mountain], cannot serve as a qualifier of it. Otherwise, just as cows such as <s>Śābaleya</s> etc. [are inferred] from the inherence of cow-ness, a mountain too would absurdly be fire from the inherence of fire-ness. If it is said that the mountain indeed has the relation of conjunct-inherence (<s>saṃyukta-samavāya</s>) with fire-ness—then without first apprehending the particular fire conjoined with the mountain, that [inference] cannot be grasped, and so the particular fire too is not inferred [directly]. And thus the fault of non-concomitance (<s>ananvaya</s>) would follow. The same reasoning should be applied to the inference of sense-organs: namely, how the specific instrument characterized as a sense-organ is established. For there too, no action performed by sense-organ-instruments is observed. Indeed, actions such as cutting are not accomplished by sense-organs, since cutting-instruments etc. are not sense-organs. Nor does the action characterized as the apprehension of form etc. admit of cutting-instruments etc. as means. Therefore, just as, given the pervasion of the generality of action-ness by mere instrumentality, the specific instrument characterized as a sense-organ is established by the force of the property-of-the-subject—so here too, even though the property of being-an-effect (<s>kāryatva</s>) is pervaded only by [being preceded by] a mere maker who knows the material cause, subsidiary cause, recipient, and purpose, the establishment [of the specific] occurs by the force of the property-of-the-subject with respect to the disputed [entities]: namely, the general [maker] who knows the material cause etc. with the specific [i.e., omniscience] subsumed. Otherwise, even the generality, held to be the pervader, would not be established, since it is impossible without a specific [instantiation], or [its] specific [instantiation] would be impossible. And since a non-omniscient being, lacking knowledge of the distinctions of unseen merit (<s>adṛṣṭa</s>) etc., cannot be the presiding controller—the specific [conclusion] of omniscience forcefully follows.

body.text: nanūpādānādyabhijñakartṛ mātreṇevāsarvajñatvadehitvādibhirapi vyāptiraśakyaparihārā, vyabhicārādarśanasya samānatvāditi cet / na sarvajñatvāsarvajñatvayordehitvādehitvayorvā kāryotpattāvanupayogāt / na hi sārvajñyaṃ kartṛṇāṃ yogyatāmupasthāpayati, asarvajñebhyaḥ kumbhakārādibhyaḥ kumbhādīnāmaprasavaprasaṅgāt / nāpyasārvajñyaṃ kumbhakārādeva keyūrādīnāmapyutpattiprasaṅgāt / tathā na dehitvaṃ kāryotpattāvupayogi kumbhakārādeva keyūrādīnāmutpattiprasaṅgāt /nādehitvaṃ kumbhakārād ghaṭādīnāmanutpādaprasaṅgāt / tataśvopādānādyabhijñapuruṣapūrvakatvameva kāryatvasya vyāpakam / tadeva ca buddhimatpuruṣapūrvakatvaśabdavācyam / tena yadyapi buddhimatpūrvakatvamātraṃ vyāptiviṣayastathāpi tadviśeṣasya sarvajñatvasya pakṣadharmatābalāt pratilambha iti viśeṣaviṣayamanumānam / na coktadoṣaprasaṅgaḥ, tasya sādhyadṛṣdāntayordharmavikalpādutkarṣāpakarṣalakṣaṇaparyanuyogasya sarvānumānasādhāraṇyenānumānamātraprāmāṇyapratikṣepahetutvāt /
body.translated_text: If it is objected: 'The pervasion by non-omniscience, embodiedness, etc. is equally irrefutable, since the non-observation of deviation is the same'—no, because omniscience/non-omniscience and embodiedness/disembodiedness are irrelevant to the production of effects. For omniscience does not establish the competence of makers—otherwise there would be the absurd consequence that pots etc. would not be produced by non-omniscient potters and the like. Nor is non-omniscience [relevant], for then armlets etc. would absurdly be produced by the potter alone. Likewise, embodiedness is not relevant to the production of effects, for then armlets etc. would absurdly be produced by the potter alone. Nor disembodiedness, for then pots etc. would absurdly not be produced by the potter. Therefore, the pervader of being-an-effect is precisely [being preceded by] a person who knows the material cause etc. And that alone is what is denoted by the term 'being preceded by an intelligent person.' Hence, although the scope of pervasion is only 'being preceded by an intelligent being' in general, the specific [conclusion of] omniscience is obtained by the force of the property-of-the-subject—thus the inference has a specific object. Nor does the stated fault arise, because the cross-examination regarding superiority and inferiority arising from the differentiation of properties in the <s>sādhya</s> and the example is common to all inferences and would undermine the authority of inference in general.

body.text: etena yaduktaṃ kaṇikāyāṃ yadi kulālādīnāṃ katipayopakaraṇādijñānaṃ, na samastopakaraṇādijñatā, tarhi tenaiva nidarśanena īśvarasyāpi tadupakaraṇādimātrajñānam / tanmātrajñāne na sarvajñatāsiddhiḥ / katipayajño hi tathā sati syāt / na vā tanmātrajñānamapīśvarasya bālādivadityāha / vālonmattādīnāṃ svakāryaprayojanāparijñāne (#Nibandh 35#) 'pi nirabhiprāyāṇāṃ tatra tatra pravṛttidarśanāt / na ca kulālādayo nidarśanam na vālādaya ityatra niyamaheturastīti tannirastam //
body.translated_text: By this, what was stated in the <s>Kaṇikā</s> [of <s>Vācaspati</s>]—'If potters etc. have knowledge of only some subsidiary instruments etc. and not knowledge of all instruments etc., then by that very illustration, God too would have knowledge of only those instruments etc. If He has knowledge of only those, then omniscience is not established; for He would then be one who knows only some things. Or else God would not have even that much knowledge, like a child'—[this objection] and his statement—'Since even infants and madmen, without knowledge of their own purpose in action, are seen to engage in various activities without deliberate intent, and there is no determining reason that potters etc. are the example rather than infants etc.'—all this is refuted.

body.text: īśvarasya hi katipayātīndriyopakaraṇādijñāne tatkāraṇasya sarvatra samānatvādaśeṣopakaraṇādijñatāyā durvāratvāt / kāraṇaṃ ca tajjñāne sattāmantareṇa nānyat, dharmādharmādīnāṃ laukikapratyāsattihetūnāṃ tatrāsaṃbhavāt / kāraṇābhede ca kāryābhedaḥ / anyathā katipayātīndriyajñānamapi na syāt / yathā hi kulālādistulyadarśanasāmagrīkeṣu nākiñcijjñāḥ tathātīndriyopakaraṇādiṣvapīśvaraḥ, sāmarthyasyāviśeṣāt / na ca bālonmattādinidarśanena katipayopakaraṇajñatāniṣedho yuktaḥ, bījadṛṣṭāntena buddhimanmātrasyāpi niṣedhābhidhānaprasaṅgāt / tasmād yathopādānādyabhijñasyāpi saṃbhavād bījādibhirna vyabhicārābhidhānam, tathā bālonmattādibhirapīti kulālādīnāmeva dṛṣṭāntatā yuktimatī, upādānādyabhijñabuddhivanmātrakāryatvayoḥ sādhyasādhanayostatra prasiddhatvāt / tathā jñānavadīśvarasya cikīrṣāprayatnaunityāvityatrāpi /
body.translated_text: For if God has knowledge of even some supersensory instruments etc., then since the cause of that knowledge is the same everywhere, His knowledge of all instruments etc. without remainder is unavoidable. And the cause of that knowledge is nothing other than [His] existence (<s>sattā</s>), since worldly proximate causes such as merit and demerit (<s>dharma-adharma</s>) etc. are impossible in His case. And when the cause is undifferentiated, the effect is undifferentiated. Otherwise, even the knowledge of some supersensory things would not obtain. For just as potters etc. are not ignorant of everything when the same perceptual conditions obtain, so too God is not [ignorant] regarding supersensory instruments etc., since there is no difference in capacity. And the denial of knowledge of some instruments by the illustration of infants and madmen is unjustified, for by the illustration of a seed [which is non-conscious], even an intelligent being in general could be denied [the capacity for knowledge]. Therefore, just as deviation is not asserted on the basis of seeds etc. because a person who knows material causes etc. is also possible [as the cause], so too [deviation is not asserted] on the basis of infants and madmen—and thus the example-status of potters etc. alone is reasonable, since the <s>sādhya</s> and <s>sādhana</s>—namely, being preceded by an intelligent being who knows material causes etc. and being-an-effect—are well-established there. The same applies to God's knowledge, desire-to-act, and effort being eternal.

body.text: yadabhihitam - nityau cet kimīśvarasya jñānena cikīrṣāprayatnopayoginā, tayornityatvāt, svotpādopayogānapekṣaṇādityādi / tadapyasāram / ajñātakartṛtvānupapatteḥ / jñānaṃ hi yatra cikīrṣāprayatnāvanityau tatra tāvupasthāpayadupakaraṇādikamupadarśayati / yatra tu tau nityau tatropakaraṇādikamupadarśayadapi saphalam / tasmāt satyapi cikīrṣāprayatnayornityatve saphalamīśvarajñānaṃ sākṣātkāryotpattāvanupayogyapi / ata eva ca so 'yamīdṛśo viśeṣo vicārāsahaḥ kathaṃ pakṣadharmatābalādapi sādhyadharmiṇyupasaṃhriyata ityādirapi pralāpa eva / īśvarajñānasyāvyāhatau sarvajñatāviśeṣasya durvāratvāt /
body.translated_text: As for the objection: 'If [desire and effort] are eternal, what use is God's knowledge, which serves desire-to-act and effort, since those being eternal, they do not depend on their own production [by knowledge]?'—that too is without substance, because agency without knowledge is impossible. For where desire-to-act and effort are non-eternal, knowledge, by presenting those [to the agent], reveals the instruments etc. Where, however, those two are eternal, [knowledge], even while revealing the instruments etc., is fruitful [in a different way]. Therefore, even though desire-to-act and effort are eternal, God's knowledge is fruitful, even if not directly useful for the production of the effect. And for this very reason, the objection 'How can such a specific [property as omniscience], which does not withstand analysis, be attributed to the subject by the force of the property-of-the-subject alone?' is mere prattle—since, given the unobstructedness of God's knowledge, the specific [conclusion of] omniscience is unavoidable.

body.text: yadabhihitam - prekṣāvatāṃ pravṛttiḥ prayojanavattayā vyāptā / na ceśvarasya prekṣāvato jagannirmāṇe prayojanamutpaśyāmaḥ, prāptanikhilaprāpaṇīyasya prāptavyābhāvāt / tadapi sāvadyam, tadabhiprāyasya durvodhatvāt, prayojanābhāvāsiddheḥ, vyāpakānupalabdheḥ, sandigdhatvāt / vicitrā hi puruṣamātrasya cetovṛttiḥ prāgeva viśvasya kartuḥ / prāptanikhilaprāpaṇīyasyāpi karūṇayāpi parārthapravṛttaḥ saṃbhāvyamānatvāt / na cāsya narakādinirmāṇapravṛttiḥ kāruṇikatāmupahanti, pratyuta pituḥ putragaṇḍapāṭanavṛttirivālpaduḥkhadānena prabhūtadāruṇaduḥkhāpanayanāt karuṇātiśayameva gamayati / prekṣāvatāmivāsyāpi niyatasthirapravṛttisiddheḥ prayojanānumitireva nyāyaprāptā //
body.translated_text: As for the objection: 'The activity of a deliberate agent is pervaded by purposefulness. And we do not see any purpose for God, a deliberate agent, in the creation of the world, since for one who has obtained everything obtainable, there is nothing to be obtained'—that too is faulty: because His intention is difficult to fathom; because the absence of purpose is unestablished; because of the non-apprehension of the pervader [i.e., purposelessness is not established]; because it is doubtful. For the mental activity of a mere person is varied—how much more so that of the creator of the universe. Even for one who has obtained everything obtainable, activity for others' sake out of compassion (<s>karuṇā</s>) is conceivable. Nor does His activity in creating hells etc. undermine His compassionate nature; rather, just as a father's act of lancing his sons' boils, by giving a small pain to remove a great and terrible suffering, indicates an excess of compassion. Since His activity, like that of a deliberate agent, is established as determined and steady, the inference of purpose is indeed warranted.

body.text: yaccedamudīritam - yadi hi sarvakāryāṇāmekaḥ kartā syāt tato 'jñasya (#Nibandh 36#) tattvānupapatteḥ sarvajñatā syāt / atha punarekaikaṃ kāryamekaikena kartrā janyata iti yo yajjanayati sa tatkāraṇamātrajña eva na tu sarvajña iti /
body.translated_text: As for the objection: 'If all effects had a single maker, then since an ignorant being cannot be that, omniscience would follow. But if each effect is produced by a separate maker, then each one who produces something knows only the causes of that thing, and is not omniscient'—

body.text: atrocyate / kāryaliṅgāviśeṣādekaḥ kartā saditi jñānāviśeṣāt sattaikatvavat / kutaścilliṅgādanumitasya vastuno nānātvasya liṅgāntarānumeyatvāt, nānātvamupapādayituṃ pramāṇāntaraṃ vaktavyam / yathātmanānātvamavasthāpayadbhiḥ sukhādi (bhirnānātva) vyavasthāpanamucyate / na ceha karturanekatvādhigame pramāṇāntaramasti / ekatve tu na pramāṇāntaramanveṣṭavyam, ekasya karturabhāve bahūnāṃ vyāhatamanasāṃ svātantreṇa parasparavirodhena mithaḥ svānukūlābhiprāyānavabodhena yugapatkāryānutpatiḥ, utpannasya vā vilopādiprasaṅgaḥ syāditi / ekatve tu siddhe sarvajñatāsiddhiravirodhinī / na ceścarasya sakalakṣetrajñasamavāyidharmādharmajñānakāraṇābhāvena tadajñānam, tatsamavetānāṃ jñānacikīrṣāprayatnānāṃ nityatvāt / na ca buddhitannityatvayoḥ kaścidvirodhaḥ / na ca buddheranityatāyāstatra tatropalabdherīśvarabuddherapi tathātvaṃ yuktam, rūpādīnāmapyanityānāṃ tatra tatropalabdhestoyādiparamāṇusamavetānāmapi rūpādīnāmanityatvaprasaṅgāt / parapuruṣasamavetadharmādharmādhiṣṭhānamapyasya yuktameva, saṃyuktasaṃyogisamavāyasya sambandhasya sadbhāvāt / saṃyuktāḥ khalvīśvareṇa paramāṇavaḥ, taiśca kṣetrajñāḥ, tatsamavetau ca dharmādharmāviti //
body.translated_text: to this we reply: From the non-differentiation of the inferential mark of being-an-effect, [the conclusion] 'there is one maker' arises without differentiation of cognition—just as [the inference of] existence and unity. Since the multiplicity of an entity inferred from one mark is to be inferred from another mark, one must state a separate <s>pramāṇa</s> to establish multiplicity. Just as those who establish the multiplicity of the self cite pleasure etc. as establishing the differentiation. But here there is no other <s>pramāṇa</s> for apprehending multiplicity of the maker. For unity, however, no other <s>pramāṇa</s> need be sought: in the absence of a single maker, many [makers] with conflicting intentions, independently [acting] in mutual opposition, not comprehending each other's favorable intentions, would fail to produce effects simultaneously, or there would be the consequence of destruction etc. of what is produced. But when unity is established, the establishment of omniscience follows without contradiction. Nor is God ignorant of the merit and demerit (<s>dharma-adharma</s>) inherent in all individual souls, since the knowledge, desire-to-act, and effort inherent in those [souls] are eternal. And there is no contradiction between intelligence and its eternity. Nor is it proper to infer that God's intelligence is non-eternal merely because intelligence is observed [as non-eternal] here and there, for that would absurdly entail the non-eternity of form etc. inherent in atoms of water etc., since non-eternal forms etc. are also observed here and there. His presiding over the merit and demerit inherent in other individual souls is also justified, since the relation of conjunct-conjunct-inherence (<s>saṃyukta-saṃyogi-samavāya</s>) obtains: God is indeed conjoined with atoms, and [atoms are conjoined] with individual souls, and merit and demerit are inherent in them.

body.text: tadevaṃ kaṇikāyāṃ vācaspaterīśvaradūṣaṇaṃ yathāsāramutthāpya vyudastamasmābhiḥ / aparaṃ ca busaprāyamanabhyupagamaprasiddhasiddhāntagrastamiha granthavistarabhayānna likhitam / tadevamabhimatasyaiva sarvajñatālakṣaṇasya viśeṣasya siddhernaiṣa viśeṣaviruddho hetuḥ / nāpi karmabhiḥ siddhasādhanamiti sthitam //
body.translated_text: Thus, having raised the substance of <s>Vācaspati's</s> refutation of <s>Īśvara</s> in the <s>Kaṇikā</s>, it has been demolished by us. The rest, being mostly chaff, swallowed by principles that are unaccepted and well-known [as refuted], has not been written here for fear of prolixity. Thus, since the specific [property] of omniscience, which is precisely what we intend [to prove], is established, this inferential reason is not contradicted by the specific [conclusion]. Nor is it a case of proving what is already established through <s>karma</s>. This is settled.

body.text: na cānaikāntikaḥ / sa hi bhavannasādhāraṇo vā syāt, yathā nityā pṛthvī gandhavatvāditi; anupasaṃhāryo vā, yathā sarvaṃ nityaṃ prameyatvāditi; sādhāraṇo vā yathā nityaḥ śabdaḥ, asparśavattvāditi /
body.translated_text: Nor is [the inferential reason] inconclusive (<s>anaikāntika</s>). For if it were, it would be either uncommon (<s>asādhāraṇa</s>), as in 'the earth is eternal because it has smell'; or unsubsumable (<s>anupasaṃhārya</s>), as in 'everything is eternal because it is knowable'; or common (<s>sādhāraṇa</s>), as in 'sound is eternal because it is intangible.'

body.text: tatra na tāvadādimau pakṣau, sapakṣasadbhāvadarśanena pratikṣiptatvāt / nāpyantimaḥ, adhigatakartṛnivṛttervyomādervipakṣād vyāvṛtterupalabdheḥ /
body.translated_text: The first two alternatives are refuted by the observation of [the reason's] presence in the positive example (<s>sapakṣa</s>). Nor does the last [alternative hold], because it is observed that [being-an-effect] is excluded from the counter-example (<s>vipakṣa</s>)—namely, space etc., from which an ascertained maker is absent.

body.text: nanu puruṣavyāpāramantareṇa tṛṇādīnudayamānānavalokayan lokaḥ kāryamātraṃ puruṣapūrvakamiti vyāptimeva na pratipadyata iti cet / evaṃ tarhi prasiddhānumānasthitirapi dattajalāñjaliḥ / tatrāpi hi vyāptipratītikāla eva vyāghrādiparyākulātidurgapradeśe vahnivyāpāramantareṇa dhūmaṃ puruṣavyāpāraṃ vinā pūrvaṃ siddhaṃ ghaṭaṃ vā vilokayan loko dhūmamātraṃ vahnipūrvakaṃ ghaṭamātraṃ vā puruṣapūervakamiti vyāptimeva na pratipadyata iti vaktuṃ śakyatvāt /
body.translated_text: If it is objected: 'Observing the arising of grass etc. without any human activity, the world does not accept the pervasion that all effects are preceded by a person'—then the stability of well-known inferences too has bid farewell [i.e., is equally undermined]. For even there, at the very time of apprehending the pervasion, observing smoke without the activity of fire in a place that is extremely inaccessible and infested with tigers etc., or a pot previously established without human activity, one could say that the world does not accept the pervasion that mere smoke is preceded by fire, or that mere pots are preceded by a person.

body.text:
(#Nibandh 37#)
tatra vahnipuruṣayordeśakālaviprakṛṣṭatvādapratikṣepa iti cet / yadyevaṃ tṛṇādāvapi puruṣasya svabhāvaviprakṛṣṭatvādapratikṣepa iti sarvaṃ samānamanyatrābhiniveśāt / puruṣavyāpārapūrvakatā tāvanna pratīyate tṛṇādīnām / sā ca puruṣasyādṛśyatvādasattvād vā na pratīyatām, kimanena vicāritena / sarvathā kiñcitkāryamapūrvapuruṣapūrvakamapaśyanna vyāptiṃ kāryamātrasya puruṣeṇa kaścit cetanāvānavagacchatīti cet / yadyevaṃ vahnimātrapūrvakatā tāvanna pratīyate dhūmasya, puruṣamātrapūrvakatā ca ghaṭasya / sā ca vahnerdeśaviprakṛṣṭatvādasattvād vā puruṣasya kālaviprakṛṣṭatvādasattvād vā na pratīyatām, kimanena vicāritena / sarvathā dhūmamātraṃ vahnivyāpārapūrvakamapaśyan ghaṭamātraṃ vā puruṣapūrvakamapaśyannavyāptimeva dhūmasya vahnimātreṇa ghaṭasya puruṣamātreṇa vā kaściccetanāvānadhigacchatītyapyucyamānaṃ na vaktraṃ vakrīkaroti / tat kimanena prasiddhānumānāpalāpinā jātyuttareṇa //
body.translated_text: (Nibandha 37) On this matter, if one says: 'There is no counter-argument because fire and a person are distant in space and time' — if so, then since a person is distant in intrinsic nature from grass and so forth, there is no counter-argument [there either], and everything is the same, except for [your] bias. The being-preceded-by-a-person's-activity is, to begin with, not perceived in the case of grass and the like. And let it not be perceived because the person is invisible or because [they are] non-existent — what use is this investigation? 'In any case, not seeing any particular effect preceded by a previously unknown person, no intelligent being comprehends the invariable concomitance of effects in general with a person' — if one says this: then the being-preceded-by-fire-in-general is, to begin with, not perceived in the case of smoke, nor is the being-preceded-by-a-person-in-general [perceived] in the case of a pot. And let it not be perceived because fire is distant in space or non-existent, or because the person is distant in time or non-existent — what use is this investigation? 'In any case, not seeing any smoke whatsoever preceded by the activity of fire, or not seeing any pot whatsoever preceded by a person, no intelligent being comprehends the invariable concomitance of smoke with fire in general, or of a pot with a person in general' — even when this is said, it does not make the speaker's face contorted [with embarrassment]. So what use is this sophistical rejoinder (<s>jātyuttara</s>) that denies well-established inference?

body.text: syādetat / na sapakṣāsapakṣayordarśanādarśanamātreṇāvyabhicāraniścayaḥ, atadātmano 'tadutpatteścāvyabhicāraniyamābhāvāt / tadidaṃ kāryatvaṃ sandigdhavipakṣavyāvṛttikatvenāsādhanam /
body.translated_text: One might say this: 'The ascertainment of non-deviation is not [established] merely by seeing and not-seeing in the <s>sapakṣa</s> (homologous) and <s>asapakṣa</s> (heterologous) instances, because there is no certainty of non-deviation for that which is not of that nature and not arisen from that.' Therefore this <s>kāryatva</s> (effect-ness) is not a valid proof, since its exclusion from the <s>vipakṣa</s> (contrary instance) is doubtful.

body.text: atrocyate / nāsti vipakṣāddhetorvyāvṛttisandehaḥ, dhūmānalayoriva kāryabuddhimatorupalambhānupalambhasādhanasya kāryakāraṇabhāvasya siddhatvāt /
body.translated_text: To this we reply: There is no doubt about the exclusion of the reason from the <s>vipakṣa</s>, because — just as with smoke and fire — the causal relation (<s>kāryakāraṇabhāva</s>), which is the means of proof through [the method of] observation and non-observation, is established for one who possesses the cognition of an effect.

body.text: kāryaviśeṣasyaiva tadutpādasiddhirna kāryasāmānyasya, yathā dhūmādivartino vastutvādernānalādijanyatvaniścaya iti cet / na / viśeṣahetvabhāvāt / upalambhānupalambhayostadutpattisādhanatveneṣṭayoraviśeṣāt kāryaviśeṣasyeva kāryasāmānyasya prabodhāśrayāyattatāsiddheḥ / yathā hi kāryaṃ vastrādyupādānavad dṛṣṭam, kāryāntaramapyadṛṣṭopādānamupādānavat kāryatvādyupasthāpyate tathā tadeva kāryaṃ vastrādi dṛṣṭakartṛkamityadṛṣṭakartṛkamapi kāryatvāt kartṛmadvyavasthāpyate / upādānasyeva karturapikāryeṇānukṛtānvayavyatirekatvāt / tanmātranibandhanatvācca sarvatra kāryakāraṇavyavahārayoḥ / tasmād yathā kāryaṃ ca syānnirupādānaṃ ceti na śakyamāśaṅkitum, kāryamātrasyopādānamātrādutpādasiddheḥ tathā kāryaṃ ca bhavedakartṛkaṃ ceti nāśaṅkanīyam, kāryamātrasya kartṛmātrādutpādasiddheraviśeṣāt //
body.translated_text: If one objects: 'The origination is established only for a specific effect, not for the universal [class of] effects — just as from the substance-ness (<s>vastutvādi</s>) inherent in smoke and the like, there is no certainty of being produced by fire and the like' — no, [we reply], because there is no special reason [for the distinction]. Since observation and non-observation, accepted as establishing the origination of that [effect], are without distinction [between specific and general effects], the establishment of the dependence [of all effects] on a conscious substratum is [proven] for the universal [class of] effects just as for the specific effect. For just as an effect such as cloth is seen to have a material cause (<s>upādāna</s>), another effect whose material cause is unseen is inferred to have a material cause because of its effect-ness — similarly, that same effect such as cloth is seen to have a maker; [therefore] even an effect whose maker is unseen is established as having a maker because of its effect-ness. Because, just like the material cause, the maker too has [its] positive concomitance and negative concomitance traced out by the effect. And because the transactional usage of cause and effect everywhere depends on precisely that [concomitance]. Therefore, just as one cannot suspect 'it might be an effect and yet be without a material cause' — since the origination of every effect from some material cause is established — similarly, one should not suspect 'it might be an effect and yet be without a maker,' since the origination of every effect from some maker is established without distinction.

body.text: nanu brūyā nāma kiñcit / tathāpi na kāryamātrād buddhimadanumānam, api tu kāryaviśeṣādeva / yaddarśanādakriyādarśino 'pi kṛtabuddhiḥ syāt / na cānapekṣitatattvānugamācchabdamātrasāmyāt sādhyasiddhiryuktā / gośabdavācyatāmātreṇa vāgādīnāṃ viṣāṇitvānumitiprasaṅgāditi cet / tadetat khasthottaramanuttarārham, kāryasāmānyasyaiva vyāptiprasādhanāt / api ca kā punariyaṃ kṛtabuddhiḥ, kimapekṣitaparavyāpārāvasāyo 'tha puruṣakṛtametaditi pauruṣeyatvaniścaya iti /
body.translated_text: Well, let someone say something [to that effect]. Even so, the inference of an intelligent [being] is not from effect-ness in general, but rather from a specific effect — [namely, that] the seeing of which would produce the cognition of 'made' even in one who does not perceive the activity [of making]. And it is not proper that the accomplishment of the <s>sādhya</s> (thesis to be proven) should follow merely from a verbal similarity without regard for the actual nature [of things] — for there would be the absurd consequence of inferring horns for speech and the like merely because they are denoted by the word 'go' (which means both 'cow' and 'speech'). This [objection] is a groundless rejoinder that deserves no answer, since the <s>vyāpti</s> (invariable concomitance) of effect-ness in general has been established. Moreover, what exactly is this 'cognition of being made'? Is it the ascertainment that depends on observing another's activity? Or is it the definite cognition 'this was made by a person,' i.e., of being produced by a person?

body.text:
(#Nibandh 38#)
yadyādyaḥ pakṣaḥ sa kathaṃ kṣityādiṣu nāsti, kāraṇavyāpārātmalābhalākṣaṇasya kāryatvasya kumbhādivat kṣityādiṣvaviśeṣāt / atha puruṣeṇa kṛtamiti pauruṣeyatvaniścayaḥ kṛtabuddhirabhimatā, tadāpi tādṛśī kṛtabuddhiḥ kasya nāstīti vaktavyam / kiṃ kāryatvāditi hetoravinābhāvavedina āhosvit tadviparītasya / nādyaḥ pakṣaḥ / avinābhāvavedinaḥ sādhyāpratipatterayogāt / atha tadviparītasya sādhyabuddhirna bhavatīti kṛtabuddhihetukatvamavanitanumahīruhādiṣu nāstīti buddhimato 'numānaṃ pratikṣipyate /
body.translated_text: (Nibandha 38) If the first alternative [is meant], how is it not present in the earth and so forth, since there is no distinction between earth and the like and pots and the like with respect to effect-ness, whose defining characteristic is the obtaining of existence through the activity of a cause? If, however, what is meant by 'cognition of being made' is the definite cognition of being produced by a person, i.e., 'made by a person' — then too, it must be stated for whom such a 'cognition of being made' is absent. Is it for one who knows the invariable concomitance of the reason, i.e., effect-ness? Or for one who is in the opposite position? Not the first alternative, because it is impossible for one who knows the invariable concomitance not to cognize the <s>sādhya</s> (what is to be proven). If, however, [it is said] that one in the opposite position does not have the cognition of the <s>sādhya</s>, and therefore the being-caused-by-a-'cognition-of-being-made' is absent in earth, trees, and the like — [then] the inference of an intelligent [being] is rejected.

body.text: nanvevaṃ sati sarvānumānoccheda syāt / sarvahetūnāmagṛhītāvinābhāvaṃ prati agamakatvāt / tasmānna kṛtabuddhihetutvaṃ viśeṣaḥ / bhavatu vā kaścidanirūpitarūpo viśeṣastathāpi kimanena / kāryamātrasyaiva dhūmamātrasyeva vyāptipratīteḥ / na ca kāryatvena hetunā saha mṛddhikārasya samakakṣatā / tasya svasādhyena dṛśyakumbhakāreṇa saha vyabhicārasya śataśo darśanāt / kāryatvasya tu dṛśyādṛśyasādhāraṇena buddhimanmātreṇa tadyogāditi nāyamanaikāntikaḥ /
body.translated_text: But if so, there would be the destruction of all inference, because all reasons are incapable of proving [anything] for one who has not grasped their invariable concomitance. Therefore the requirement of the 'cognition of being made' as a reason is no distinguishing factor. Or even if there is some distinguishing factor whose nature has not been determined, what use is it? Since the <s>vyāpti</s> (invariable concomitance) is perceived of effect-ness in general, just like that of smoke in general. And the [argument from a] potter is not on par with the reason of effect-ness, because deviation of the potter from his own <s>sādhya</s> (the visible potter) is seen hundreds of times. But effect-ness, being connected with an intelligent being in general — common to both visible and invisible [makers] — is not inconclusive (<s>anaikāntika</s>).

body.text: nāpi prakaraṇasamaḥ, apratipakṣatvāt / na hyasya pratipakṣopasthāpakaṃ dharmāntaramasti / yathā nityaḥ śabdo vastutve satyanupalabhyamānanityadharmatvādityasya, anityaḥ śabdo vastutve satyanupalabhyamānanityadharmatvāditi pratipakṣakṛtaṃ dharmāntaramasti / na cedaṃ bādhakaṃ vaktavyam / neśvarakartṛkaṃ jagat / vastutvasattvādityādi / īśvarakartṛkatvasya vastutvāditi virodhābhāvāt / iti gāyaṃ prakaraṇasamo 'pi /
body.translated_text: Nor is it a <s>prakaraṇasama</s> (balancing the controversy), because it has no counter-argument. For there is no other property that would present a counter-argument to it — as there is for [the argument]: 'Sound is permanent, because, given that it is a real entity, no property of impermanence is observed' — where the counter-argument exists: 'Sound is impermanent, because, given that it is a real entity, no property of permanence is observed,' created by a contrary property. Nor should this be called a <s>bādhaka</s> (contradictory proof), [such as]: 'The world is not created by <s>Īśvara</s> (God), because it possesses real-entity-ness' and so on — because there is no contradiction in '<s>Īśvara</s>-createdness' and 'real-entity-ness.' Thus [such an attempt to show it is] a <s>prakaraṇasama</s> also [fails].

body.text: na ca kālātyayāpadiṣṭaḥ pratyakṣānumānāgamairbādhitaviṣayasya tathābhāvāt / asya ca tairavirodhāt / tatra pratyakṣaviruddhaḥ, anuṣṇastejo 'vayavī kṛtakatvāt / anumānaviruddhaḥ, sāvayavāḥ paramāṇavo mūrtatvāt / āgamaviruddhaḥ, śuci na(ra) śiraḥ kapālaṃ prāṇyaṅgatvāditi / tatra na tāvadayaṃ pratyakṣaviruddhaḥ, sādhyaviparyayasya pratyakṣāviṣayatvāt / nāpyanumānaviruddhaḥ, dharmigrāhiṇānumānenābādhitaviṣayatvāt / na cāgamaviruddhaḥ, āgamena sādhyaviparya(ya) syāparicchedāt / saugatādyāgamairviparītaparicchedāditi cet / na, teṣāṃ kṣaṇikatvādyarthavisaṃvādopalambhena prāmāṇyābhāvāt / vedāgamo 'pi bādhakatvena nāśaṅkanīyaḥ,
body.translated_text: Nor is it <s>kālātyayāpadiṣṭa</s> (a reason whose time has passed), since the subject matter is not contradicted by perception, inference, and scripture — and there is no conflict of this [reason] with those [sources of knowledge]. In that regard: 'contradicted by perception' [would be like]: 'Fire is not hot, because it is a product'; 'contradicted by inference': 'Atoms have parts, because they are material'; 'contradicted by scripture': 'A human skull is pure, because it is a limb of a living being.' Now, this [reason] is not contradicted by perception, because the opposite of the <s>sādhya</s> is not an object of perception. Nor is it contradicted by inference, because its subject matter is not refuted by an inference that apprehends the <s>dharmin</s> (subject). Nor is it contradicted by scripture, because scripture does not determine the opposite of the <s>sādhya</s>. If one objects: 'The opposite is determined by the scriptures of the Buddhists and others' — no, because those [scriptures] lack authority, since a discrepancy with reality is observed [in them] regarding momentariness and other doctrines. Nor should the Vedic scripture be suspected of being a contradicting [authority],

body.text: sahasraśīrṣā puruṣaḥ
body.translated_text: 'The <s>Puruṣa</s> (Cosmic Person) has a thousand heads' —

body.text: ityādinā tatra kartureva pratipādanāt / tathābhūtapuruṣātiśayapūrvakatvābhāve satyaprāmāṇyācceti nāyamatikrāntakālo hetuḥ / tadevamapanītahetvābhāsavibhramādataḥ sādhanādupādānādyabhijño buddhimānabhimataḥ kartā sidhyati / sa eva bhagavānasmākamīśvara iti sthitam //
body.translated_text: because of the teaching therein of a creator [in passages] like this. And because [the Veda] lacks authority if there is no [such] extraordinary person as its source — therefore this is not a reason whose time has passed (<s>atikrāntakāla</s>). Thus, having cleared away the confusion of pseudo-reasons (<s>hetvābhāsa</s>), from this proof, the intended maker — an intelligent being who knows the material cause and other [factors] — is established. He alone, the Blessed One, is our <s>Īśvara</s> (Lord) — this is established.

body.text:
(#Nibandh 39#)
tathāsya siddhaye śaṅkaraḥ sādhanamidamabhipraiti -
body.translated_text: (Nibandha 39) Likewise, for the establishment of this [Īśvara], <s>Śaṅkara</s> propounds this proof:

body.text: jagadetat prabodhāśrayāyattaprasavamabhilāṣaprītiparamāṇumūrtyādhāraparatvāparatrvānumeyasāmānyasamavāyāntyaviśeṣatadekārthasamavetaparimāṇaikatvapṛthaktvagurutvasnehāpārthivarūparasasparśāpyadravatvāmūrtasaṃyogataditaretarābhāvānutpattirūpārūpamasmadādivinirmitetarat /
body.translated_text: This world — which is other than what is fashioned by us and the like, [and which possesses] desire, pleasure, atoms, material form, space as substrate, spatial and temporal remoteness and proximity, universals ascertainable [by inference], inherence, ultimate <s>viśeṣas</s> (individuators), measures coinhering with a single substance, unity, separateness, weight, fluidity, non-earthy color, taste, and touch, as well as non-fluidity, immaterial conjunction, mutual absence, and non-origination — [which has] both form and formlessness — has its origination dependent on a conscious substratum.

body.text: acetanopādānatvāt /
body.translated_text: Because it has an unconscious material cause (<s>acetanopādāna</s>).

body.text: yaditthaṃ tat tathā, yathā kalasaḥ /
body.translated_text: Whatever is of this nature is so [i.e., has a conscious cause], like a pot.

body.text: tathā cedam /
body.translated_text: And this [world] is of this nature.

body.text: tasmādidamapi tatheti /
body.translated_text: Therefore this too is so [i.e., has a conscious cause].

body.text: asyāyamarthaḥ / jagaditi dharmī / prabodhāśrayāyattaprasavamiti sādhyam / abhilāṣetyādi anutpattirūpārūpaparyantena dharmiviśeṣaṇenākāśādinityavargaparihāraḥ / asmadādivinirmitetaradityanenāpi dharmiviśeṣaṇena prasiddhakartṛkaghaṭādiparihāraḥ / abhilāṣaśca prītiśca paramāṇumūrtiśca / āsāmadhāraḥ ākāśa ātmā paramāṇuḥ / paratvāparatvānumeyau dikkālau / sāmānyādayastu yathāprasiddhā grahītavyāḥ /
body.translated_text: The meaning of this [argument] is as follows: 'the world' is the <s>dharmin</s> (subject); 'having its origination dependent on a conscious substratum' is the <s>sādhya</s> (what is to be proved).
