Nor is there here, when there is doubt whether the co-occurrence of smoke with fire is permanent or merely accidental like that of two friends, any support from another <s>pramāṇa</s> establishing permanent co-occurrence, nor is any effect of that [relationship] observed. Nor should one say 'Then the distinguishing characteristic will be that of being subject to invalidation versus not being subject to invalidation,' because the invalidation of repeated observation, which grasps non-deviation (<s>avyabhicāra</s>), is not established. For mere non-invalidation is a simple negation (<s>prasajyapratiṣedha</s>) and is not a <s>pramāṇa</s>. And the nominative exclusion (<s>paryudāsa</s>) — namely, the support of another <s>pramāṇa</s> or the obtaining of causal efficacy — is not established. Therefore the first position does not hold. Nor the second, because even in the absence of a fixed [relation], repeated observation is possible with respect to earthiness and the like — and therefore pervasion is not ascertainable through repeated observation.

body.text: trilocanacodye 'pi brūmaḥ / yadi pratyakṣaṃ svalakṣaṇaviṣayamityayogavyavacchedenocyate tadā siddhasādhanam / anyayogavyavacchedastvasiddhaḥ, pratyakṣānumānādisarvajñānānāṃ grāhyāvaseyabhedena viṣayadvaividhyānatikramāt / yadvi yatra jñāne pratibhāsate tad grāhyam / yatra tu tat pravartate tadadhyavaseyat / tatra pratyakṣasya svalakṣaṇaṃ grāhyam / adhyavaseyaṃ tu sāmānyam, atadrūpaparāvṛttasvalakṣaṇamātrātmakam / anumānasya tu viparyayaḥ / tataśca sāṃvyavahārikapramāṇāpekṣayā rūparasagandhasparśasamudāyātmakasya ghaṭasya rūpabhedamātragrahaṇe 'pi pratyakṣataḥ samudāyasiddhivyavasthā / tathaikasyātadrūpaparāvṛttasya grahaṇe 'pi sādhyasādhanasāmānyayoratadrūpaparāvṛttavastumātrātmanorayogavyavacchedena viṣayabhūtayorvyāptigraho yukta eva / ata eva vikalpānāmavastveva viṣayaḥ, vastu tu teṣāṃ parokṣamevetyapi durjñānam, sarvavikalpānāmadhyavaseyāpekṣayā vastuviṣayatvāt / śāstre 'pi tathaiva pratipādanāt / na ca manasā tajjātīyānāṃ vyāptigrahaḥ śakyaḥ, manaso bahirasvātantryāt / anyathā andhabadhirādyabhāvaprasaṅgāt / na ca vahnivyabhicāre dhūma upādhirahitaṃ āṃbandhamatikrāmediti vaktumucitam, svakapolakalpitasvābhāvikasaṃbandhasya yācitakamaṇḍanatvāditi //
body.translated_text: We also respond to <s>Trilocana</s>'s objection. If 'perception has the particular (<s>svalakṣaṇa</s>) as its object' is stated by way of exclusive connection (<s>ayogavyavaccheda</s>), then it proves what is already established. But exclusive connection with something else (<s>anyayogavyavaccheda</s>) is unestablished, because all cognitions — perception, inference, and so forth — do not transcend the twofold nature of their objects by the distinction of apprehended (<s>grāhya</s>) and determined (<s>avaseya</s>). For whatever appears in whatever cognition, that is its apprehended [object]. And that toward which it directs [activity], that is its determined [object]. In this framework, for perception, the particular is the apprehended; but the determined is the universal, consisting merely in a particular turned away from what is not of that form. For inference, it is the reverse. And therefore, with respect to conventional valid cognition, even when apprehending only a portion of form — a pot being an aggregate of form, taste, smell, and touch — the establishment of the aggregate is determined through perception. Similarly, even when apprehending a single [thing] turned away from what is not of that form, the apprehension of the pervasion between the general properties of the proved and the prover — which are objects by way of exclusive connection, consisting merely in real things turned away from what is not of that form — is entirely justified. For exactly this reason, [the claim that] the object of conceptual thoughts is unreal, and that real things are beyond their reach, is also a misunderstanding — because all conceptual thoughts have real things as their object with respect to what they determine. In the treatise too, it is taught in just this way. Nor can the mind (<s>manas</s>) grasp the pervasion of things of the same class, because the mind has no independence regarding external [objects]; otherwise there would be the absurd consequence of there being no blind or deaf persons. And it is not appropriate to say that in the deviation of smoke from fire, smoke would not transgress the relation that is free from adventitious conditions (<s>upādhi</s>) — because the so-called natural relation (<s>svābhāvikasaṃbandha</s>), fabricated by one's own imagination, has the status of borrowed ornament.

body.text: yadapi vācaspatijalpitam, yo yatropādhinā niyatastatra tasya svābhāvikaḥ saṃbandhaḥ / yathā dahane dhūmasya / tadupādherdṛśyasyānupalabhyamānatvāt kvacid vyabhicārasyādarśanādityatredaṃ vicāryate / yasyādarśanataḥ svābhāvikaḥ saṃbandho vyavasthāpanīyaḥ, sa khalu dhūmasvarūpādarthāntaramupādhirvaktavyo yathā dahanādindhanam / arthāntaraṃ ca kiñcid dṛśyamadṛśyaṃ ca kiñcit, na tu sarvameva dṛśyatāniyatam / tataśca dhūmasyāpi hutāśane syādupādhiḥ, na copalabhyate ityupādhimātrānupalabdhiranaikāntikī / tatkathamadarśanamātrānnāstyevopādhiḥ, yataḥ svābhāvikasaṃbandhasiddhiḥ (#Nibandh 110#) syāt / dṛśyopādhyabhāvasādhane tu siddhasādhanam / paramadṛśyopādhiśaṅkāsaṃbhave svābhāvikatvapratirodhastadavastha eva / kvacid vyabhicārādarśanādityasaṃbaddhameva, upādhivat vyabhicārasyāpyadarśanamātrādabhāvāsiddheḥ / vyabhicārasya sarvadeśakālayoḥ saṃbhave 'pi dṛśyatve 'pi sarvadā sarvatra sarveṇa sāmagryabhāvādapi niścetumaśakyatvāt / brāhmaṇyādivyabhicāravadevāhatyādarśane 'pi deśakālāntare taddarśanasya niṣeddhumaśakyatvāt /
body.translated_text: As for what <s>Vācaspati</s> chatters — 'That which is restricted to something through an adventitious condition (<s>upādhi</s>) has a natural relation there; for example, smoke with respect to combustion; since the adventitious condition, though visible, is not observed, deviation is not seen anywhere' — here we examine this: The adventitious condition that is to be stated, the non-observation of which is supposed to establish a natural relation, must surely be something other than the nature of smoke itself — like fuel in relation to combustion. And this something else may be either visible or invisible — not everything is necessarily limited to being visible. Therefore there could be an adventitious condition even for smoke's [relation] with fire, and it is not observed — hence the mere non-observation of an adventitious condition is inconclusive (<s>anaikāntika</s>). How then, from mere non-observation alone, [can one conclude] that there is simply no adventitious condition, such that the natural relation would be established? (Nibandhāvalī 110) And in proving the absence of a visible adventitious condition, this proves what is already established. But the obstruction to the [claim of] natural relation due to the possibility of suspecting an invisible adventitious condition remains exactly as it was. [The claim] 'because deviation is not seen anywhere' is simply incoherent — because, just like an adventitious condition, the mere non-observation of deviation does not establish its absence. For even though deviation is possible at all places and times, and even though visible, it cannot be ascertained [to be absent] because the complete conditions [for observation] may not be present always, everywhere, for everyone. Just as, even when deviation in the form of Brahminhood and the like is not seen, one cannot prohibit the seeing of it in another place or time.

body.text: nanu yadi dhūmasyāpekṣaṇīyamarthāntaramupādhiḥ syāt kathaṃ dhūma ityeva pāvakasattāniyama iti cet / nanvidameva cintyate kiṃ dhūme satyavaśyamagniḥ saṃbhavīna veti / kadācidarthāntaramupādhimapekṣya dhūmo 'pi syānnāgniriti kimatra niṣṭabdhaṃ kāraṇam / tasmāt pāvakaparādhīnodayo dhūmaḥ pariniṣṭhitaḥ kathaṃ tadabhāve bhāvaṃ svīkuryādityeva sādhu /
body.translated_text: Objection: If there were an adventitious condition, something other than smoke, to be considered, how could there be the rule 'Where there is smoke, there is fire'? Reply: This is precisely what is being examined — whether, when smoke exists, fire necessarily exists or not. Sometimes, depending on some other adventitious condition, there may be smoke but not fire — what fixed reason is there here? Therefore, [the statement] 'Smoke is established as having its arising dependent on fire; how could it accept existence in the absence of that?' — just this is correct.

body.text: atha vyaktau jātau vā vahnivyabhicāro na dṛṣṭaḥ, kathaṃ tatra śaṅkayata iti cet / tat kiṃ sthāṇuvyaktau jātau vā puruṣatvaṃ dṛṣṭaṃ yena sthāṇau śaṅkayate / anyatrordhvatāliṅgite dṛṣṭamiti cet / ihāpyanyatra bhūyaḥ sahacāriṇi pārthivatvādau dṛṣṭa eva vyabhicāraḥ / yatraiva tu yat saṃśayyate tatraiva tasya darśanamapekṣyata ityalaukikam / yadi dhūmavyaktau vyabhicāro dṛṣṭastadā dhūmasāmānyaṃ vyāptau bahirbhūtameva, kathaṃ saṃśayaḥ / atha jātau dṛṣṭastadāpi vyabhicāraniścaya eva, kathaṃ saṃśayaḥ / ato dhūmajātāvadṛśyamāno 'pi vyabhicāra upādhirvā darśanāyogyatayā niṣeddhumaśakya iti saṃśayo durvāraprasaraḥ / sa cedānīmupādhervyabhicārasya vā saṃśayaḥ svābhāvikatvasaṃśayasvabhāvaḥ svābhāvikatvaniścayaṃ tāvadavaśyaṃ pratibadhnāti / tasmāt svābhāvikatvaniścayapratibandha evārthataḥ, niścayamantareṇa gamakasya svayamakiñcitkaratvāt / tadevamupādhyanupalabdhirvyabhicārasyānupalabdhirvānaikāntikī na tayorabhāvaṃ sādhayati, yataḥ saṃbandhasya svābhāvikatvasiddhiḥ syāt / asiddhā ceyamupādhyanupalabdhiḥ / yathā dahano nendhanena vinā dhūmena saṃbadhyate tathā dhūmo 'pi na tena vināgninā saṃbadhyata iti samānamupādhitvamindhanasyobhayatra /
body.translated_text: If [one objects:] deviation from fire is not seen in the individual or the universal [of smoke]; how can there be doubt about that? [We reply:] What, has personhood been seen in the individual or universal of a post, that there is doubt [whether a post is a person]? If [you say] 'It was seen elsewhere, in what is marked by uprightness' — here too deviation is seen elsewhere, in earthiness and the like, which is a more frequent co-occurrent. And [to say] that the seeing [of deviation] is required precisely where and with respect to what is doubted is extraordinary. If deviation is seen in the individual of smoke, then the universal of smoke is entirely outside the pervasion — how can there be doubt? If it is seen in the universal, then there is certainty of deviation — how can there be doubt? Therefore, deviation not seen in the universal of smoke, or an adventitious condition, cannot be negated due to being unfit for observation — and thus doubt is of irrepressible momentum. And this doubt now — whether of an adventitious condition or of deviation — being by nature a doubt about natural relation, necessarily obstructs the certainty of natural relation. Therefore the obstruction of certainty of natural relation is the real point — because without certainty, the indicator itself is powerless. Thus the non-observation of adventitious conditions and the non-observation of deviation are inconclusive and do not establish their absence, from which the natural relation of the connection would be proved. And this non-observation of adventitious conditions is itself unestablished. Just as combustion is not connected with smoke without fuel, so too smoke is not connected with fire without that [fuel] — the adventitious-condition-status of fuel is the same in both cases.

body.text: atha siddhasyāgnerindhanasāhityena dhūmalābha ityupādhivyavasthā, asiddhasya tu dhūmasya tannimittātmalābhatayāvyabhicārāt svābhāvikaḥ saṃbandha iti vyavasthā pyata iti cet / evamapi saiva tadutpattirāyātā / saiva svābhāvikaḥ saṃbandhaḥ / na punaḥ pratijñāsiddhaḥ sahacāramātrātmakaḥ / kiṃ ca svābhāvikatvādavyabhicāraḥ sarvatra, sarvatrāvyabhicārācca svābhāvikatvamitītaretarāśrayatvamanivāryam / yasya tu sakṛttadutpattipratītireva sarvatrāvyabhicārapratītistasya nāyaṃ prasaṅgaḥ /
body.translated_text: If [one says:] the determination of the adventitious condition is that smoke is obtained together with fire that is established, while the natural relation is determined [for smoke] because, as an unestablished [thing], it obtains its existence through that cause and thus does not deviate — even so, that very arising [of smoke from fire] is what has arrived at. That itself is the natural relation. Not one established merely by assertion, consisting in mere co-occurrence. Moreover, [the argument that] non-deviation everywhere [follows] from natural relation, and natural relation [follows] from non-deviation everywhere — the mutual dependence (<s>itaretarāśrayatva</s>) is unavoidable. But for one for whom the single cognition of arising from that is itself the cognition of non-deviation everywhere, this problem does not arise.

body.text: yadyevaṃ mamāpi bhūyodarśanādavyabhicārasiddhiriti cet / na / bhūya ityapariniṣṭhitavārasaṃkhyatvāt kiyatā darśanena lakṣaṇānusārī nirvṛtimāsādayet / asmākaṃ (#Nibandh 111#) tu pratyakṣānupalabdhau parigaṇitasaṃkhyāveva / yadāhuḥ
body.translated_text: If so, [you might say:] for me too, non-deviation is established through repeated observation (<s>bhūyodarśana</s>). No, because 'repeated' (<s>bhūyas</s>) has an indeterminate number of instances — with how much observation would one who follows the [proper] criterion achieve satisfaction? For us, however, (Nibandhāvalī 111) there are precisely enumerated numbers in perception and non-observation. As they say:

children.translated_text: Seeing sequentially what was previously unseen, one ascertains the causal relation;
or not seeing sequentially what was [previously] seen — otherwise there is no stability.

body.text: yattvanupalabhyamānasyāpi kalpanānupapatteriti vilapitam, tadvālasyāpyasāmpratam / anupalabhyamāne 'rthe ca kalpanāvakāśāt / na hi dṛśyamāno ghaṭaḥ kalpita ucyate / na ca sandihyamāna upādhiḥ saṃbandhasya svābhāvikatvaṃ pratibadhnātīti yuktam, sādhakabādhakābhāva eva saṃśayasya nyāyaprāptatvāt / ata eva na sarvatra śaṅkāpiśācāvakāśaḥ / tatkathaṃ nāyaṃ pravartetaṃ /
body.translated_text: As for the lamentation that 'even of what is not observed, there is no justification for supposition (<s>kalpanā</s>)' — that is untimely even for a child. Because there is room for supposition regarding an unobserved object. For a pot that is being seen is not called 'supposed.' And it is not justified [to say] that a doubted adventitious condition does not obstruct the natural relation — because doubt, in its proper sense, arises precisely from the absence of both proof and refutation. For exactly this reason, there is not room everywhere for the demon of doubt. How then would this [inferential process] not proceed?

body.text: pramāṇaviṣaye 'pi śaṅkā kartuṃ śakyata iti cet / na / svīkṛtapramāṇasya hi niścayaphalatvāt pramāṇasyāvipratipannapramāṇaviṣaye niścayasvīkāranāntarīyaka eva tatsvīkāraḥ / na ca śaṅketyeva na pravṛttiḥ, arthasaṃśayenāpi pravṛtteranivāryatvāt snigdhānnapānopayogavat / tadupayoge kadācinmaraṇadarśane 'pi koṭiśo jīvitadarśanāt / na ca prāmāṇikalolayātrākṣatiḥ, prāmāṇikaireva pramāṇābhāve saṃśayasya vihitatvāt / yathādarśanamāśaṅkanīyamityādyapi siddhasādhanam, anyatra dṛṣṭasyaivopādhervyabhicārasya vā śaṅkitatvāt / kiṃ ca bādhakādarśane 'pi sādhakabhāvādapi śaṅkā syādeva /
body.translated_text: If [one objects:] doubt can be raised even regarding what is the object of a valid cognition — no, because for one who has accepted a <s>pramāṇa</s> (valid means of knowledge), since the <s>pramāṇa</s> has certainty as its result, accepting the <s>pramāṇa</s> necessarily entails accepting the certainty regarding its undisputed object. And it is not that one simply does not act because of doubt — because activity, even from doubt about the object, is irrepressible, like the consumption of agreeable food and drink. Even when death is sometimes seen from consuming that, due to seeing life [result from it] millions of times. Nor is there damage to the livelihood of the logicians — because doubt, in the absence of a <s>pramāṇa</s>, has been enjoined by the logicians themselves. [The statement] 'One should suspect as far as one has seen' and so forth also proves what is already established — because it is precisely the adventitious condition or deviation seen elsewhere that is suspected [here]. Moreover, even in the absence of invalidation, doubt could arise due to the absence of proof.

body.text: yadapi syādetaditi valgitaṃ tadapi niḥsāram / pramāṇasiddhe hi rūpe svābhāvāvalambanam / natu svabhāvāvalambanenaiva vastusvarūpavyavasthā / tadyadi niyataviṣayānvayavyatirekagrāhakapratyakṣānupalambhapramāṇasiddhe hetuphalabhāve svabhāvavādastat kimāyātaṃ svābhāvikasaṃbandhe / yatra tadutpattisāmagrīṃ hṛdayena dūrīkṛtyānyataḥ sahacaritadvayād viśeṣaṃṇa pratītau pratyupāya eva devīyān / tatsāmagryapekṣaṇe ca tadutpattireva sā / kimāhopuruṣikayā nāmāntarakaraṇena / kena punaḥ pramāṇena eṣa svābhāvikaḥ saṃbandho gṛhyata ityādistadgrahaṇaprakāraḥ pūrvameva nirākṛtaḥ / tathā svābhāvikatvāsiddhau svabhāvataśca pratibaddhā hetava ityādyupasaṃhāropi manorājyamātram / tasmādarthāntare gamye kāryahetustadbhāvasiddhiśca pratyakṣānupalambhāditi sthitam / tadevaṃ svābhāvikavādena hṛdayānulepanamaśucineva parihāryaṃ dūrata iti /
body.translated_text: As for the boast 'This would be [the case],' that too is without substance. For regarding a form established by a <s>pramāṇa</s>, reliance on nature is [justified]. But the determination of the real nature of a thing is not [achieved] by mere reliance on nature. Therefore, if the nature-doctrine (<s>svabhāvavāda</s>) [applies] to the causal relation established by the <s>pramāṇa</s> of perception, non-observation, [and] apprehension of invariable positive and negative concomitance with a fixed object — then what is achieved with respect to [the claim of] natural relation? For where, having cast aside from the heart the aggregate of conditions for that arising, one does not apprehend the distinction from a pair of co-occurrents [found] elsewhere — the remedy is divine indeed. And in considering the aggregate of conditions, that is itself that arising. What is the point of the bravado of merely giving another name? 'By what <s>pramāṇa</s> is this natural relation grasped?' — this and the manner of its apprehension have already been refuted above. Likewise, 'when natural relation is not established, and causes are obstructed by their own nature' — this conclusion too is mere daydreaming. Therefore it is established that when something else is to be inferred, the causal reason and the proof of its existence [are achieved] through perception and non-observation. Thus, the smearing of the heart with the natural-relation-doctrine should be avoided from afar, like [smearing with] impurity.

body.text: // vyāptinirṇayaḥ samāpto ratnakīrtipādānām //
body.translated_text: Thus concludes the <s>Vyāptinirṇaya</s> (Determination of Pervasion) of the venerable <s>Ratnakīrti</s>.

(Nibandhāvalī 112)
Section 8.

body.text: // sthirasiddhidūṣaṇam //
body.translated_text: <s>Sthirasiddhidūṣaṇam</s> (Refutation of the Proof of Permanence)

body.text: namastārāyai //
body.translated_text: Homage to <s>Tārā</s>!

children.translated_text: That which, through the connection [of ignorance], like a blind man, causes the world to wander in <s>saṃsāra</s> (the cycle of rebirth) —
that sinful permanent establishment (<s>sthirasiddhi</s>) is cast away by those under the sway of compassion.

body.text: iha pare sakalapadārthasthairyaprasādhanārthaṃ pratyakṣamanumānamarthāpattiṃ(ca) pramāṇānyācakṣate / tathā hi sa evāyaṃ ghaṭasphaṭikādiriti pratyabhijñākhyaṃ pratyakṣamudīyamānaṃ sthairyamutthāpayati / na cedamapramāṇamabhighātavyam / aprāmāṇyaṃ hi bhavadaprāmāṇyakāraṇopapattyā vā bhavet, prāmāṇyalakṣaṇavirahād vā / yadyādyaḥ pakṣaḥ kimaprāmāṇyakāraṇam, mithyātvamajñānaṃ saṃśayo vā / na tāvadatra mithyātvam / mithyātvaṃ hi tadviṣaye bādhakapratyayād vā hetūtthadoṣato vā saṃbhāvyeta / na tāvad bādhagandho 'pi saṃbhavati, deśakālanarāntareṣvapyasaṃbhavāt / na cānavagatāpi bādhā kadācidapi bhaviṣyatīti śaṅkā yuktimatī, nirbījaśaṅkānupapatteḥ /
body.translated_text: Here, opponents cite <s>pratyakṣa</s> (perception), <s>anumāna</s> (inference), and <s>arthāpatti</s> (presumption) as <s>pramāṇas</s> (valid means of knowledge) for the purpose of establishing the permanence of all things. Thus: the <s>pratyakṣa</s> called <s>pratyabhijñā</s> (recognition), which arises in the form 'This is that very same pot, crystal, etc.,' establishes permanence. And this is not to be assailed as a non-<s>pramāṇa</s>. For its non-validity would arise either from the applicability of a cause of invalidity as you [Buddhists] understand it, or from the absence of the defining characteristics of <s>prāmāṇya</s> (validity). If the first alternative — what is the cause of invalidity? Falsity, ignorance, or doubt? First, there is no falsity here. For falsity could be suspected either from a sublating cognition regarding that object, or from a defect arising from the cause [of cognition]. But not even a trace of sublation is possible, since [no sublation] occurs in any other place, time, or person. Nor is the suspicion rational that sublation, though not yet observed, will someday arise, since a groundless suspicion is untenable.

body.text: avaśyaṃ śaṅkayā bhāvyaṃ niyāmakamapaśyatām /
body.translated_text: "Those who see no determining factor must necessarily entertain doubt" —

body.text: iti dattāvakāśā saṃśayapiśācī labdhaprasarā na kvacinnāstīti nāyaṃ kvacitpravarteta / antataḥ snigdhānnapānopayoge 'pi maraṇadarśanena sarvatra śaṅkānivṛtteḥ / tasmāt prāmāṇikalokayātrāmanupālayatā yathādarśanameva śaṅkanīyaṃ nādṛṣṭapūrvamapi / yaduktaṃ kārikāyāṃ
body.translated_text: thus, once given scope, the demon of doubt, having gained free rein, would be nowhere absent, and one would never engage in any activity. For ultimately, even in the consumption of nourishing food and drink, doubt would not cease anywhere, since death is observed [even there]. Therefore, one who upholds the worldly conduct grounded in <s>pramāṇas</s> should doubt only in accordance with what is observed, not even what has never been seen before. As stated in the <s>kārikā</s>:

body.text: nāśaṅkā niṣpramāṇikā /
body.translated_text: "Doubt without a [supporting] <s>pramāṇa</s> is not [valid]."

body.text: iti /
body.translated_text: Thus.

body.text: bṛhaṭṭīkāyāmapi
body.translated_text: And in the <s>Bṛhaṭṭīkā</s> as well:

children.translated_text: "He who, out of delusion, would imagine a sublating cognition even of an unknown kind —
That person, being of a doubting nature, would come to ruin in all practical affairs."

body.text: iti /
body.translated_text: Thus.

body.text: kṣaṇabhaṅgasādhanaṃ bādhakamasyeti cet / na / anumānasya paramparayāpi pratyakṣapūrvakatvāt pratyakṣaṃ pradhānam / prādhānyāccānumānasya bādhakam / na tvanumānamasya / pratyakṣāntaraṃ tu bādhakaṃ bhavati / yathā sarpādipratyayasya rajvādipratyakṣam / taccātra na saṃbhavati /
body.translated_text: If [the Buddhist objects:] the proof of <s>kṣaṇabhaṅga</s> (momentary destruction) is the sublating [cognition] of this [<s>pratyabhijñā</s>] — [we reply:] No. Since <s>anumāna</s> (inference), even indirectly, is always preceded by <s>pratyakṣa</s> (perception), <s>pratyakṣa</s> is primary. And because of its primacy, it can sublate <s>anumāna</s>, but <s>anumāna</s> cannot sublate it. Another <s>pratyakṣa</s>, however, can serve as a sublater — as the perception of a rope [sublates] the cognition of a snake and so forth. But that [another sublating <s>pratyakṣa</s>] does not occur here.

body.text: nanu pratyakṣe 'pi bādhake kasmānna bhavati parasparapratibandhena dvayorapyapratyakṣatā / na / arthakriyāsamarthavastuviṣayāviṣayatvena samānatvābhāvādekasya pratyakṣābhāsatvāditi na (#Nibandh 113#) sadviṣayatvaṃ bādhakapratyayānmithyātvam / nāpi hetūtthadoṣattaḥ, deśakālanarāntare 'rthavisaṃvādāt / nāpyajñānamaprāmāṇyakāraṇamatrāsti, pratyabhijñānasaṃvedanasaṃbhavāt / na ca saṃśayaḥ / na hi tadevedaṃ syād vā na veti sphaṭikādiṣūdayati matiḥ,kiṃ tu tadevedaṃ sphaṭikādikamiti nirastavibhramāśaṅkā / tannāprāmāṇyakāraṇopapattyā pratyabhijñānasyāprāmāṇyam / nāpi lakṣaṇakṣayāt / yadeva hi utpannamasandigdhamaduṣṭakāraṇajanyaṃ deśakālanarāntareṣvabādhitaṃ ca tadeva pramāṇamiti naḥ siddhāntaḥ / taduktam
body.translated_text: Objection: If even <s>pratyakṣa</s> can serve as a sublater, why is it not the case that, through mutual obstruction, both are rendered non-perceptual? [Reply:] No, because there is no parity between them, since one has a real object capable of <s>arthakriyā</s> (causal efficacy) and the other does not, and one is a mere semblance of <s>pratyakṣa</s>. (#Nibandh 113#) Therefore, there is no falsity [in <s>pratyabhijñā</s>] due to a sublating cognition, since it has a real object. Nor is there [falsity] due to a defect arising from the cause, since it does not fail to correspond with the object in any other place, time, or person. Nor is ignorance present here as a cause of invalidity, since the self-awareness of the <s>pratyabhijñā</s>-cognition is possible. Nor is there doubt; for the thought 'This might or might not be that very same thing' does not arise regarding crystals and so forth; rather, [the cognition is] 'This is indeed that very same crystal' — with the suspicion of error eliminated. Therefore, there is no invalidity of <s>pratyabhijñā</s> through the applicability of a cause of invalidity. Nor through the absence of the defining characteristics [of <s>pramāṇya</s>]. For our established position is that whatever cognition has arisen, is free from doubt, is born from an unimpaired cause, and is not sublated in any other place, time, or person — that alone is a <s>pramāṇa</s>. As stated:

children.translated_text: "Therefore, that cognition which, having arisen firmly, does not encounter discordance
From any other cognition — let that be accepted as a <s>pramāṇa</s>."

body.text: tathā bṛhaṭṭīkāpi
body.translated_text: Likewise, the <s>Bṛhaṭṭīkā</s> too [states]:

children.translated_text: "Therein, a cognition of a novel object, certain, free from sublation,
Arisen from an unimpaired cause — that is a <s>pramāṇa</s>, accepted by the world."

body.text: iti / etacca lakṣaṇamuktanyāyena pratyabhijñāne 'pi saṃbhavatīti pramāṇamevedam / nanvidamekameva na bhavati, kāraṇabhedāt, viṣayabhedāt, svabhāvavirodhācca / tathā hi sa iti saṃskārakāryam, ayamiti cendriyakāryam / na ca kāraṇabhede 'pi kāryābhedo viśvavaicitryāhetukatvaprasaṅgāt / tathā satyapi sphaṭikaḥ sphaṭika iti vyapadeśābhede pūrvadeśakālasaṃbandhāparadeśakālasaṃbandhābhyāṃ viruddhadharmābhyāṃ yogāt sphaṭikaḥ pūrvāparakālayorbhidyata iti viṣayabhedo vaktavyaḥ / tathā sa iti parokṣam, ayamiti sākṣātkāraḥ / na cānayoḥ svabhāvaviruddhayordahanatuhinayoriva śakyā śakreṇāpyekatā āpādayitum, trailokasyaikyaprasaṅgāt / na cāsya prāmāṇyam, vikalpatvenāvastunirbhāsitvāt,smārtādaviśeṣācca / tasmāt pratyabhijñā ekatvaṃ sthāpayati bhāvānāmiti manorathamātram //
body.translated_text: Thus. And this definition, by the reasoning stated, obtains in <s>pratyabhijñā</s> as well; hence this is indeed a <s>pramāṇa</s>. [Objection:] But this [<s>pratyabhijñā</s>] is not a single [cognition], due to the difference of causes, the difference of objects, and the inherent contradiction [of its components]. For 'that' (<s>sa</s>) is the product of a <s>saṃskāra</s> (dispositional imprint), and 'this' (<s>ayam</s>) is the product of a sense-organ. And when the causes differ, there cannot be identity of the effects, on pain of the diversity of the world being causeless. Likewise, even though the designation 'crystal, crystal' is the same, since it is associated with contradictory properties — namely, connection with a prior place and time versus connection with the present place and time — it must be said that the crystal at earlier and later times is different, hence the objects differ. Also, 'that' (<s>sa</s>) is mediate [knowledge], and 'this' (<s>ayam</s>) is direct apprehension. And the unity of these two, which are mutually opposed in nature like fire and frost, cannot be effected even by <s>Śakra</s> (<s>Indra</s>), on pain of the entire three worlds being identical. Nor does this [<s>pratyabhijñā</s>] have <s>prāmāṇya</s> (validity), since, being a <s>vikalpa</s> (conceptual construction), it does not apprehend a real thing, and since it is no different from memory. Therefore, [the claim] that <s>pratyabhijñā</s> establishes the unity of things is mere wishful thinking.

body.text: atrocyate / ekamevedaṃ pratyabhijñānaṃ samākhyātam / yadyapīndriyaṃ kevalamasamartham, yadyapi saṃskāramātram, saṃskārasadhrīcīnaṃ tu indriyaṃ bhāvayiṣyati pratyabhijñānam, tadbhāvābhāvānuvidhānāt pratyabhijñābhāvābhāvayoḥ / na hi nājījanad bījamātramaṅkuramiti mṛdādisahitamapi na janayati / atha bhavatu deśakālayostatsaṃsargayorvā parasparanānātvam, na tadavacchinnasya padmarāgasya, tasya tābhyāṃ tatsaṃsargābhyāṃ cānyatvāt //
body.translated_text: To this we reply: This <s>pratyabhijñā</s> is declared to be a single [cognition]. Although the sense-organ alone is incapable [of producing it], and although the <s>saṃskāra</s> (dispositional imprint) alone [is also incapable], the sense-organ concordant with the <s>saṃskāra</s> will generate the <s>pratyabhijñā</s>, since the presence and absence of the <s>pratyabhijñā</s> conform to the presence and absence of that [combination]. For it is not the case that a seed alone did not generate a sprout, therefore even when accompanied by earth and so forth it does not generate one. Now, let there be mutual distinctness of place and time, or of their connections — but not of the ruby (<s>padmarāga</s>) as delimited by them, since the ruby is different from those [place, time] and from their connections.

body.text: tato 'nyatve tatsaṃsargayoḥ kutastadīyatvamiti cet / svabhāvādeveti saṃsargaparīkṣāyāṃ nipuṇataramupapādayiṣyate / na ca svabhāvavirodhaḥ, anumānasyāpyanekatvaprasaṅgāt / tadapi hi pratyakṣamapratyakṣaṃ ca, avikalpo vikalpaśca, asamāropaḥ samāropaśca / svānubhavāvasthāpitābhedasya svarūpatadgrāhyabhedāpekṣayā pratyakṣādīnāmavirodha iti cet / na, ihāpi sāmyāt / na khalvetadapi vijñānaṃ (#Nibandh 114#) tattedantādhikaraṇamekamābhyāmanuraktaṃ sphaṭikaṃ gocarayadabhinnaṃ nānubhūyate nāvasīyate vā / ekatve 'pi ca vastunastadanurañjakatattedantābhedāpekṣayā pratyakṣatāparokṣate na virotsyete, sahasaṃbhavāt, vijñānaikatvasya ca pramāṇasiddhatvāt / na ca sa iti pūrvadeśakālasaṃsargo 'yamiti ca sannihitadeśakālasaṃsargaṃ ekasya virudhyate, yato yuktaṃ yatpadmarāgasya svarūpe paricchidyamāne tadabhāvo vyavacchidyata iti tadavyavacchede tatsvarūpāparicchedāt svapracyutivyavacchedyasvabhāvatvāt padmarāgabhāvasya tadanavacchede tatparicchedānupapatteḥ //
body.translated_text: If [the Buddhist objects:] given that [the ruby] is different from those [place, time] and their connections, whence comes its belonging to them? — [we reply:] From its very nature, as will be demonstrated more precisely in the examination of relations. Nor is there an inherent contradiction [in <s>pratyabhijñā</s>], since even <s>anumāna</s> would face the same consequence of multiplicity. For it too is both perceptual and non-perceptual, both non-conceptual and conceptual, both non-superimposed and superimposed. If [the Buddhist says:] since the unity [of inference] is established by one's own experience, there is no contradiction of <s>pratyakṣa</s> and so forth with respect to the distinction between its own nature and the apprehended [object] — [we reply:] No, since the same applies here. For this cognition too — which has 'that' and 'this' as its substrate, and which is a single [cognition] colored by both, having the crystal as its undifferentiated object — is both experienced and ascertained [as a unity]. And even though the thing is one, <s>pratyakṣatā</s> (perceptual character) and <s>parokṣatā</s> (non-perceptual character), with respect to the non-difference of the 'that'- and 'this'-coloring [elements], will not conflict — since they are co-possible, and since the unity of the cognition is established by <s>pramāṇa</s>. Nor is there a contradiction in one [thing]'s having the connection with a prior place and time (through 'that') and the connection with the present place and time (through 'this'), since when the own-nature of the ruby is being cognized, its [non-existence] is excluded. If it is not excluded, then the own-nature of the ruby is not cognized — since the being of the ruby has the nature of being excluded from its own non-being. If that [non-being] is not excluded, the cognition of that [ruby] is untenable.

body.text: kasmāt punastadanye puṣparāgādayo vyavacchidyante / tadabhāvāvinābhāvāditi cet / sa eva kutaḥ / pratyakṣeṇa kadācidapi puṣparāgapadmarāgayostādātmyānupalambhāditi cet / yatra tarhi tatastādātmyapratītiḥ, na tatra tadavinābhāvaḥ / samasti ca so 'yaṃ padmarāga iti deśakālāvasthānugatamekaṃ padmarāgamavabhāsayantī sākṣātkāravatī pratītiḥ / na vikalparūpatayāsyā aprāmāṇyam, abhilāpasaṃsargapratibhāsatvaprāmāṇyayoravirodhāt / na cedaṃ smārtam, adeśakālāvasthāvato 'yaṃ deśakālāvasthānugatatvenādhikyāditi //
body.translated_text: Why, then, are others such as the topaz (<s>puṣparāga</s>) excluded? If [you say:] because of the invariable absence of that [ruby] without the [exclusion of topaz] — then whence [is that invariable absence known]? If [you say:] because the identity of topaz and ruby is never apprehended by <s>pratyakṣa</s> — then wherever there is a cognition of identity regarding that [same thing], there is no invariable absence of that. And there exists the cognition 'This is that very same ruby,' which, manifesting a single ruby pervading multiple places, times, and conditions, has the character of direct apprehension. Nor is this invalid because it has the form of a <s>vikalpa</s>, since there is no contradiction between the appearance of verbal association and validity. Nor is this a mere memory, since it exceeds [memory] by apprehending [the object] as endowed with place, time, and conditions — unlike [memory, which apprehends] one devoid of place, time, and conditions.

body.text: atha keśakuśakadalīstambādau satyapi bhede pratyabhijñānamutpannamiti cet / utpadyatāṃ ko doṣaḥ / kimanena pratipāditaṃ bhavati / kiṃ pratyabhijñāyāḥ sādhāraṇānaikāntikatvam, atha śabdasāmyādubhayorapyaprāmāṇyam, uta saṃśayāpādanamātram / prathamaḥ pakṣo 'nabhyupagamādeva nirastaḥ / na hīyamanumānatvenopanyastā / anumānatve 'pyabādhitatvāditi viśeṣaṇe na doṣa iti pratipādayiṣyāmaḥ / nāpi dvitīyaḥ pakṣaḥ, dṛṣṭāntamātrataḥ sādhyasiddherayogāt / keśoṇḍukādiviṣayasya cakṣurvijñānasyāpyaprāmāṇye ghaṭādipratyakṣasyāprāmāṇyaprasaṅgāt / saṃśayamātraṃ tu vyavahārocchedakatvānnāśrayaṇīyamevati pratipāditamiti na tṛtīyo 'pio pakṣaḥ //
body.translated_text: If [the Buddhist objects:] but in the case of hair, grass, plantain stalks, and so forth, <s>pratyabhijñā</s> arises even though there is [actual] difference — [we reply:] Let it arise; what is the fault? What does this [objection] prove? Does it prove that <s>pratyabhijñā</s> is a common inconclusive [reason]? Or that both [the genuine and false cases] are invalid due to verbal similarity? Or merely the introduction of doubt? The first alternative is refuted by the very fact that [<s>pratyabhijñā</s>] is not presented here as an inferential reason. Even if it were inferential, we shall demonstrate that there is no fault in the qualifying condition 'being unsublated.' Nor does the second alternative hold, since the <s>sādhya</s> cannot be established from a mere example alone — for if the visual cognition of hair-balls and such were invalid, there would be the absurd consequence that the perception of pots and so forth would also be invalid. And mere doubt, since it would destroy all practical activity, is not to be relied upon — as has been demonstrated. So the third alternative also does not hold.

body.text: kiṃ ca keśādau yadi pratyabhijñā vyabhicāriṇo, kāryakāraṇapratītiḥ kiṃ na vyabhicāriṇī / yā vyabhicāriṇo sā kāryakāraṇapratītireva na bhavatīti cet / yadyevaṃ yā visaṃvādinī sā pratyabhijñaiva na bhavati tadābhāsatvāditi samānam / pratyabhijñānasya ca sati prāmāṇye 'numānādiṣvanantarbhāve pratyakṣataiva, saṃskārasahāyendriyānvayavyatirekānuvidhāyitvācca / satsaṃprayoge satīndriyāṇāṃ bhāvācca / tadiyaṃ pratyabhijñā anekadeśakālāvasthāsaṃbaddhamekaṃ sphaṭikādikaṃ gocarayantī sthairyaṃ vyavasthāpayati //
body.translated_text: Moreover, if <s>pratyabhijñā</s> deviates in the case of hair and so forth, does not the cognition of cause and effect also deviate? If [the Buddhist says:] whatever deviates is simply not a cognition of cause and effect — [we reply:] if so, then likewise whatever is discordant is simply not a <s>pratyabhijñā</s> but a semblance thereof — the same [logic applies]. And when the validity of <s>pratyabhijñā</s> is established, since it is not subsumed under <s>anumāna</s> and other [means of knowledge], it is simply a form of <s>pratyakṣa</s> (perception), since it conforms to the positive and negative concomitance of a sense-organ assisted by a <s>saṃskāra</s> (dispositional imprint). And since the sense-organs are operative when there is contact [with the present object]. Therefore, this <s>pratyabhijñā</s>, manifesting a single crystal and so forth connected with multiple places, times, and conditions, establishes permanence.

body.text: tathānumānato 'pi sthiratāsiddhiḥ / prayogaḥ - vivādādhyāsitaḥ sa evāyaṃ sphaṭikaṃ ityādipratyabhijñāpratyayo yathārthaḥ, abādhitapratyayatvāt / yāvānabādhitapratyayaḥ sa sarvo yathārtha upalabdhaḥ / yathā svasaṃvedanapratyayaḥ / abādhitaścāyam / tasmāttatheti / abādhitatvaṃ ca parodbhāvitakṣaṇikatvasādhanabādhakoddhārānniśceyam //
body.translated_text: Likewise, permanence is established through <s>anumāna</s> (inference) as well. The formal argument: the cognition of <s>pratyabhijñā</s> (recognition), such as 'This is that very same crystal,' which is the subject of dispute, is veridical — because it is an unsublated cognition. Whatever is an unsublated cognition, all of that has been found to be veridical — like the cognition of self-awareness. And this [<s>pratyabhijñā</s> cognition] is unsublated. Therefore it is so. And the unsublated character is to be ascertained from the refutation of the sublating proofs of momentariness raised by the opponent.

body.text:
(#Nibandh 115#)
athāparaḥ prayogaḥ / vivādādhyāsitā bhāvāḥ pūrvāparakālayorekasvabhāvāḥ, abādhitapratyabhijñayā pratyabhijñāyamānatvāt / yadyadabādhitapratyabhijñayā pratyabhijñāyate tatsarvamabhinnam / yathā yastvayā dṛṣṭo nīlo 'rthaḥ sa eva mayā dṛṣṭa iti nīlo 'rthaḥ pratyabhijñāyate / tathā caite bhāvāḥ / tasmāttatheti / pūrvaṃ pratyayasya dharmitā, adhunā bhāvānāmiti viśeṣaḥ /
body.translated_text:
(#Nibandh 115#)
Now another formal argument: The things that are the subject of dispute are of a single nature at earlier and later times, because they are recognized by an unsublated <s>pratyabhijñā</s>. Whatever is recognized by an unsublated <s>pratyabhijñā</s>, all of that is non-different — just as the blue object that you have seen is recognized as 'This blue object seen by me is that very same one.' And these things are likewise. Therefore they are so. Previously the property-possession was stated of the cognition [as subject]; now it is stated of the things — this is the distinction.

body.text: kiṃ ca sahetukatvādvināśasya sthairya siddham / prayogaḥ - vivādāspadībhūtā bhāvā yathāsvaṃ vināśahetusannidheḥ prāṅ na vināśinaḥ, sahetukavināśatvāt / yadyaddhetukaṃ tattadasannidhau na bhavati / yathā vahnyādyabhāve dhūmādiḥ / sahetukavināśāścāmī bhāvāḥ / tasmāttatheti / sahetukavināśatvaṃ ca ghaṭasyāgnidhūmayoriva pratyakṣānupalambhato mudgaravināśayorapi kāryakāraṇabhāvasiddhau siddham / na ca vināśahetorasāmarthyavaiyarthyābhidhānamucitam, aṅkurādihetorapi tathātvaprasaṅgāt / śakyaṃ hi vaktumarthasyābhaviṣṇutāyāmasamartho janmahetuḥ, bhaviṣṇutāyāṃ vyartha iti / api ca akṣaṇikāḥ santaḥ, kāraṇavattvāt / yat kāraṇavattadakṣaṇikam / yathā bhāvavināśaḥ / kāraṇavantaśceme santaḥ / tasmādakṣaṇikā iti /
body.translated_text: Moreover, the permanence of things is established from the fact that destruction has a cause. The formal argument: The things that are the subject of dispute do not perish prior to the proximity of their respective causes of destruction, because destruction is caused. Whatever has a caused destruction does not occur in the absence [of that cause] — like smoke and so forth in the absence of fire and so forth. And the destruction of these things is caused. Therefore they are so. And the caused nature of destruction is established, just as in the case of a pot, or of fire and smoke, through the perception and non-perception [of the cause and effect] — so too the causal relation between a mallet and the destruction [of the pot] is established. Nor is it proper to assert the incapacity or purposelessness of the cause of destruction, since the same absurd consequence would apply to the cause of a sprout and so forth. For one could equally say: the cause of birth is incapable when the thing is destined not to exist, and purposeless when it is destined to exist. Furthermore: existing things are non-momentary, because they possess causes. Whatever possesses a cause is non-momentary — like the destruction of a thing. And these existing things possess causes. Therefore they are non-momentary.

body.text: kāraṇavattvasya sādhyaviparyaye vṛttiśaṅkā vināśasya sahetukatvameva nivartayatīti prasiddhavyāptikāt kāraṇavattvādakṣaṇikatvasiddhiriti //
body.translated_text: The suspicion that 'having a cause' might apply to the opposite of the <s>sādhya</s> [i.e., to momentary things] itself negates the caused nature of destruction. Hence, from 'having a cause,' whose <s>vyāpti</s> is well-established, the non-momentariness is proven.

body.text: tathā śaṅkaraḥ sthirasiddhau prāha / notpattyanantaravināśī bhāvaḥ, prameyatvāt, vastuvyāvṛttivaditi / avidyamānavipakṣatvādanvayyeva hetuḥ / prameyatvasya kṣaṇikatvena virodhābhāvāt sandigdhavyatirekitvamiti cet / na khalu kṣaṇikatve kasyacitprameyatvaṃ sidhyati, kṣaṇasthitidharmaṇaḥ pramāṇakāle 'pātāt / atītasya ca prameyatve 'tiprasaṅgāditi /
body.translated_text: Likewise, <s>Śaṅkara</s> states in the <s>Sthirasiddhi</s>: A thing does not perish immediately upon arising, because it is a <s>prameya</s> (knowable object) — like the exclusion from non-things (<s>vastuvyāvṛtti</s>). Since there is no [actual] counter-instance, the <s>hetu</s> is purely positive (<s>anvaya</s>). If [the Buddhist objects:] since there is no contradiction between <s>prameyatva</s> (knowability) and <s>kṣaṇikatva</s> (momentariness), the negative concomitance is doubtful — [we reply:] Surely, on the thesis of momentariness, no knowability of anything is established, since a thing whose property is to endure [only] a moment falls outside the scope of a <s>pramāṇa</s> at the time of cognition. And if a past thing were knowable, there would be an absurd over-extension.

body.text: evameva prayogamupastuvan trilocano 'pyāha / akṣaṇikāḥ sarvabhāvāḥ, prameyatvāt / yat pramīyate tadakṣaṇikam / yathā bhāvavināśaḥ / prameyāśca sarvabhāvāḥ / tasmādakṣaṇikā iti /
body.translated_text: Praising this very proof, <s>Trilocana</s> also says: 'All entities are non-momentary, because they are knowable. Whatever is knowable is non-momentary — for example, the destruction of an entity. And all entities are knowable. Therefore they are non-momentary.'

body.text: asiddho dṛṣṭāntadharmīti cet / na / svakāraṇakalāpādutpannavato bhāvasyāntareṇa nivṛttiprasavaṃ sarvadāvasthānaprasaṅgāt / tadaiva bhāvo 'sti na pūrvaṃ na praścādityapi śabdaḥ kṣaṇikaparyāyatveneṣyamāṇaḥ kṣaṇādūrdhvaṃ sattvāvicchedopajananamantareṇa nārthavān devairapi śakyaḥ parikalpayitum / vināśakālāpekṣayā hi kṣaṇo 'lpīyān kālaḥ / tena so 'syāstīti kṣaṇiko vaktavyaḥ / itarathā janmavināśayorekasmin kāle bhavatoḥ tulyahetukatvenaikatvaprasaṅgaḥ / ekatve tu dvayorekataraḥ prahātavyaḥ / tatra janmaprahāṇe bhāvā niḥsvabhāvāḥ prasajyeran / nivṛttiparityāge ca janmino bhāvā nityā iti durnivāraḥ prasaṅgaḥ / tat siddho dṛṣṭāntaḥ //
body.translated_text: Objection: The subject of the example is unestablished. Reply: No. For an entity that has arisen from its own aggregate of causes, without the production of cessation [by an external cause], would have the absurd consequence of persisting forever. And the statement 'the entity exists at that very time, not before and not after' — even when intended as a synonym for 'momentary' — cannot be meaningfully conceived, even by the gods, without the generation of an unbroken continuation of existence beyond the moment. For a moment is the shortest duration in relation to the time of destruction. Therefore, one should say that the entity possessing that [minimal duration] is momentary. Otherwise, since origination and destruction, occurring at the same time, would have the same cause, there would be the absurd consequence of their being identical. And if they were identical, one of the two would have to be abandoned. If origination is abandoned, entities would turn out to be without intrinsic nature. If cessation is abandoned, then entities that have originated would be permanent — an unavoidable absurd consequence. Therefore, the example is established.

body.text:
(#Nibandh 116#)
nanu prameyatvakṣaṇikatvayorvirodhāsiddheḥ sandigdhavipakṣavyāvṛttikaṃ prameyatvamiti cet / naitadasti / yasmādarthaṃ kañcit prāpayat pratyakṣaṃ tena pratyāsannatvātprāpayati / pratyāsattiśca tadutpatirevāvakalpate, na tādātmyam, sākāranirākāravādayoraprakṛtatvāt / anyatra nirākṛtatvācca / sā ca niyatavastupratibhāsākṣiptā kāryakāraṇabhāvalakṣaṇā pratyāsattistulyakālaṃ pramāṇaprameyayoranupapannā, savyetaraviṣāṇayoriva / tataḥ pramāṇamarthasattāṃ bodhayattadadhīnotpādatayā bodhayati / kāraṇabhāvamātrānubandhitvācca tasya pūrvakālasattayā bhavitavyam / ataḥ pūrvakālasattvena vyāptaṃ prameyatvam / pūrvakālasattvaṃ ca kṣaṇikatve 'nupapannamiti vyāpakānupalabdhyā vipakṣāt kṣaṇikatvād vyāvartamānaṃ prameyatvamakṣaṇikatvena vyāpyata iti asandigdho vyatirekaḥ / tadevamanumānapramāṇasiddho 'kṣaṇika iti //
body.translated_text: Objection: Since the contradiction between knowability and momentariness is not established, knowability has doubtful exclusion from the counter-instance. Reply: This is not so. For perception, when it brings someone to an object, does so by virtue of proximity to that object. And proximity is to be understood as the arising [of the cognition] from that [object], not as identity — since the theories of cognition-with-form and cognition-without-form are not at issue here, and have been refuted elsewhere. And that proximity, characterized by the causal relation — which is implied by the appearance of a determinate object — is impossible for the means of knowledge and the knowable at the same time, just as [it is impossible] for the right and left horns [to be simultaneous]. Therefore, the means of knowledge, when it reveals the existence of the object, reveals it as having an existence dependent on it [i.e., arising from it]. And since it is connected solely with the causal relation, the object must have existence at a prior time. Therefore, knowability is pervaded by prior-time existence. And prior-time existence is impossible under momentariness. Thus, by the non-apprehension of the pervader (<s>vyāpakānupalabdhi</s>), knowability — being excluded from the counter-instance, namely momentariness — is pervaded by non-momentariness. Hence the negative concomitance is not doubtful. Thus, non-momentariness is established by the <s>pramāṇa</s> of inference.

body.text: evamarthāpattirapyasya sādhikā / tathā hi kāryakāraṇabhāvagrahaṇaṃ kramayaugapadyagrahaṇasmaraṇam abhilāṣaḥ svayaṃnihitapratyanumārgaṇaṃ duṣṭārthakutūhalaviramaṇaṃ karmaphalasaṃbandhaḥ saṃśayapūrvakanirṇayaḥ bandhamokṣaḥ mokṣaprayatnaḥ śubhodarke karmaṇi pravṛttiḥ pratyabhijñā kāryakāraṇabhāvaḥ upādānopādeyabhāvaprabhṛtayaḥ sthirasattāmantareṇānupapadyamānāḥ sthairya sādhayanti / pratikṣaṇaṃ bhede satyanubhaviturvinaṣṭatve 'nyasya kāryakāraṇabhāvagrahaṇādyanupapatteriti kathaṃ kṣaṇabhaṅgaśaṅkāpi //
body.translated_text: <s>Arthāpatti</s> (presumption) too serves as a proof for this. For the apprehension of the causal relation, the apprehension and recollection of succession and simultaneity, desire, the search for something previously deposited by oneself, the cessation of curiosity about a harmful object, the connection between action and its fruit, determinate judgment preceded by doubt, bondage and liberation, effort toward liberation, engagement in action that has an auspicious outcome, recognition, and the causal relation — all these and the material-cause relation

body.text: atrābhidhīyate / apramāṇamevāyaṃ pratyabhijñākhyo vikalpo mithyātvaṃ ca sadviṣayatvabādhakapratyayāt / nanvasya bādhakaṃ pratyakṣamasambhavi, anumānaṃ cāsamarthamāveditamiti cet / nanvasya pratyabhijñānasya svārthāvinābhāvadārḍhye pratyakṣasahasreṇāpi kim / saṃvādaśaithilye tu bādhakapratyakṣavadanumānamapi prāptāvakāśam, pramāṇasyaiva siddhibādhayoradhikārāt / tathā hi māyākāraḥ śirasi nimajjitaṃ golakamāsyena niḥsārayatīti pratyabhijñā śirasi cchidraprasaṅgasaṅgatenānumānena bādhyamānā pratītaiva / bādhyamānā na pratyabhijñeti prastute 'pyastu / yathāvanatākāśapratibhāsaḥ sarvasaṃpratipattāvapi bādhya eva tadvadekatāgrahaḥ sarvasaṃpratipattāvapi bādhyo 'stu / tasmādasyāḥ pratyakṣatākīrtanaṃ yācitakamaṇḍanamātramatrāṇam / kathamataḥ sthairyasthitirastu / tataścānumānatvamapyasyā dhvastam, uktakrameṇa abādhitatvaviśeṣaṇaviruddhabādhyamānatāyāḥ prasādhanāditi viśeṣaṇāsiddho hetuḥ / yadāpi kṣaṇabhaṅgasādhakaṃ bādhakaṃ nocyate asyāstadāpīyamapramāṇameva, lūnapunarjātakeśapāśādau vyabhicāropalambhāt //
body.translated_text: To this we reply: This conceptual judgment called 'recognition' (<s>pratyabhijñā</s>) is not a <s>pramāṇa</s> (valid means), and its falsity is established by a cognition that contradicts its having a real object. Objection: Perception as its contradicting cognition is impossible, and inference has been shown to be incapable. Reply: If the firmness of the indispensable connection between this recognition and its own object is strong, what can even a thousand perceptions do? But if the concordance is weak, then just as a contradicting perception, so too an inference

body.text: nanūktaṃ yā vyabhicāriṇī sā na pratyabhijñetyādi / yuktametat, yadi kāryakāraṇabhāvapratītivallakṣaṇabhedaḥ pratipādayituṃ śakyeta / yathā hyanvayavyatirekagrahaṇapravaṇapratyakṣānupalambhādupapanno niścayaḥ kāryakāraṇabhāvapratīteranyastadābhāsapratītirityanayorlakṣaṇabhedaḥ, tathā yadi pratyabhijñāne 'pi lakṣaṇabhedo darśitaḥ syāt, darśayituṃ (#Nibandh 117#) vā śakyo vyabhicārāvyabhicāropayogī, tadā bhavatu pratyabhijñātadābhāsayorvivekaḥ / na tvevamasti, sarvatrātyantasadṛśe vastuni pṛthagjanapratyabhijñāyā ekarasatvāt //
body.translated_text: Objection: It was stated that 'what is deviant is not recognition' and so forth. Reply: That is valid only if a definitional distinction can be demonstrated, as in the case of the cognition of the causal relation. For just as the certainty arising from perception and non-apprehension inclined toward grasping positive and negative concomitance constitutes the cognition of the causal relation, while the other — its apparent semblance — is [merely] the appearance of such a cognition, and thus the definitional distinction between these two exists; so too, if in the case of recognition

body.text: saṃvāditvāsaṃvāditve lakṣaṇabheda iti cet / na / aliṅgasya hi vikalpasya saṃvādo nāma pramāṇāntarasaṅgatirarthakriyāprāptirvā / tatra na tāvadādyaḥ pakṣaḥ, paścādapi sa evāyamiti svatantraikādhyavasāyamātrādaparasya pramāṇagandhasyāpyabhāvāt /
body.translated_text: Objection: The definitional distinction lies in concordance and non-concordance. Reply: No. For the concordance of a conceptual judgment that is not a logical mark means either agreement with another <s>pramāṇa</s> or the attainment of causal efficacy. The first alternative does not hold, because after the independent unitary determination 'this is that very same thing,' there is not even a trace of another <s>pramāṇa</s>.

body.text: nāpi dvitīyaḥ pakṣaḥ saṃgacchate / na hi pūrvāparakālayorekavastupratibaddhā siddhā kācidarthakriyāḥ, bhinnenāpi tatsamānaśaktinā tādṛgarthakriyāyāḥ karaṇāvirodhāt / tathā hi yathaiko ghaṭo vāri dhārayatīti tatkālabhāvino 'pyanyasya deśāntaravartino na vāridhāraṇavāraṇam tathā dvitīyādikṣaṇopyanyo yadi vāri dhārayati, kīdṛśo doṣaḥ syāt / visadṛśakriyāyāṃ tu cintaiva nāsti / tatkathaṃ pratyabhijñānasya saṃvādasaṃbhavaḥ //
body.translated_text: Nor does the second alternative work. For no causal efficacy connected to a single entity across earlier and later times has been established, since there is no contradiction in a different entity of the same capacity performing the same causal efficacy. For just as, when a single pot holds water, this does not prevent another pot existing at the same time in a different place from holding water; likewise, another entity at the second and subsequent moments, which

body.text: nanu yadyekaṃ pratyabhijñānaṃ bisaṃvādi dṛṣṭamiti sarvameva pratyabhijñānaṃ visaṃvādi śaṅkyate, tadaikamindriyajñānaṃ keśoṇḍukadvicandrādau visaṃvādyupalabdhamiti ghaṭādiṣvapi sarvameva pratyakṣaṃ visaṃvādi saṃbhāvyatām, indriyajanyatvasyaikalakṣaṇasya sarvatra saṃbhavāditi cet / na / tatrāpi lakṣaṇabhedasya sadbhāvāt / tathā hi bahirarthasthitāvindriyārthakāryatayā sākṣādarthākārānukāritvaṃ pratyakṣatvam / taccābhyāsaviśeṣāsāditapaṭimnā pratyakṣeṇa niścīyate / kvacittvarthakriyāprāptijñānāditi pratyakṣatvamanavadyameva / dvicandrādau tvarthavinākṛtena timirādiviplutacakṣuirmātreṇa tajjñānaṃ janitamiti pratyakṣābhāsameva / dvicandrādyarthābhāvastu deśakālanarāntarairdvicandrāderarthasya bādhitatvādavyāhata iti pratyakṣābhāsaparihāre 'pi pratyakṣeṣu ka āścāsavirodhaḥ / pratyabhijñāne 'pi sarvamidamastīti na yuktam //
body.translated_text: Objection: If one recognition is seen to be discordant, then all recognition would be suspected of being discordant. In that case, since a single sensory cognition is found to be discordant in the case of hair-like floaters, double moons, and the like, let all perception of pots and the like also be suspected of being discordant, since the single defining characteristic of being born from sense-organs is present everywhere. Reply: No. In that case too, a definitional distinction

body.text: yathā hi pūrvaṃ pāvakādau pākādikriyā pratibaddhā siddhā paścādanubhūyamānā dahanajñānasya saṃvādamāvedayati, anyathā bāhyārthocchedānnirīhaṃ jagajjāyate, na tathā prathamacaramakālayorekīmāvapratibaddhā kācidarthakriyā upalabdhigocarā pūrvāparakālayorekatvamantareṇa vā pravṛttyādikṣatiryenaikatāvagraho 'pi saṃvādī syāt / tadiyamanumānabādhitatvād vyabhicāraśaṅkākalaṅkitatvāccana pratyakṣamanumānaṃ veti kathamataḥ sthairyasiddhiranumānapratihatirvā //
body.translated_text: For just as the cooking activity and the like, which were previously established as connected with fire, when subsequently experienced, demonstrate the concordance of the cognition of fire — otherwise, with the elimination of external objects, the world would become inert — so too, no causal efficacy within the scope of apprehension that is connected with the identity of something at the first and last moments [has been established]. Without the identity across earlier and later times, there is no impairment of engagement and the like, by which the cognition of identity

body.text: yat punarvācaspatirūvāca saṃskārendriyayormilitayoreva pratyabhijñānaṃ prati kāraṇatvamiti, tadayuktam, bhinnasāmagrīprasūtatvādanayorjñānayoḥ / tathā hi nimīlite cakṣuṣi sa ityatrendriyavinākṛtasyaiva saṃskārasya sāmarthyamupalabdham / prathamadarśane tvayamityatra saṃskārarahitasyaivendriyasya sāmarthyaṃ dṛṣṭam / tasmāt sāmagrīdvayapratibaddhaṃ (#Nibandh 118#) jñānadvayamidamavadhāritam / kathamubhābhyāṃ militvaikameva pratyabhijñānamutpāditamityudghuṣyate / bījakṣityādyostu pṛthak sāmarthyaṃ na dṛṣṭamityekaiva sāmagrītyaṅkuro 'pyeka evāstu / tathā pūrvadeśakālāparadeśakālābhyāṃ tatsaṃbaddhābhyāmanyatvāt padyarāgasyābheda ityapyasaṅgatam / viruddhayordharmayoḥ padmarāgādanyatve 'pi viruddhadharmayogāt padmarāgasya bhedaḥ kathamapahnayate, trailokyaikatvaprasaṅgasya durvāratvāt / na hi dharmadharmiṇoranyatve 'pi brāhmaṇatvacāṇḍālatve ekādhāre bhavitumarhata iti padmarāgasya bhedo duratikramaḥ / tathā ca na svabhāvavirodho 'numānasyāpyanekatvaprasaṅgāt / tadapi pratyakṣamapratyakṣaṃ cāvikalpo vikalpaścāsamāropaḥ samāropaścetyapyayuktam / anumānasya hi paramārthataḥ svasaṃvedanapratyakṣātmano 'vikalpasyāsamāropasvabhāvasyāpratyakṣatvavikalpatvasamāropatvādeḥ parāpekṣayā prajñaptatvād viruddhadharmādhyāsābhāvāt kathaṃ bhedasiddhiḥ / sa e vāyamiti tu pratyabhijñānasya sa ityaspaṣṭākārayogitvam, ayamiti spaṣṭākārayogitvamiti viruddhadharmadvayaṃ bhedakam //
body.translated_text: As for what <s>Vācaspati</s> said — that the causality of recognition belongs to the combination of impressions and sense-organs — that is improper, since these two cognitions arise from different aggregates of conditions. For when the eyes are closed, the capacity of the impression alone, without the sense-organ, is observed in the [recognition] 'that one.' But in the first perception, the capacity of the sense-organ alone, without the impression, is observed in the [cognition] 'this one.'

body.text: na caivaṃ vaktavyam tattedantāpekṣayā pratyabhijñānasyāpyekasyaiva pārokṣyāpārokṣyamaviruddhamiti / na hodamekākāratayā vyavasthitam, yenānumānavadasyāpi pārokṣyāpārokṣyavyavasthāmātraṃ syāt / yāvadatītārthākārānukāro vartamānārthānukāraśca svadharmo na bhavati tāvattadarthagocarataiva nāsti / kutaḥ pārokṣyāpārokṣyavyavahāro bhaviṣyati / tasmāt spaṣṭāspaṣṭākāradvayaviruddhadharmādhyāsāt pratyabhijñānaṃ
body.translated_text: And it should not be said that, with reference to 'that' and 'this,' the single recognition may have both directness and indirectness, without contradiction — as in the case of inference. For this [recognition] is not constituted as having a single form, such that, like inference, a mere distinction of directness and indirectness would apply. As long as the imitation of the form of the past object and the imitation of the form of the present object are not its own properties, its having those objects as its domain does not even exist. How then

body.text: pratyayadvayametaditi sthitam //
body.translated_text: It is established that these are two [distinct] cognitions.

body.text: tathā sahetukavināśatvādayamapyasiddho hetuḥ / yatpunaratroktam sahetukavināśatvaṃ ghaṭasyāgnidhūmayoriva pratyakṣānupalambhato mudgaraghaṭavināśayorapi kāryakāraṇabhāvasiddhau siddhamiti, tadasaṅgatam, agnidhūmayordvayorapi dṛśyatvāt, pratyakṣānupalambhato dhūmasya vahnikāryatā sidhyatu / vināśaśabdavācyastvartho na kaścididantayā dṛṣṭaḥ / karparameva ghaṭamudgarābhyāmutpadyamānamupalabdham / yadāhurguravaḥ
body.translated_text: Likewise, because destruction has a cause, this reason too is unestablished. As for what was said here — that destruction-having-a-cause is established from perceptual non-apprehension, just as the causal relation between fire and smoke is established, and similarly between the hammer and the pot's destruction — that is incoherent, because both fire and smoke are visible; let the smoke's being an effect of fire be established through perceptual non-apprehension. But the word 'destruction'

children.text: dṛṣṭastāvadayaṃ ghaṭo 'tra ca patan dṛṣṭastathā mudgaro
children.translated_text: "This pot was seen here, and the hammer was likewise seen falling;

children.text: dṛṣṭā karparasaṃhatiḥ paramato nāśo na dṛṣṭaḥ paraḥ /
children.translated_text: and a mass of sherds was seen — but beyond that, no further 'destruction' was seen."

children.text: tenābhāva iti śrutiḥ kva nihitā kiṃ vātra tatkāraṇaṃ
children.translated_text: By that, 'absence' — where has this testimony been placed? What then is the cause of it here?
Only this row of potsherds, produced by its own cause — the mallet — has been seen.

body.text: tadayamabhāvo dṛśyānupalabdhibādhitaḥ kathaṃ pratyakṣato mudgarādikāryamavadhāryaḥ //
body.translated_text: Thus, this absence, being contradicted by the non-apprehension of the visible, how can the effect of the mallet and the like be determined through direct perception?

body.text: yatpunarasminnadṛśyamāne 'pi dṛśyata iti vāgjālaṃ sā bhaṇḍavidyā / tadvacanād gṛhṇānnapi paśureva / tathā hi
body.translated_text: And as for the verbal jugglery that 'even though this is not visible, it is seen' — that is a conjurer's trick. One who accepts [it] on the basis of such a statement is no better than an animal. For:

body.text:
kasyacit pratibhāsena sādhyate 'pratibhāsi yat /
pratibhāso 'sya nāsyeti nopapattestu gocaraḥ // iti /
body.translated_text: That which is not manifest is proved by the manifestation of something [else]; but 'its manifestation is not its own' — this is not within the scope of reason. Thus.

body.text:
(#Nibandh 119#)
athaivaṃ vaktavyam kimanyena dhvaṃsena, karparameva ghaṭadhvaṃso 'stu, tathā ca sati mudgarādyabhāve karparābhāvāt ghaṭasthairyamavyāhatamiti / durāśā khalveṣā / tathā hi yathā nāśaśabdena karparamucyate tathā yadyabhāvaśabdenāpi karparamevocyate tadaikatra pradeśe ghaṭamekamapanīya ghaṭāntaranyāse tatrāpanītaghaṭasyābhāvavyavahāro na syāt, tatpradhvaṃsakapālayostatrānutpādāt / tasmādyathāpanītaghaṭasya pracyutimātrāpekṣayā nyastaghaṭe 'bhāvavyavahārastathā mudgarādikāraṇābhāvāt pradhvaṃsakarparayoranutpāde 'pi pracyutimātrāpekṣayaiva pratikṣaṇamanyānyatvavyavahāro ghaṭasya sidhyatīti kutaḥ sthairyasiddhiḥ / tasmāt pradhvaṃsakarparābhāve 'pi pracyutimātrātmakabhāvāpekṣayāpyasmanmatamavyāhatam / yadāhurguravaḥ
body.translated_text: (Nibandh 119) Now, it might be said: what need for a separate destruction? Let the potsherd itself be the destruction of the pot. And in that case, since in the absence of the mallet there would be no potsherds, the permanence of the pot would be unrefuted. This is indeed a vain hope. For if, just as 'destruction' denotes the potsherd, so too if 'absence' also denotes only the potsherd, then when one pot is removed from a certain place and another pot placed there, there would be no usage of 'absence' with respect to the removed pot, since neither the destruction-potsherd nor the [replacement] potsherd has arisen there. Therefore, just as the usage of 'absence' with respect to the removed pot is based merely upon its departure in relation to the placed pot, so too, even when the destruction-potsherds have not arisen due to the absence of a cause such as a mallet, the usage of being different at each moment is established for the pot on the basis of mere departure alone — so from where does permanence follow? Therefore, even in the absence of destruction-potsherds, our position is unrefuted with respect to the entity whose nature is mere departure. As the masters say:

body.text:
āstāṃ karparapaṃktireva kalaśadhvaṃso na ceyaṃ purā
tena sthairyamapi prasidhyatu tato bhinnena nāśena kim /
body.translated_text: Let the row of potsherds itself be the destruction of the water-jar, and let that not have existed before — then let permanence too be established; what need then for a separate destruction?

body.text: atrottaram,
body.translated_text: To this, the reply:

body.text:
nāśaḥ saiva yathocyate yadi tathābhāvo 'pi kumbhāntar
anyāse 'bhāvavacaḥ kathaṃ matamataḥ sidhyatyabhāvo 'pi na //
body.translated_text: If destruction is said to be that very thing [the potsherds], then 'absence' too — when another pot is placed inside, how does the word 'absence' apply? Therefore, from this [argument], absence too is not established.

body.text: iti /
body.translated_text: Thus.

body.text: nanu yadi svahetujanito nāśo nāsti, kathaṃ kvacideva deśe kāle ghaṭo naṣṭa iti pratītiniyamaḥ / na ca mudgarādanyo nāśasya heturvaktavyaḥ, prāgapi nāśasaṃbhave naṣṭaghaṭabuddhisaṃbhavaprasaṅgāt / yadāhuḥ
body.translated_text: Objection: If destruction produced by its own cause does not exist, how is there the regularity of the cognition 'the pot is destroyed' at a particular place and time? And no cause of destruction other than the mallet can be stated, because there would be the absurd consequence that the cognition of a destroyed pot could arise even before [the mallet strikes]. As they say:

children.text: nāśo nāsti yadi svahetuniyataḥ kiṃ deśakāle kvacit
children.translated_text: If destruction, determined by its own cause, does not exist, why at a certain place and time

children.text: kumbho naṣṭa iti pratītiniyamastenāsti kāryaśca saḥ /
children.translated_text: is there the regularity of the cognition 'the pot is destroyed'? Therefore it exists and is an effect.
Nor is there any other cause; for if destruction were possible even before the powerful blow of the stick,

children.text: nāśoktā na kṛtā vinaṣṭaghaṭadhīḥ kenoddhurā vāryate //
children.translated_text: the cognition of a destroyed pot — stated as [arising through] destruction — would not have been made; by whom would that wild [cognition] be restrained?

body.text: iti cet / tarhīdānīmarthāpattyā pradhvaṃsaṃ prasādhya mudgarādhīnatvamasya sādhayitumārabdham / tathā ca sati dhūmāgnivat pratyakṣataḥ pradhvaṃsasya mudgarādikāryatvaṃ siddhamityutphullagallamullapitaṃ vyāluptam //
body.translated_text: If so objected: Then, having established destruction by <s>arthāpatti</s> (presumption), you have begun to prove its dependence on the mallet. And in that case, the puffed-up assertion that 'the effect-nature of destruction with respect to the mallet and the like is established directly through perception, like smoke and fire' has been demolished.

body.text: na cārthāpattito 'pi tatsiddhiḥ saṃdyapate, kumbho naṣṭa iti pratīteranyathāpyupapadyamānatvāt / vināśaṃ vināpi hi ghaṭadarśanavato mudgarakṛtakapālānubhava evanaṣṭaghaṭāvasāyasādhanaḥ, kimapareṇa nāśena kartavyam, ghaṭo naṣṭa iti buddherghaṭaniścayapūrvakamudgarakṛtakapālānubhavamātrānvayavyatirekānuvidhānadarśanāt / na ceyaṃ sāmagrīpūrvamapyasti / mudgarābhāve karparapaṃkterevābhāvāt kathaṃ prāgapi naṣṭaghaṭabuddhiprasaṅgaḥ saṃgato nāma / yadāhurguravaḥ
body.translated_text: Nor is its establishment achieved even through <s>arthāpatti</s> (presumption), O doubter, since the cognition 'the pot is destroyed' can be accounted for in another way even without it. For even without postulating destruction, for one who has seen the pot, the mere experience of potsherds produced by the mallet is sufficient to bring about the determination of a destroyed pot — what need for an additional destruction? For it is observed that the cognition 'the pot is destroyed' invariably follows only upon the experience of potsherds produced by the mallet preceded by the prior ascertainment of the pot. And this aggregate [of conditions] did not exist before — since in the absence of the mallet, the row of potsherds itself does not exist, how can there be the absurd consequence of the cognition of a destroyed pot arising earlier? As the masters say:

body.text:
dṛṣṭe 'mbhobhṛti mudgarādijanitā dṛṣṭā kapālāvalī
saṅketānugamādvinaṣṭaghaṭadhīstāvat samutpādyate /

children.translated_text: (Nibandh 120)

children.text: sāmagryāmiha nāśanāma na kimapyaṅgaṃ na cāsyāmapi
children.translated_text: In this aggregate, destruction is no component whatsoever; nor in this [aggregate]

children.text: syādeṣā na kadāpi nāpi ca purāpyeṣā samagrā sthitiḥ //
children.translated_text: would this [cognition] ever arise [without the aggregate]; nor was this aggregate ever present before.

body.translated_text: When the water-bearer [pot] is seen, the row of potsherds produced by the mallet and the like is seen; by the following of convention, the cognition of a destroyed pot is then produced.

body.text: arthāpattirato gatā kṣayamiyaṃ na dhvaṃsasiddhau prabhuḥ // iti //
body.translated_text: <s>Arthāpatti</s> (presumption) has thus come to naught — it has no power to establish destruction. Thus.

body.text: yadi nāśānubhavo nāsti kapālānubhavāt kapālakalpanaiva syāt, na naṣṭaghaṭabuddhiriti cet / tadetadatisāhasam, ghaṭaniścayapūrvakakapālavalayadarśanādeva naṣṭaghaṭabuddheḥ sākṣādevānubhūyamānatvāt / tadapalāpe dhūmādīnāmapi dahanādipūrvakatvaniścayo na syādityatiprasaṅgaḥ //
body.translated_text: If [objected]: 'If the experience of destruction does not exist, then from the experience of potsherds there would be only the postulation of potsherds, not the cognition of a destroyed pot' — this is utter recklessness, since the cognition of a destroyed pot is directly experienced simply from seeing the ring of potsherds preceded by the prior ascertainment of the pot. If one denies that, then the absurd consequence would be that the ascertainment that smoke and the like are preceded by fire would also not hold — this is over-extension.

body.text: nanu ghaṭo naṣṭa iti buddhirviśeṣyabuddhiḥ / sā ca vināśaṃ viśeṣaṇamākṣipatīti cet / tadasat, yataḥ
body.translated_text: Objection: The cognition 'the pot is destroyed' is a qualified cognition (<s>viśeṣyabuddhi</s>), and as such it demands destruction as a qualifier. Reply: This is wrong, because:

body.text: svabuddhyā rajyate yena viśeṣyaṃ tadviśeṣaṇam /
body.translated_text: A qualifier is that by which the qualificand is coloured through its own cognition.

body.text: ucyate / na cāvidyamānamadṛśyaṃ vā svabuddhyā kiñcidrañjayati / prayogo 'trayasya na svarūpanirbhāsastanna kasyacit svānurakta pratītinimittam / yathā karikeśaraḥ / nāsti ca svarūpanirbhāso dhvaṃsasyeti vyāpakānupalabdhiḥ / nāsyā asiddhiḥ, abhāvasya svarūpeṇaivedantayā nirbhāsābhāvāt / na ca viruddhatā, sapakṣe bhāvāt / nāpyanaikāntikatvam, pratibhāsābhāve 'pi svānuraktapratītihetutve śaśaviṣāṇāderapi tathātvaṃ syādityatiprasaṅgaḥ /
body.translated_text: It is called [a qualifier]. But something non-existent or invisible does not colour anything through its own cognition. Its application here has no manifestation of its own form; therefore it is not the cause of a cognition attached to anything — like the mane of a hare. And the non-manifestation of the self-form of destruction is a case of <s>vyāpakānupalabdhi</s> (non-apprehension of the pervader). This is not unestablished, because absence, being of the nature of non-being, lacks manifestation by its very nature. Nor is it contradictory, because it is present in the concordant instance. Nor is it inconclusive, because if something were the cause of a cognition attached to itself even in the absence of manifestation, then a hare's horn and the like would also be so — which is over-extension.

body.text: nanu
body.translated_text: Objection:

children.text: na dhvaṃsena vinā vinaśyati jagad bhāvena sārdhaṃ sacet
children.translated_text: Without destruction, the world would not perish; if it coexists with being,
let it be both existent and non-existent, determined by reality; it is born after being, therefore
being of different causation from being, and in the impossibility of its cause,
from non-being — then the otherness produced by it too has collapsed; how then can there be momentary destruction?

body.text: atrocyate / kāraṇāntarādutpadyamāno dhvaṃso 'bhinno bhinno vā / nādyaḥ pakṣaḥ, bhinnakāraṇatvāt, tairanabhyupagatatvācca / atha dvitīyaḥ pakṣa / tadā kaḥ punarbhāvasya pradveṣo yena pradhvaṃsākhye vastuni svahetorutpanne nivartate nāma //
body.translated_text: To this we reply: Destruction, arising from a different cause, is either identical with [the entity] or different. The first option does not hold, because it has a different cause and because the opponents themselves do not accept it. Now, if the second option [is adopted], then what grudge does the entity have such that it ceases when a thing called 'destruction' arises from its own cause?

body.text: yatpunaretaducyate - nābhāvasyotpāde bhāvasyāparā nivṛttiḥ, kiṃ tvabhāvotpattireva tannivṛttiriti / kathamanyasyotpāde 'nyasya nivṛttiḥ / atra svabhāvabhedairuttaraṃ vācyam ye parasparaparihārasthitayaḥ svahetubhyo jāyante / na hi svato 'nyasyāṅkurasya vahnirna kāraṇamityanyatvāviśeṣād bhasmano 'pi na kāraṇam / svabhāvabhedenatu kāryakāraṇabhāvasamarthanaṃ parasparaparihārasthitiniyame 'pi tulyam / yathā cotpādasya purastādakhilasāmarthyarahitasyāṅkuraprāgabhāvasyāpakāraṃ kañcidakurvanto 'pi bījādayo 'ṅkuramārabhamāṇāḥ prāgabhāvaṃ nivartayanti, tadutpādasyaiva tatprāgabhāvanivṛttirūpatvāt; evaṃ tadabhāvahetavo 'pi bhāvarūpe 'kiñcitkarā (#Nibandh 121#) api tadabhāvamādadhānāstannivartayanti, abhāvotpādasyaiva bhāvanivṛttirūpatvāt / tena pūrvavannārthakriyākaraṇaprasaṅga iti / taducitaṃ syād yadi kāryakāraṇayorivāsyā pyātmā pramāṇapratītaḥ syāt, kevalaṃ dṛśyānupalambhagraste 'pyetasminnupalabhyata iti pralāpo vyaktamiyaṃ bhaṇḍavidyetyuktam / arthāpattirapi kṣīṇetyapi prāgabhāvasya ca dṛṣṭāntatvenopanyāso bhaṇḍālekhyanyāyaḥ /
body.translated_text: And as for the further statement: 'Upon the arising of non-being, there is no additional cessation of the entity; rather, the arising of non-being is itself its cessation' — how does the cessation of one thing [follow] from the arising of another? Here the answer must be given through differences of nature, which are established in mutual exclusion and arise from their own causes. For fire is not a non-cause of a sprout that is other than itself — and since there is no difference in otherness, it would also not be a cause of ashes. The justification of the causal relation through differences of nature is equally applicable to the regularity of mutual exclusion. And just as the seed and the like, while not causing any harm to the prior-absence of the sprout — which is devoid of all efficacy — before its production, yet upon beginning [to produce] the sprout they remove the prior-absence, since the production of that [sprout] is itself of the nature of the cessation of its prior-absence; so too the causes of its non-being, (Nibandh 121) while effecting nothing with respect to the being-form [of the entity], yet by establishing its non-being they remove it, since the production of non-being is itself of the nature of the cessation of being. Therefore, the objection of causal efficacy as before does not apply. That would be proper if the nature of this [mutual exclusion] too, like the causal relation, were cognised through a <s>pramāṇa</s>; but prattle about perceiving that which is swallowed up by the non-apprehension of the visible — this is clearly a conjurer's trick, as already stated. The <s>arthāpatti</s> argument too has been exhausted. And the introduction of prior-absence as an example is the logic of the conjurer's painting.

body.text: kiṃ ca kaḥ punaratra virodhaḥ
body.translated_text: Moreover, what is the contradiction here?

children.translated_text: If your [notion of] contradiction between entity and non-entity is their impossibility of co-location,
just as cold and fire cannot co-exist even for a moment,

children.text: sa ca dhvaṃso dhvaṃsāntaramupanayan saṃprati bhaved
children.translated_text: then that destruction, which brings about another destruction, would now itself be

children.text: virodhī so 'pyanyaṃ kṣayamiti na nāśaḥ kathamapi //
children.translated_text: contradictory [to the entity]; and since it too [requires] another cessation, there is no destruction whatsoever.

body.text: anyathā siddhasattāmātreṇa virodhitve sarvaṃ sarveṇa viruddhaṃ prasajyeta / svabhāvālambanamapyadarśanādeva nirastamiti /
body.translated_text: Otherwise, if contradiction arose merely from the established existence [of something], everything would be contradictory with everything. And the claim that the [contradiction] rests on nature is also refuted simply by its not being observed.

children.translated_text: If then, the entity being of the nature of mutual absence,
let the absence of destruction itself co-exist [with being], or [let it follow] from the force of the cause;
by this, the destruction under discussion is struck down, and since it does not arise,
the entity itself is indeed stronger — for its own decay, what need of another here?

body.text: saccāsacca kimastu vastviti tu prasaṅgaḥ trilocanaprastāve nirākaraṇīyaḥ / ata evātra prastāve bhuvanaikagurūn bhagavataḥ kīrtipādānavamanyamānaḥ śaṅkaraḥ paśorapipaśuriti kṛpāpātramevaiṣa jālmaḥ /
body.translated_text: As for the objection 'let a thing be both existent and non-existent' — this consequence is to be refuted in the context of <s>Trilocana</s>'s [discussion]. In this very context, <s>Śaṅkara</s>, who disrespects the venerable <s>Kīrtipāda</s> [<s>Dharmakīrti</s>], the sole preceptor of the world, is an animal among animals — this wretch is merely an object of compassion.

body.text: yadapyāha trilocanaḥ bhāvavyatiriktāṃ nivṛttimanicchadbhiraśakyā svarūpanivṛttiravasthāpayitum / yā hi tasya prāktanī kācidavasthā bhavadbhirarthakriyānirvartanayogyā dṛṣṭā saiva yadyuttarakālamapyanuvartate tarhi svarūpeṇaiva nivṛtto bhāvaḥ kathamavasthāpyate / tadānīmayaṃ naṣṭo nāma yadi svahetupratilabdhasvarūpavyatirekiṇī tasya kācidavasthotpadyeta, utpattau saiva tasyātmāntaraṃ jātamityatādavasthyamevāsya vināśaṃ brūmaḥ / tādavasthye tādātmye ca svarūpeṇa nivṛtto bhāva ityasya śabdasya satyamarthaṃ na vidmaḥ / svarūpanivṛttiḥ khalviyaṃ bhavantī bhāva eva syāt, bhāvādanyā vā / tattve svakāraṇebhyo niṣpannasyārthasyānyathānupapattāvutpatterārabhya sattvānnityatvaṃ prasajyeta / anyatve ca tadeva nivṛtteranyatvanivṛtti(riti) priyamanuṣṭhitaṃ priyeṇa / tasmādutsṛjya vibhramaṃ nāśotpattireva naṣṭatvamabhyupagantavyamiti /
body.translated_text: And as for what <s>Trilocana</s> says — 'Those who do not accept a cessation distinct from the entity cannot establish cessation by its own nature. For if some prior state of it, observed by you as capable of accomplishing causal efficacy, continues at a later time as well, then how can the entity, which has ceased by its own nature, be established? At that point, this is called destroyed — namely, if some state of it, having a nature different from the nature obtained through its own cause, arises; upon its arising, we call its having become a different self — its change of state — its destruction. But if there is constancy of state and constancy of nature, then truly we do not know the meaning of the expression "the entity has ceased by its own nature." This cessation by its own nature is either the entity itself or other than the entity. If identical, since the thing produced from its own causes cannot be otherwise, permanence would follow from the fact of its existence from the time of its production onward. If different, then the otherness of cessation is just otherness — thus the beloved has fulfilled the wish of the beloved.' Therefore, abandoning confusion, one must accept that destruction-arising itself constitutes being-destroyed.

body.text:
(#Nibandh 122#)
tadetadajñānaphalam / tathā hi
body.translated_text: (Nibandh 122) This is the fruit of ignorance. For:

children.translated_text: Just as an entity arises from its own cause with its form excluded from another place,
so too, with its occurrence excluded from a different moment — does it not arise from its own cause in just the same way?
If, from non-being, the objection of being a different entity [is raised] — there too another entity is to be examined.
The example of the lamp is not appealing, because of the separation from the observation of its own form.
